layers.name: Motivation Layer
layers.scope: Captures why the system exists: stakeholders and their drivers, assessments, goals and outcomes, principles, requirements and constraints, and the meaning and value attached to them (ArchiMate 3.2 motivation elements). Motivation elements are expressed in documents, decision records and requirement text rather than in executable code; every lower layer should be traceable back to an element here. Modelling rules: realization runs through motivation, as in ArchiMate: requirements realize the outcomes, goals and principles they make concrete, and outcomes realize goals. Decomposition is same-type only: an element aggregates the narrower elements of its own type that make it up, and specializes a more general one. Influence is one motivation element shaping another: drivers, assessments, stakeholders, goals, principles and constraints influence goals, outcomes, principles, requirements and constraints, and a constraint constrains the requirements it limits. Association is kept for concerns and interpretation: a stakeholder is associated with the drivers, goals, requirements, principles, outcomes and constraints it cares about, an assessment with the drivers it evaluates, and meaning and value are associated with any concept and are always the source of that association. Other layers trace to motivation with one predicate per meaning: they satisfy requirements, constraints and principles; an element realizes a goal or outcome it exists to achieve and supports one it contributes to alongside others; services and features deliver value, and user workflows deliver the outcomes they produce. A stakeholder is not served: business actors and roles, like personas, reference the stakeholder whose concerns they stand for.

types.title: Assessment
types.description: A recorded finding or judgement produced by analysing the current state of the enterprise, a system, or its environment, such as an identified strength, weakness, risk, gap, or feasibility verdict. It states what is the case, not a desired end state, a result to achieve, or an obligation on the solution. Use Driver instead when the element names the motivating condition or concern itself (e.g. 'GDPR compliance', 'rising cloud cost') rather than an analytical finding about it (e.g. 'current logging stores PII unencrypted'). Use Outcome instead when the statement describes an end result the organization plans to achieve or has achieved, with a lifecycle status, rather than a diagnosis of the present situation. Use Constraint instead when the statement restricts which design or implementation options are allowed, rather than reporting an evaluated fact about the current state. Use Requirement instead when the statement prescribes a need the system must satisfy (e.g. 'must encrypt PII at rest') instead of describing the observed deficiency that prompted it.
evidence: The 'Context' or 'Problem Statement' section of an ADR stating an observed weakness, limitation, or risk of the existing design that the decision responds to.
Entries in a risk register, threat model (e.g. STRIDE table in threat-model.md), or security/audit findings file listing identified threats or vulnerabilities with likelihood or severity.
A tech-debt, gap-analysis, or readiness/feasibility document (or tracked issue labelled tech-debt/gap) recording that a current capability is missing, inadequate, or viable.

distinguish.motivation.driver: the element names the motivating condition or concern itself (e.g. 'GDPR compliance', 'rising cloud cost') rather than an analytical finding about it (e.g. 'current logging stores PII unencrypted').
distinguish.motivation.outcome: the statement describes an end result the organization plans to achieve or has achieved, with a lifecycle status, rather than a diagnosis of the present situation.
distinguish.motivation.constraint: the statement restricts which design or implementation options are allowed, rather than reporting an evaluated fact about the current state.
distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement prescribes a need the system must satisfy (e.g. 'must encrypt PII at rest') instead of describing the observed deficiency that prompted it.

types.title: Constraint
types.description: A stated restriction on the solution space, such as a mandated or forbidden technology, a deadline, a budget ceiling, a jurisdiction or a contractual term, that limits which design or implementation options are permissible without describing a capability or quality the system must deliver. It is stated in decision records, policies or requirement text; code such as a fitness test may enforce it, but is not where it is defined. Use Requirement instead when the statement describes a function or quality the system must provide (what it must do or how well), rather than ruling options in or out for how it is built. Use Principle instead when the statement is a general normative rule meant to guide many decisions across systems (e.g. 'prefer managed services') rather than a specific, checkable limit on one solution. Use Driver instead when the item is the underlying condition or force (a new regulation, a market shift) that motivates change, rather than the concrete restriction derived from it. Use Assessment instead when the item is an analytical finding about the current state (a risk, gap or weakness) rather than a binding limit on design choices.
evidence: An ADR or design doc section titled 'Constraints' or 'Decision drivers' with mandatory wording such as 'must use PostgreSQL 14', 'no GPL dependencies' or 'must ship before Q3'
Code comments or config justified by a cited rule, e.g. cloud region pinned to eu-* with a comment referencing GDPR data residency, or a deny-list of licences in a dependency-audit config

Architecture fitness tests or lint rules (ArchUnit, dependency-cruiser, import-linter) that forbid certain imports, libraries or runtime versions, together with documentation naming the restriction they enforce

distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement describes a function or quality the system must provide (what it must do or how well), rather than ruling options in or out for how it is built
distinguish.motivation.principle: the statement is a general normative rule meant to guide many decisions across systems (e.g. 'prefer managed services') rather than a specific, checkable limit on one solution
distinguish.motivation.driver: the item is the underlying condition or force (a new regulation, a market shift) that motivates change, rather than the concrete restriction derived from it
distinguish.motivation.assessment: the item is an analytical finding about the current state (a risk, gap or weakness) rather than a binding limit on design choices

types.title: Driver
types.description: A motivation element naming an external or internal condition or force (e.g. a regulation coming into effect, market pressure, rising operating cost, technical debt) that prompts the organization to set or change goals, requirements or architecture. It names the condition itself, not an evaluation of it and not the response to it. Use Assessment instead when the element records the result of analysing a condition (a SWOT finding, risk rating, gap or feasibility conclusion) rather than naming the condition itself. Use Goal instead when the statement expresses a desired end state or direction the organization intends to pursue in response to the condition. Use Constraint instead when the element is a fixed restriction on design or implementation choices (e.g. 'must run on-prem') rather than a force that motivates change. Use Stakeholder instead when the element is the person, team or organization holding the concern, not the concern or condition itself.
evidence: An ADR or design doc 'Context' / 'Motivation' / 'Background' section naming an external or internal condition, such as 'GDPR enforcement deadline' or 'p95 latency complaints from customers', as the reason for the change.
Issue tracker epics or labels (e.g. 'compliance', 'tech-debt', 'cost-reduction') whose description cites a regulation, market event or operational problem that triggers a body of work.
Code comments or README notes that justify a module's existence by citing a condition, e.g. '// Required due to PCI-DSS 4.0 rollout' or 'Introduced because vendor X API is deprecated in 2025'.

distinguish.motivation.assessment: the element records the result of analysing a condition (a SWOT finding, risk rating, gap or feasibility conclusion) rather than naming the condition itself.
distinguish.motivation.goal: the statement expresses a desired end state or direction the organization intends to pursue in response to the condition.
distinguish.motivation.constraint: the element is a fixed restriction on design or implementation choices (e.g. 'must run on-prem') rather than a force that motivates change.
distinguish.motivation.stakeholder: the element is the person, team or organization holding the concern, not the concern or condition itself.

types.title: Goal
types.description: A motivation statement of an end state or direction that stakeholders intend to reach, expressed qualitatively and at a level general enough that it does not prescribe a specific system property or measurable result, and is refined by requirements and outcomes. Use Outcome instead when the statement names a concrete, measurable or time-bound result, or tracks one that is planned, in progress or achieved, such as 'checkout p95 latency under 300 ms by Q3'. Use Requirement instead when the statement specifies a need that a particular system, component or solution must satisfy and that can be verified against it, such as 'the API shall support OAuth2 client credentials'. Use Principle instead when the statement is a standing rule that governs how all designs in a context are made, such as 'prefer managed services', rather than an end state to reach. Use Driver instead when the statement describes the condition or force prompting change, such as a new regulation or market pressure, rather than the intended end state that responds to it.
evidence: A 'Goals', 'Objectives' or 'Vision' section in a README, design document or product brief that lists intended end states without acceptance criteria.
An 'Objective' entry in an OKR or roadmap file (e.g. okrs.yaml, ROADMAP.md) that sits above its measurable key results.

An ADR or RFC 'Context' or 'Motivation' section stating what the change is meant to achieve, such as 'enable self-service onboarding for partners', and referenced by the requirements or decisions that follow.

distinguish.motivation.outcome: the statement names a concrete, measurable or time-bound result, or tracks one that is planned, in progress or achieved, such as 'checkout p95 latency under 300 ms by Q3'.
distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement specifies a need that a particular system, component or solution must satisfy and that can be verified against it, such as 'the API shall support OAuth2 client credentials'.
distinguish.motivation.principle: the statement is a standing rule that governs how all designs in a context are made, such as 'prefer managed services', rather than an end state to reach.
distinguish.motivation.driver: the statement describes the condition or force prompting change, such as a new regulation or market pressure, rather than the intended end state that responds to it.

types.title: Meaning
types.description: A motivation element recording the interpretation or knowledge that stakeholders attach to a specific concept (a term, data item, artifact, or other architecture element) within a stated context, expressed as an explanatory statement of what the concept signifies rather than as an intent, need, condition, or worth. Use Value instead when the statement expresses how much a concept is worth or how useful it is to a stakeholder (financial, strategic, reputational benefit), not what it signifies. Use Principle instead when the statement is normative, prescribing how systems or decisions should behave, rather than explaining what a concept means. Use Requirement instead when the statement declares a need that a system must satisfy, including a requirement that a term be interpreted a certain way. Use Assessment instead when the statement is a finding from analysing the current state of affairs (strength, weakness, risk, gap), not the interpretation of a concept.
evidence: a glossary or ubiquitous-language document (e.g. GLOSSARY.md, docs/domain-terms.md) defining business terms as used in a specific bounded context
a docstring or comment on a domain class, enum value, or field explaining the business interpretation of the concept, e.g. 'An "active" customer means one with a purchase in the last 90 days'
a data dictionary or schema description entry (e.g. dbt schema.yml column description, JSON Schema 'description', OpenAPI field description) stating what a field signifies for its consumers

distinguish.motivation.value: the statement expresses how much a concept is worth or how useful it is to a stakeholder (financial, strategic, reputational benefit), not what it signifies
distinguish.motivation.principle: the statement is normative, prescribing how systems or decisions should behave, rather than explaining what a concept means
distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement declares a need that a system must realize, including a requirement that a term be interpreted a certain way
distinguish.motivation.assessment: the statement is a finding from analysing the current state of affairs (strength, weakness, risk, gap), not the interpretation of a concept

types.title: Outcome
types.description: A motivation element stating a concrete, preferably measurable end result that the organization or a system has achieved or intends to achieve, usually with a target value, threshold or time frame. It describes a state that can be checked as reached or not reached, not a direction of intent or a capability the system must provide. Use Goal instead when the statement expresses a desired direction or end state without a measurable target or verifiable completion point (e.g. 'improve customer satisfaction'). Use Requirement instead when the statement specifies what a system or solution must do or exhibit (a need to be realized by design), rather than the business or system result that follows from it. Use Value instead when the element expresses the worth or utility to a stakeholder (e.g. 'lower operating cost'), not the concrete result that produces that worth. Use Assessment instead when the statement records a finding about the current state of affairs (a SWOT item, risk or gap) rather than an intended or achieved result.
evidence: A key result or success criterion in an OKR, roadmap or epic document stating a measurable target with a date, e.g. 'checkout abandonment below 20% by Q4'
A 'Success metrics' or 'Expected outcome' section in a PRD, RFC or ADR describing the verifiable result after delivery, often tagged with a tracking status such as done, on-track or at-risk
An SLO or KPI objective in monitoring or dashboard configuration (e.g. a Datadog/Prometheus SLO target) whose name and description reference a business result and link to a stated goal

distinguish.motivation.goal: the statement expresses a desired direction or end state without a measurable target or verifiable completion point (e.g. 'improve customer satisfaction')
distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement specifies what a system or solution must do or exhibit (a need to be realized by design), rather than the business or system result that follows from it
distinguish.motivation.value: the element expresses the worth or utility to a stakeholder (e.g. 'lower operating cost'), not the concrete result that produces that worth
distinguish.motivation.assessment: the statement records a finding about the current state of affairs (a SWOT item, risk or gap) rather than an intended or achieved result

types.title: Principle
types.description: A normative statement, applying across all systems or decisions within a stated scope (enterprise, domain, or programme), that prescribes how design and implementation choices should generally be made, without targeting one specific system or being directly verifiable as met by it. Use Requirement instead when the statement names a specific system, component or solution and can be verified as satisfied or not for that system (e.g. 'the Orders API must use OAuth 2.0'). Use Constraint instead when the statement is an externally imposed or fixed restriction on the solution space for a particular realization (e.g. a mandated vendor, deadline or budget) rather than a self-adopted guideline. Use Goal instead when the statement expresses a desired end state or direction to reach (e.g. 'reduce time-to-market') rather than a rule for how decisions are made. Use Value instead when the element captures the worth or importance of something to stakeholders rather than a prescription governing choices.
evidence: An architecture-principles document or ADR section listing broad prescriptive statements (e.g. 'API-first', 'Data is owned by a single service') each with rationale and implications.
An engineering handbook or CONTRIBUTING.md passage stating repository-wide conventions phrased as 'we always/never …' that are cited as justification in multiple ADRs or code reviews.
An architecture fitness test or lint rule set (e.g. ArchUnit, dependency-cruiser, eslint config) whose comments or names cite a named principle enforced across all modules rather than one feature.

distinguish.motivation.requirement: the statement names a specific system, component or solution and can be verified as satisfied or not for that system (e.g. 'the Orders API must use OAuth 2.0').
distinguish.motivation.constraint: the statement is an externally imposed or fixed restriction on the solution space for a particular realization (e.g. a mandated vendor, deadline or budget) rather than a self-adopted guideline.
distinguish.motivation.goal: the statement expresses a desired end state or direction to reach (e.g. 'reduce time-to-market') rather than a rule for how decisions are made.
distinguish.motivation.value: the element captures the worth or importance of something to stakeholders rather than a prescription governing choices.

types.title: Requirement
types.description: A statement of need that a system, component, or solution must satisfy, phrased as a specific, verifiable behavior or property (typically a 'shall/must' statement with acceptance criteria) and traceable to the stakeholders, drivers, or goals that motivate it. Use Goal instead when the statement expresses a high-level desired direction or end state that cannot be directly verified against a specific system, rather than a concrete need the system must meet. Use Constraint instead when the statement limits the design or implementation options (e.g. a mandated technology, budget, deadline, or regulation) rather than stating something the system must do or exhibit. Use Principle instead when the statement is a general normative rule that applies to all systems in a context and guides decisions, rather than a need assigned to a particular system or solution. Use Outcome instead when the statement describes a measurable end result the organization intends or has achieved, rather than a property the system must have to contribute to it.
evidence: A requirements document, PRD, or SRS entry with a stable identifier (e.g. REQ-042, FR-7, NFR-3) and 'shall'/'must' wording
A user story or issue tracker ticket labeled as a requirement, with acceptance criteria that tests or reviewers check against
Test annotations, docstrings, or traceability matrices that reference a requirement ID (e.g. @Requirement("REQ-042"), '# Verifies NFR-3') linking code or tests back to the stated need

distinguish.motivation.goal: the statement expresses a high-level desired direction or end state that cannot be directly verified against a specific system, rather than a concrete need the system must meet
distinguish.motivation.constraint: the statement limits the design or implementation options (e.g. a mandated technology, budget, deadline, or regulation) rather than stating something the system must do or exhibit
distinguish.motivation.principle: the statement is a general normative rule that applies to all systems in a context and guides decisions, rather than a need assigned to a particular system or solution
distinguish.motivation.outcome: the statement describes a measurable end result the organization intends or has achieved, rather than a property the system must have to contribute to it

types.title: Stakeholder
types.description: A motivation element naming a person, group, team, organization, or class of such parties, by its role or perspective, whose interests or concerns about the architecture are what drivers, goals, and requirements are traced back to. It captures who cares and why, not who performs behavior. Use Driver instead when the element states the concern or condition itself (e.g. 'GDPR fines', 'customer churn') rather than the party who holds it. Use Requirement instead when the text is a need the system must satisfy, such as a user story 'As a clerk I want…', where the clerk is only the associated stakeholder. Use Value instead when the element expresses the worth or benefit a party gains, rather than the party itself. Use business BusinessActor or BusinessRole instead when the party performs behaviour in the business; the actor or role references the stakeholder whose concerns it stands for.
evidence: A 'Stakeholders' section or RACI table in a README, architecture document, or ADR that lists named roles or teams together with their concerns
MADR or ADR front-matter fields such as 'deciders', 'consulted', or 'informed' that list teams, roles, or external bodies
Compliance or requirements documents that name an external authority or audience (e.g. 'PCI SSC', 'data protection officer', 'merchant partners') as the source of an obligation or concern

distinguish.motivation.driver: the element states the concern or condition itself (e.g. 'GDPR fines', 'customer churn') rather than the party who holds it
distinguish.motivation.requirement: the text is a need the system must satisfy, such as a user story 'As a clerk I want…', where the clerk is only the associated stakeholder
distinguish.motivation.value: the element expresses the worth or benefit a party gains, rather than the party itself

types.title: Value
types.description: A motivation element stating the worth, benefit, or utility that a specific concept, service, feature, or outcome has for one or more named stakeholders, expressed from the stakeholder's perspective (for example 'saves customers ten minutes per order') rather than as a target, a result, or a need. Use Outcome instead when the statement describes an end result the organization intends or has achieved, such as a measurable state change, rather than why that result is worth something to a stakeholder. Use Goal instead when the statement expresses a desired direction or end state the organization strives toward, not the benefit a stakeholder derives. Use Meaning instead when the statement gives the interpretation or definition of a concept in a context, not its worth or importance. Use Driver instead when the statement describes a condition or force that motivates change, such as market pressure or regulation, rather than a benefit delivered.
evidence: A 'Value proposition', 'Benefits' or 'Why this matters' section in a product spec, PRD or README that names a stakeholder and the benefit they receive
A business case, OKR or ADR 'Consequences/Benefits' entry quantifying worth to a stakeholder, such as cost saved, revenue enabled or time reduced
A feature, epic or service catalogue entry with a 'value', 'benefit' or 'business value' field describing what a user or customer gains

distinguish.motivation.outcome: the statement describes an end result the organization intends or has achieved, such as a measurable state change, rather than why that result is worth something to a stakeholder
distinguish.motivation.goal: the statement expresses a desired direction or end state the organization strives toward, not the benefit a stakeholder derives
distinguish.motivation.meaning: the statement gives the interpretation or definition of a concept in a context, not its worth or importance
distinguish.motivation.driver: the statement describes a condition or force that motivates change, such as market pressure or regulation, rather than a benefit delivered

layers.name: Business Layer
layers.scope: Describes what the organization does independently of the software that supports it: business actors and roles, collaborations and interfaces, processes, functions, interactions and events, business services and business objects, and the business capabilities the organization has (ArchiMate 3.2 business layer, with the strategy layer's Capability). Elements here are realized by application services and consume no implementation detail. Modelling rules: actors fill roles, and roles and collaborations are assigned to the processes, functions and interactions they perform (assigned-to); behaviour is never assigned to an actor directly. Internal behaviour realizes business services, which interfaces offer (assigned-to) and which serve actors, roles and processes. Only behaviour accesses business objects and contracts; actors, roles and interfaces reach information through the behaviour assigned to them. Events trigger processes and interactions, and behaviour raises events (triggers); a hand-off between behaviours is flows-to, and a function, having no start, is reached by flows rather than triggered. A business capability is an ability the organization has: business functions and processes realize it, capabilities aggregate narrower capabilities, and software capabilities (product layer) contribute by realizing the business functions behind it. Business services and business capabilities carry the main link to motivation: services realize goals and outcomes, satisfy requirements and deliver value; capabilities support goals and realize outcomes; processes may also realize outcomes and satisfy requirements.

types.title: BusinessActor
types.description: An active structure element denoting a specific, nameable organizational entity (an individual person, a team or department, or an external organization such as a customer or supplier) that exists independently of any responsibility it holds and can be assigned to BusinessRoles to perform behavior. It denotes who the entity is, not what responsibility it carries. Use BusinessRole instead when the element names a set of responsibilities or authorizations, such as 'Approver' or 'Account Holder', that different people or organizations could fill, rather than a concrete entity. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element is a temporary or contextual grouping of roles that act jointly, such as a review board formed per case, rather than a standing organizational entity with its own identity. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is a channel or access point, such as a call center, web portal or front desk, through which services are offered, rather than the entity offering or using them. Use BusinessObject instead when the code symbol is a data record about a party, such as a Customer table row, and the model needs the information itself rather than the organizational entity acting on it.
evidence: A domain or party-model class or enum value naming an organizational entity, such as Customer, Supplier, Partner, Department or Organization, that holds identity fields (legal name, org ID, tax number) and is referenced as the initiator or owner of business transactions.

Requirements, use-case or BPMN documentation that lists named participants or pools (e.g., 'Actors: Customer, Finance Department, Payment Provider'), or a swimlane labeled with a department or external company.

Integration or tenant configuration that identifies concrete external organizations or internal units, such as partner IDs, tenant or organization records, or supplier onboarding entries, on whose behalf the system acts.

distinguish.business.businessrole: the element names a set of responsibilities or authorizations, such as 'Approver' or 'Account Holder', that different people or organizations could fill, rather than a concrete entity.
distinguish.business.businesscollaboration: the element is a temporary or contextual grouping of roles that act jointly, such as a review board formed per case, rather than a standing organizational entity with its own identity.
distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is a channel or access point, such as a call center, web portal or front desk, through which services are offered, rather than the entity offering or using them.
distinguish.business.businessobject: the code symbol is a data record about a party, such as a Customer table row, and the model needs the information itself rather than the organizational entity acting on it.

types.title: BusinessCapability
types.description: An ability the organization possesses or intends to possess, stated as what the business can do (e.g. 'Share data with partners', 'Settle insurance claims', 'Onboard new customers'), independent of how, by whom or with what software it is done. It is stable while the processes, functions, people and systems behind it change, and capabilities nest into a capability map. The business functions and processes that carry out the ability realize it, and software capabilities contribute through those business functions. Use SoftwareCapability (product layer) instead when the ability belongs to the software platform (e.g. 'Save documents to files'), which realizes a business function, rather than to the organization. Use BusinessFunction instead when the element is a standing area of work grouped by the competency or resources it needs (e.g. 'Claims Handling'), performed by a role, rather than the ability that such work realizes. Use BusinessService instead when the element is externally visible behaviour offered to a consumer, rather than an internal ability of the organization. Use Goal (motivation layer) instead when the element states an end the organization wants to reach rather than an ability it has.
evidence: a business capability map, enterprise architecture document or strategy deck listing what the organization is able to do (e.g. a level-1/level-2 capability decomposition)
architecture decision records, roadmaps or OKRs that name an organizational ability to build or improve (e.g. 'become able to settle claims in one day') independent of any system
README or docs sections that map the software's modules to the business abilities they support

distinguish.product.softwarecapability: the ability belongs to the software platform (e.g. 'Save documents to files') rather than to the organization
distinguish.business.businessfunction: the element is a standing area of work performed by a role and grouped by competency, rather than the ability that work realizes
distinguish.business.businessservice: the element is externally visible behaviour offered to a consumer rather than an internal ability
distinguish.motivation.goal: the element states an end to reach rather than an ability the organization has

types.title: BusinessCollaboration
types.description: An active structure element that is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more BusinessRoles (which BusinessActors fill) jointly assigned to collective behavior that none of them performs alone. It has no identity apart from its participants: removing participants below two dissolves it. Use BusinessRole instead when the element is a single set of responsibilities assignable to one actor, even if many actors may fill it. Use BusinessActor instead when the grouping is a standing organizational unit (department, team, partner company) with its own identity, independent of which roles it combines. Use BusinessInteraction instead when you are modelling the joint behavior itself (e.g. 'negotiate terms') rather than the group of participants that performs it. Use Contract instead when you are modelling the recorded agreement binding the parties rather than the parties acting together.
evidence: a BPMN collaboration diagram or workflow definition declaring two or more participant pools/lanes (e.g. Buyer and Seller) that exchange messages within one flow

a domain class or config entity such as ReviewBoard, Partnership or JointVenture whose fields reference multiple distinct participant role types and which is used to gate a multi-party step (e.g. requires approvals from each role)
approval or sign-off rules (e.g. a four-eyes or dual-control policy) listing several named roles that must act together before a business step completes

distinguish.business.businessrole: the element is a single set of responsibilities assignable to one actor, even if many actors may fill it
distinguish.business.businessactor: the grouping is a standing organizational unit (department, team, partner company) with its own identity, independent of which roles it combines
distinguish.business.businessinteraction: you are modelling the joint behavior itself (e.g. 'negotiate terms') rather than the group of participants that performs it
distinguish.business.contract: you are modelling the recorded agreement binding the parties rather than the parties acting together

types.title: BusinessEvent
types.description: A behavior element that denotes an instantaneous, named occurrence of a business state change (e.g., order placed, contract signed, month-end reached) with no duration and no performer of its own. It exists only to trigger a BusinessProcess or BusinessInteraction, or to be raised by a BusinessProcess, BusinessFunction or BusinessInteraction; it is never accessed like information, and a hand-off between behaviours that involves no named occurrence is a flow, not an event. Use BusinessProcess instead when the element has duration, ordered steps, or a performing actor or role, rather than marking a single point in time. Use BusinessObject instead when the thing being modelled is the information record or message payload that carries the facts (e.g., the Order document), not the occurrence itself (OrderPlaced). Use BusinessInteraction instead when the element is collective behavior jointly carried out by several roles in a collaboration, not the moment that starts or ends that behavior.
evidence: Past-tense domain-event classes or records such as OrderPlaced or ContractSigned that are published to an event bus, outbox or message broker topic named after a business occurrence.
Cron or scheduler entries (e.g., a month-end or renewal-due job) whose firing starts a business workflow, indicating a timer-type event.
Start, intermediate or end events in BPMN or workflow-engine definitions, or business-named channels in an AsyncAPI or event-catalog document.

distinguish.business.businessprocess: the element has duration, ordered steps, or a performing actor or role, rather than marking a single point in time.
distinguish.business.businessobject: the thing being modelled is the information record or message payload that carries the facts (e.g., the Order document), not the occurrence itself (OrderPlaced).
distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the element is collective behavior jointly carried out by several roles in a collaboration, not the moment that starts or ends that behavior.

types.title: BusinessFunction
types.description: A business behavior element that groups ongoing internal behavior by the competency, skill, knowledge or resource it requires (e.g. Accounting, Claims Handling, Procurement), performed by the BusinessRole assigned to it, with no defined start, end or ordered sequence of steps, so it is not triggered by an event; work reaches it through flows from processes and other functions. Use BusinessProcess instead when the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a trigger and a defined end result (e.g. 'Handle Insurance Claim from submission to payout') rather than a standing area of competence. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes externally visible behavior from the consumer's perspective (what is offered), rather than the internal grouping of work that realizes it. Use BusinessInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles in a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor. Use BusinessRole instead when the element names who holds responsibility (e.g. 'Claims Handler', 'Finance Department') rather than the behavior they perform (e.g. 'Claims Handling', 'Financial Accounting'). Use BusinessCapability instead when the element names an ability the organization has (e.g. 'Share data with partners'), independent of the competency area or roles whose work realizes it.
evidence: top-level packages, modules or bounded contexts named after organizational competency areas (e.g. billing/, hr/, accounting/, procurement/) that own many related workflows rather than a single one

CODEOWNERS, team-ownership or service-catalog entries mapping a department or functional team to a group of modules, or permission scopes/menu sections grouped by functional area (e.g. 'finance:*', a 'Human Resources' navigation section)

architecture docs, capability or function maps, or ADRs listing functional areas of the business (e.g. a 'Business Functions' table or level-1 functional decomposition) referenced by code comments or module READMEs

distinguish.business.businessprocess: the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a trigger and a defined end result (e.g. 'Handle Insurance Claim from submission to payout') rather than a standing area of competence.
distinguish.business.businessservice: the element describes externally visible behavior from the consumer's perspective (what is offered), rather than the internal grouping of work that realizes it.
distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles in a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor.
distinguish.business.businessrole: the element names who holds responsibility (e.g. 'Claims Handler', 'Finance Department') rather than the behavior they perform (e.g. 'Claims Handling', 'Financial Accounting').
distinguish.business.businesscapability: the element names an ability the organization has, independent of the work and roles that realize it, rather than a standing area of work.

types.title: BusinessInteraction
types.description: A behavior element describing a unit of collective business behavior that two or more business roles carry out jointly within a BusinessCollaboration, such as negotiating terms or jointly approving a deal. It cannot be completed by any single participant acting alone. Use BusinessProcess instead when a single role or actor can carry the behavior through to its result, even if other parties are consulted or notified along the way. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element names the grouping of participating roles (who works together) rather than the joint behavior they perform (what they do together). Use BusinessFunction instead when the behavior is a stable, competency-based grouping (e.g., 'Partner Management') rather than a specific joint activity with a result. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes externally visible value offered to a consumer, with the joint internal behavior that delivers it hidden.
evidence: A workflow, saga or state machine for one business transaction (e.g., Negotiation, JointApproval) whose transitions are guarded by different roles, and which reaches its terminal state only after actions from each party, such as buyer accepts and seller countersigns.
A BPMN collaboration or choreography diagram, or a use-case document listing two or more primary actors, that describes one shared activity spanning both parties' lanes.

API endpoints on a shared resource (e.g., /negotiations/{id}/offer and /negotiations/{id}/counter-offer) protected by distinct role authorizations, where completion requires calls from users holding each role.

distinguish.business.businessprocess: a single role or actor can carry the behavior through to its result, even if other parties are consulted or notified along the way
distinguish.business.businesscollaboration: the element names the grouping of participating roles (who works together) rather than the joint behavior they perform (what they do together)
distinguish.business.businessfunction: the behavior is a stable, competency-based grouping (e.g., 'Partner Management') rather than a specific joint activity with a result
distinguish.business.businessservice: the element describes externally visible value offered to a consumer, with the joint internal behavior that delivers it hidden

types.title: BusinessInterface
types.description: An active structure element representing a channel or point of access, such as a branch counter, call centre, customer portal or mailroom, through which a BusinessService is offered to and used by actors in the environment. It identifies where and how the service is reached, not the service itself or the person or role who staffs it. Use BusinessService instead when the element describes what value or behavior is offered to the consumer, independent of the channel through which it is reached. Use BusinessRole instead when the element is a set of responsibilities performed behind the access point, such as a call-centre agent, rather than the access point itself. Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form of information exchanged, such as an on-screen form or a printed letter, rather than the channel through which the service is accessed. Use BusinessActor instead when the element is the concrete organizational unit or person, such as a customer-service department, rather than the channel it operates.
evidence: an enum or lookup table of customer contact channels (e.g. Channel { WEB, PHONE, BRANCH, EMAIL, PARTNER_PORTAL }) used to tag incoming requests or orders
channel-specific intake configuration, such as IVR or call-routing menus, a contact-centre queue definition, or a branch/portal entry module that routes customers to a named service
product or support documentation stating how customers reach a service (e.g. 'claims can be filed via the self-service portal, by phone, or at a branch')

distinguish.business.businessservice: the element describes what value or behavior is offered to the consumer, independent of the channel through which it is reached
distinguish.business.businessrole: the element is a set of responsibilities performed behind the access point, such as a call-centre agent, rather than the access point itself
distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form of information exchanged, such as an on-screen form or a printed letter, rather than the channel through which the service is accessed
distinguish.business.businessactor: the element is the concrete organizational unit or person, such as a customer-service department, rather than the channel it operates

types.title: BusinessObject
types.description: A passive structure element representing a business concept or unit of information (e.g., Order, Invoice, Claim, Customer record) that business behavior creates, reads, updates or deletes. It is identified by its business meaning and lifecycle, independent of storage format, schema or presentation. Use Contract instead when the information is specifically an agreement that sets out obligations, rights or terms between a provider and a consumer (e.g., SLA, policy terms, subscription agreement). Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form or media format in which the information is shown or exchanged (a PDF invoice, an HTML order form), not the information concept itself. Use BusinessEvent instead when the thing being modelled is a state change or occurrence (an order was placed) rather than the information entity that the occurrence concerns (the order). Use Product instead when the element is a bundle of services and contracts offered to customers as a value proposition, rather than a piece of information acted upon.
evidence: a domain-model class or aggregate root named with a business noun (Order, Invoice, Claim) in a domain/model package, referenced by several workflow or use-case handlers
a lifecycle status enum or state machine on that entity (e.g., DRAFT, SUBMITTED, APPROVED, CANCELLED) whose transitions are driven by business process steps
an entry in a business glossary, ubiquitous-language document or requirements spec that defines the term, with matching names in database tables, API schemas or JSON Schema titles

distinguish.business.contract: the information is specifically an agreement that sets out obligations, rights or terms between a provider and a consumer (e.g., SLA, policy terms, subscription agreement)
distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form or media format in which the information is shown or exchanged (a PDF invoice, an HTML order form), not the information concept itself
distinguish.business.businessevent: the thing being modelled is a state change or occurrence (an order was placed) rather than the information entity that the occurrence concerns (the order)
distinguish.business.product: the element is a bundle of services and contracts offered to customers as a value proposition, rather than a piece of information acted upon

types.title: BusinessProcess
types.description: A business behavior element, performed by the BusinessRole assigned to it (BusinessActors take part by filling that role), that consists of an ordered sequence of business activities with a defined start (a BusinessEvent or internal initiation) and a defined end state yielding a specific result, such as a delivered BusinessObject or a fulfilled request, for a customer or stakeholder. Use BusinessFunction instead when the behavior is a stable grouping of work by competency, skill or resource (e.g. 'Accounts Payable') with no inherent start trigger, step order or end result. Use BusinessInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles acting as a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor. Use BusinessService instead when you are describing the externally visible value offered to a consumer (what is provided), not the internal sequence of steps that delivers it (how it is done). Use BusinessEvent instead when the element is an instantaneous state change (e.g. 'Order Placed') that starts or ends a process, not the activity that runs between such changes.
evidence: A workflow or orchestration definition (BPMN file, Camunda/Temporal/Step Functions workflow, saga class) named after a business outcome, e.g. OrderFulfillmentWorkflow, whose steps run in a declared order.
A state machine or status enum on a business entity whose transitions follow a business lifecycle (e.g. SUBMITTED → APPROVED → SHIPPED) and are driven by a single orchestrating service method.
Documentation, runbooks or user stories that describe a numbered sequence of business steps from a trigger to a completion criterion, owned by a named role (e.g. 'claims handler').

distinguish.business.businessfunction: the behavior is a stable grouping of work by competency, skill or resource (e.g. 'Accounts Payable') with no inherent start trigger, step order or end result.
distinguish.business.businessinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more roles acting as a BusinessCollaboration rather than by a single role or actor.
distinguish.business.businessservice: you are describing the externally visible value offered to a consumer (what is provided), not the internal sequence of steps that delivers it (how it is done).
distinguish.business.businessevent: the element is an instantaneous state change (e.g. 'Order Placed') that starts or ends a process, not the activity that runs between such changes.

types.title: BusinessRole
types.description: An active structure element naming a responsibility position in the organization (e.g., Claims Adjuster, Approver, Customer) that business behavior is assigned to and that one or more BusinessActors can fill. It is defined by what is expected of whoever occupies it, not by the identity of a particular person, department or organization. Use BusinessActor instead when the element is a specific, identifiable person, department, team or external organization, such as 'Finance Department' or 'Acme Ltd', rather than a position that different actors could fill. Use BusinessCollaboration instead when the element is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more roles acting jointly, such as 'Buyer–Seller Negotiation', rather than a single responsibility position. Use BusinessFunction instead when the name denotes a capability-based grouping of behavior, such as 'Claims Handling', rather than the position responsible for performing it, such as 'Claims Handler'. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is a channel or access point through which a service is offered, such as a call center, portal or front desk, rather than the responsibility held by whoever staffs it.
evidence: An enum, constant set or lookup table of job-like user categories (e.g., APPROVER, UNDERWRITER, CASE_WORKER, CUSTOMER) that workflow or task-assignment logic uses to route work, rather than to name individual users.

Workflow or BPMN definitions that name a responsibility as a swimlane, candidateGroup or task assignee (e.g., camunda:candidateGroups="claims-adjuster"), or approval-chain configuration such as 'requires sign-off by Finance Approver'.
Requirements artifacts or user stories phrased 'As a <role>, I want…', or RACI and responsibility matrices listing positions against processes or tasks.

distinguish.business.businessactor: the element is a specific, identifiable person, department, team or external organization, such as 'Finance Department' or 'Acme Ltd', rather than a position that different actors could fill.
distinguish.business.businesscollaboration: the element is a temporary or permanent grouping of two or more roles acting jointly, such as 'Buyer–Seller Negotiation', rather than a single responsibility position.
distinguish.business.businessfunction: the name denotes a capability-based grouping of behavior, such as 'Claims Handling', rather than the position responsible for performing it, such as 'Claims Handler'.
distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is a channel or access point through which a service is offered, such as a call center, portal or front desk, rather than the responsibility held by whoever staffs it.

types.title: BusinessService
types.description: A behavior element that names an explicitly defined, externally visible unit of business behavior offered to customers or other stakeholders, such as 'Claims Handling' or 'Order Delivery'. It is described by the value and outcome the consumer receives, independent of the processes, functions, or software that realize it. Use BusinessProcess instead when the element describes the internal ordered steps, triggers, and hand-offs that produce a result, rather than the offering as the consumer sees it. Use BusinessFunction instead when the element is an internal grouping of behavior by competency or organizational capability, such as Finance or HR, that is not offered to a consumer as a named service. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is the access point or channel through which the service is obtained, such as a call center, web portal, or branch counter, rather than the behavior itself. Use Product instead when the element is a marketed bundle of one or more services together with contracts or terms, sold or offered as a single package.
evidence: A service catalog, SLA, or operating-level document entry that names a customer-facing offering (e.g. 'Claims Handling') with its consumers, availability hours, and service levels.
An OpenAPI tag, bounded-context module, or top-level domain package whose description states a business outcome for external consumers and groups several operations that support it.
A pricing page, terms-of-service text, or plan/entitlement configuration listing named services a customer is entitled to receive (e.g. 'Premium Support', 'Same-day Shipping').

distinguish.business.businessprocess: the element describes the internal ordered steps, triggers, and hand-offs that produce a result, rather than the offering as the consumer sees it.
distinguish.business.businessfunction: the element is an internal grouping of behavior by competency or organizational capability, such as Finance or HR, that is not offered to a consumer as a named service.
distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is the access point or channel through which the service is obtained, such as a call center, web portal, or branch counter, rather than the behavior itself.
distinguish.business.product: the element is a marketed bundle of one or more services together with contracts or terms, sold or offered as a single package.

types.title: Contract
types.description: A business object that records an agreement between two or more parties, typically a service provider and a consumer, stating the obligations, rights, and terms (e.g., SLA levels, pricing, durations, penalties) that govern how a business service or product is delivered and used. It is information acted upon, not behavior or an actor. Use BusinessObject instead when the information has business relevance but does not bind identified parties to obligations, rights, or terms (e.g., an invoice, order, or customer record). Use Representation instead when the element is the perceptible form of the agreement, such as the signed PDF, HTML terms page, or on-screen acceptance form, rather than the agreement's content. Use Product instead when the element is the offered bundle of services and contracts sold to a market, rather than the terms attached to it. Use BusinessEvent instead when the element is the state change of the agreement, such as a contract being signed, renewed, or terminated, rather than the agreement itself.
evidence: A domain class or schema named Agreement, Contract, Subscription, or ServiceLevelAgreement with fields such as parties, effectiveDate, expiryDate, termsVersion, and obligations or penalties
SLA or SLO configuration files that declare uptime, response-time, or support-tier commitments bound to a named customer plan or tier
Versioned terms-of-service, license, or data-processing-agreement documents in the repository, with code that records a user's acceptance of a specific terms version

distinguish.business.businessobject: the information has business relevance but does not bind identified parties to obligations, rights, or terms (e.g., an invoice, order, or customer record)
distinguish.business.representation: the element is the perceptible form of the agreement, such as the signed PDF, HTML terms page, or on-screen acceptance form, rather than the agreement's content
distinguish.business.product: the element is the offered bundle of services and contracts sold to a market, rather than the terms attached to it
distinguish.business.businessevent: the element is the state change of the agreement, such as a contract being signed, renewed, or terminated, rather than the agreement itself

types.title: Product
types.description: A composite element that bundles a named offering of one or more BusinessServices, optionally with application or technology services and business objects, together with the Contract that governs it, and that is offered as a whole to customers or markets. It is identified by what is sold or subscribed to, not by any single behavior or document within it. Use BusinessService instead when the element is a single externally visible unit of business behavior rather than a named, packaged offering combining several services with terms. Use Contract instead when the element is the agreement itself (terms, obligations, SLA, rights) rather than the offering those terms are attached to. Use BusinessObject instead when the element is information the business manipulates, such as a catalog entity or a 'Product' record or class in an e-commerce domain model describing goods for sale, rather than the offering bundle itself.
evidence: A plan, tier or SKU definition (e.g. a PLANS constant, Stripe product/price IDs, a billing config listing 'Basic/Pro/Enterprise') that enumerates which capabilities or services each offering includes.
An entitlements or feature-gating map keyed by subscription plan or edition, deciding which services a customer may use based on what they purchased.
Pricing-page content, product sheets or onboarding docs that present a named offering together with links to its terms of service, SLA or license agreement.

distinguish.business.businessservice: the element is a single externally visible unit of business behavior rather than a named, packaged offering combining several services with terms.
distinguish.business.contract: the element is the agreement itself (terms, obligations, SLA, rights) rather than the offering those terms are attached to.
distinguish.business.businessobject: the element is information the business manipulates, such as a catalog entity or a 'Product' record or class in an e-commerce domain model describing goods for sale, rather than the offering bundle itself.

types.title: Representation
types.description: A passive structure element that is a concrete, perceptible form (document layout, file format, printed or on-screen rendering) in which the information of a BusinessObject or Contract is conveyed to people. It captures how the information looks or is encoded, not what the information means. Use BusinessObject instead when the element is the business information concept itself (e.g., Invoice, Order) independent of any rendering or file format. Use Contract instead when the element is the agreement with its obligations and terms, rather than the signed PDF or printed form carrying it. Use BusinessInterface instead when the element is an access point (portal, counter, call centre) through which a service is offered, rather than the form of information delivered through it.
evidence: a document or report template (e.g., Jasper/Thymeleaf/Handlebars/LaTeX template, .docx template) that renders a business entity such as an invoice or statement
a PDF/CSV/XML export generator, such as a class named InvoicePdfRenderer or StatementExporter, that produces a file with a fixed layout for end users
a printable or on-screen form definition (HTML form template, print stylesheet, email template) that presents a business document to customers or staff

distinguish.business.businessobject: the element is the business information concept itself (e.g., Invoice, Order) independent of any rendering or file format.
distinguish.business.contract: the element is the agreement with its obligations and terms, rather than the signed PDF or printed form carrying it.
distinguish.business.businessinterface: the element is an access point (portal, counter, call centre) through which a service is offered, rather than the form of information delivered through it.

layers.name: Product Layer
layers.scope: Frames the system from a product-management point of view: the personas it serves, the software capabilities it must possess, the features that deliver them, the user workflows that exercise them and the milestones that schedule delivery. It adapts the ArchiMate 3.2 strategy vocabulary rather than adopting it: a software capability is an ability of the software platform, not ArchiMate's Capability, which is the organization's ability and is modelled as business.businesscapability. Product elements describe what the software offers and to whom, never how it is built. Modelling rules: realization runs upward through product. Application and technology services realize software capabilities and features, views realize features, and navigation flows and flow steps realize user workflows and their steps; product elements in turn realize business behaviour, a software capability realizing the business function it carries out and a user workflow the business process the user performs. A feature realizes the software capabilities it exercises; software capabilities aggregate narrower capabilities, and capabilities and features may depend on their own kind. Features and user workflows serve the personas they are designed for; a persona describes a kind of person, so it references the stakeholder and business role it stands for rather than realizing or serving them. A user workflow composes its steps, steps flow to steps, and each step uses the features it exercises; a workflow reaches features and software capabilities only through its steps. Software capabilities support goals; software capabilities and features satisfy requirements; features deliver value and workflows deliver outcomes. Software capabilities and features are scheduled for milestones, and milestones precede milestones.
layers.standard: ArchiMate 3.2 Strategy Extension + Product Management Practice

types.title: Feature
types.description: A unit of product functionality that a persona can directly perceive and invoke, such as a screen, command, setting or behaviour. It is described in user terms and can be prioritised, sized and scheduled on its own, and it realises one or more software capabilities. Use SoftwareCapability instead when the element names an ability the software must have regardless of which user-visible functionality provides it, and is not itself prioritised or sized as a deliverable. Use UserWorkflow instead when the element is a goal-directed sequence of user actions that passes through one or more features rather than a single piece of functionality. Use WorkflowStep instead when the element is one ordered action or experience within a specific user journey that exercises a feature, rather than the functionality itself. Use Milestone instead when the element is a dated delivery target that groups features, rather than functionality the user interacts with.
evidence: a feature-flag definition (e.g. LaunchDarkly, Unleash or a features.yml key) that gates a user-visible behaviour such as 'bulk-export' or 'dark-mode'
a Gherkin .feature file whose 'Feature:' block describes user-facing functionality with acceptance scenarios
a release-notes, changelog or user-guide entry announcing user-visible functionality (e.g. 'New: export reports to CSV') that is traceable to a set of routes, views or endpoints

distinguish.product.softwarecapability: the element names an ability the software must have regardless of which user-visible functionality provides it, and is not itself prioritised or sized as a deliverable
distinguish.product.userworkflow: the element is a goal-directed sequence of user actions that passes through one or more features rather than a single piece of functionality
distinguish.product.workflowstep: the element is one ordered action or experience within a specific user journey that exercises a feature, rather than the functionality itself
distinguish.product.milestone: the element is a dated delivery target that groups features, rather than functionality the user interacts with

types.title: Milestone
types.description: A named, time-bound delivery target, such as a release, version or roadmap phase, against which features and software capabilities are scheduled. It is defined by its target date or period and the scope assigned to it, not by any functionality of its own. Use Feature instead when the element is a user-visible unit of functionality being delivered, rather than the dated target or release it is delivered in. Use SoftwareCapability instead when the element names an ability the software has or should have, independent of when it is delivered, rather than a scheduled delivery point.
evidence: An issue-tracker milestone or fixVersion (e.g. a GitHub milestone, Jira release) with a due date and a set of linked feature issues.
A ROADMAP.md or planning document section headed by a version or quarter (e.g. 'v2.0 — Q3 2025') that lists the features targeted for it.
Feature-flag or configuration entries annotated with a target release (e.g. 'enabled_in: 3.1', 'since: v2.0'), or an 'Unreleased' or upcoming-version section in CHANGELOG.md.

distinguish.product.feature: the element is a user-visible unit of functionality being delivered, rather than the dated target or release it is delivered in.
distinguish.product.softwarecapability: the element names an ability the software has or should have, independent of when it is delivered, rather than a scheduled delivery point.

types.title: Persona
types.description: A named, fictional archetype of a class of the product's actual or intended users, characterised by shared goals, behaviours, proficiency and pain points, against which features and workflows are designed. It describes who the user is, not what they do in the product or what access they are granted. Use UserWorkflow instead when the artefact describes a goal-directed journey the user takes through the product rather than the characteristics of the user taking it. Use WorkflowStep instead when the artefact is a single action or experience a user has at one point in a journey, even if phrased as 'the admin does X'.
evidence: persona documents in the repository (e.g. docs/personas/*.md or a product brief) naming an archetype with goals, frustrations and skill level
user stories or acceptance criteria in issues or BDD feature files phrased 'As a <named user type>, I want ...' that recur across many stories

a user-segment or user-type discriminator (e.g. onboarding question 'I am a developer / designer', analytics segment definitions, feature-flag targeting rules) that tailors UI or content per user class rather than granting permissions

distinguish.product.userworkflow: the artefact describes a goal-directed journey the user takes through the product rather than the characteristics of the user taking it
distinguish.product.workflowstep: the artefact is a single action or experience a user has at one point in a journey, even if phrased as 'the admin does X'

types.title: SoftwareCapability
types.description: An ability of the software platform, stated as what the software can do (e.g. 'Save documents to files', 'Full-text search', 'Payment processing') rather than as a deliverable unit or a user journey. It is realized by one or more features, application services or technology services, and it realizes the business functions it carries out (saving documents to files realizes the business function of sharing data). Use BusinessCapability (business layer) instead when the ability belongs to the organization and would remain if different software, or none, provided it (e.g. 'Share data with partners'): a business capability is what the business can do, a software capability is what the platform can do. Use Feature instead when the element is a discrete, user-visible, prioritizable and sizable unit of functionality that ships (e.g. 'Apple Pay checkout button') rather than the enduring ability it contributes to (e.g. 'Payment processing'). Use UserWorkflow instead when the element describes an ordered sequence of user actions toward a goal rather than an ability the software has regardless of who uses it or in what order. Use WorkflowStep instead when the element is a single user action or experience at a position within a workflow rather than an ability that many steps may rely on. Use Milestone instead when the element is a dated delivery target that groups software capabilities or features rather than an ability itself.
evidence: a product capability map, roadmap or README section headed 'Capabilities' listing abilities such as 'Search', 'Billing', 'Notifications' that are realized by several features
a top-level domain module, bounded context or service named for an ability of the platform (e.g. billing/, search/, export/) whose submodules implement several distinct user-facing features

a declared capability set in a manifest or handshake (e.g. a 'capabilities' object in a plugin manifest or protocol initialization response) enumerating abilities the system offers independent of specific UI entry points

distinguish.business.businesscapability: the ability belongs to the organization and would remain if different software, or none, provided it (e.g. 'Share data with partners'), rather than an ability of the software platform (e.g. 'Save documents to files')
distinguish.product.feature: the element is a discrete, user-visible, prioritizable and sizable unit of functionality that ships (e.g. 'Apple Pay checkout button') rather than the enduring ability it contributes to (e.g. 'Payment processing')
distinguish.product.userworkflow: the element describes an ordered sequence of user actions toward a goal rather than an ability the product possesses regardless of who uses it or in what order
distinguish.product.workflowstep: the element is a single user action or experience at a position within a workflow rather than an ability that many steps may rely on
distinguish.product.milestone: the element is a dated delivery target that groups software capabilities or features rather than an ability itself

types.title: UserWorkflow
types.description: An ordered, end-to-end journey of user-facing steps that a persona performs through the product to reach one goal, described from the user's point of view and independent of screens, routes or code. It is composed of WorkflowSteps and spans the features those steps exercise. Use WorkflowStep instead when the element is a single action or experience at one position in a journey, not the whole sequence from trigger to goal. Use Feature instead when the element is a unit of functionality the user can switch on, buy or ship, rather than the ordered path a user takes to reach a goal. Use SoftwareCapability instead when the element names an ability the software has (e.g. 'password recovery') with no ordering of user actions.
evidence: an end-to-end test spec (Playwright, Cypress, Selenium) named after a user goal, such as 'checkout.e2e.ts', that drives a user across several pages in order
an analytics funnel definition (Amplitude, Mixpanel, GA4 config) listing ordered events from a start event to a goal event
a Gherkin .feature file or docs/user-journeys page describing numbered Given/When/Then steps a named user type takes to accomplish a goal

distinguish.product.workflowstep: the element is a single action or experience at one position in a journey, not the whole sequence from trigger to goal
distinguish.product.feature: the element is a unit of functionality the user can switch on, buy or ship, rather than the ordered path a user takes to reach a goal
distinguish.product.softwarecapability: the element names an ability the software has (e.g. 'password recovery') with no ordering of user actions

types.title: WorkflowStep
types.description: An ordered, user-facing action within exactly one UserWorkflow, stating what the user does or experiences at that point in the journey and its observable result, described without reference to screens, routes, components or code. Each step names one position in one workflow; the same action in a different workflow is a different step. Use UserWorkflow instead when the element is the whole goal-directed journey made up of several steps, rather than one position within it. Use Feature instead when the element is a reusable unit of user-visible functionality that may be exercised by steps in many workflows, rather than a point in a particular journey. Use SoftwareCapability instead when the element describes an ability the software has regardless of any user sequence, with no ordering or user action attached.
evidence: Numbered 'When'/'Then' lines inside a Gherkin Scenario or acceptance-criteria list that describe a user action and its visible result
test.step('...') or cy.step-style blocks inside an end-to-end test (Playwright, Cypress) named after a user action within a journey test
A user-journey, onboarding or story-map document (or wizard step config array) listing ordered steps with titles like 'Enter email' and 'Confirm code'

distinguish.product.userworkflow: the element is the whole goal-directed journey made up of several steps, rather than one position within it
distinguish.product.feature: the element is a reusable unit of user-visible functionality that may be exercised by steps in many workflows, rather than a point in a particular journey
distinguish.product.softwarecapability: the element describes an ability the software has regardless of any user sequence, with no ordering or user action attached

layers.name: Security Layer
layers.scope: Defines how the system identifies, authorizes and protects: authentication configuration, roles, permissions, secure resources and their operations, access conditions and field-level controls, declarative policies and rules, data classification and rate limits, together with goal-oriented security concepts such as actors, objectives, delegations, threats, countermeasures and accountability (NIST SP 800-53 controls with STS-ml and XACML-style policy modelling). Code that checks identity or enforces permissions is evidence for elements here. Modelling rules: the security model composes its authentication configuration, constraints container and policies, and aggregates the shared elements (actors, roles, permissions, secure resources, information entities, delegations, threats, classifications and accountability requirements); a policy composes its rules, and a secure resource composes its operations and field access controls. Actors are assigned to roles, roles aggregate permissions and specialize a parent role, and permissions authorize resource operations; access follows that chain. An authentication configuration authenticates actors, uses its password policy and protects resources. A policy rule uses the conditions it evaluates, protects its target, authorizes permissions, triggers its policy actions and generates evidence; conditions and actions do not constrain or trigger on their own. Policies (security, password, retention and data classification) mandate the countermeasures they call for, and only countermeasures mitigate threats. A threat targets resources, information entities and business processes and services, influences classifications and policies, and references the motivation driver it gives rise to. Audit configurations, policy rules and delegations generate evidence; an audit configuration monitors resources and satisfies accountability requirements, and a retention policy governs the audit trails, evidence and information it keeps. A data classification governs the information entities, secure resources and retention policies it labels; field access controls are constrained by it, and data elements in other layers reference it. Separation of duty, binding of duty and need to know constrain roles, permissions and operations; the constraints container only groups them, and other layers link to the individual rule they follow. Validation rules constrain field values; they do not decide access.

types.title: AccessCondition
types.description: A single comparison predicate that tests one named request-context attribute (subject claim, resource property, environment value) against a literal or referenced value using one operator, and yields a denial message when false. It carries no effect of its own; it is evaluated as one term within a PolicyRule, ResourceOperation or InformationRight authorization check. Use Condition instead when the logic is a reusable, free-form or compound expression (time windows, combined attribute logic) rather than one field-operator-value test. Use PolicyRule instead when the unit carries a permit/deny effect or obligations, not just a boolean test. Use ValidationRule instead when the check enforces format, range or integrity of field data rather than deciding whether a principal may access something. Use InformationRight instead when the element grants named operations on an information entity to a specific actor, even if it embeds a constraint.
evidence: A guard clause in a handler or middleware that compares one request attribute to a value and throws or returns 403 with a message, e.g. if (req.user.tenantId !== resource.tenantId) throw new ForbiddenError('Tenant mismatch')
A declarative policy or config entry holding a field/operator/value triple, e.g. { attribute: 'token.scope', op: 'contains', value: 'orders:write' } in a Casbin, OPA input or custom rules file
A route or method annotation that asserts a single claim or attribute, e.g. @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_read')") or requireClaim('email_verified', true)

distinguish.security.condition: the logic is a reusable, free-form or compound expression (time windows, combined attribute logic) rather than one field-operator-value test
distinguish.security.policyrule: the unit carries a permit/deny effect or obligations, not just a boolean test
distinguish.security.validationrule: the check enforces format, range or integrity of field data rather than deciding whether a principal may access something
distinguish.security.informationright: the element grants named operations on an information entity to a specific actor, even if it embeds a constraint

types.title: AccountabilityRequirement
types.description: A security obligation stating that the performance of one named action on one named resource must be provably attributable to the actor who performed it. It records whether non-repudiation is mandatory, the purpose that justifies the obligation, and whether the resulting proof may be disputed. Use AuditConfig instead when the element specifies which events are logged, at what verbosity, and with which fields sanitized, rather than the obligation to prove that a particular action happened. Use Evidence instead when the element is the concrete proof artifact itself (a signature, hash, timestamp or audit-trail entry), not the requirement that such proof exist. Use NeedToKnow instead when the declared purpose is a precondition an actor must state before being granted access, rather than a justification attached to proving an action after it occurs. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the concern is how long the proof or logs are kept and how they are disposed of.
evidence: A sensitive operation, such as payment approval, contract acceptance or record deletion, that signs a payload with the acting user's key or a server HSM and persists the signer ID, signature and timestamp alongside the record.

An append-only or write-once audit table, ledger, or hash-chained log that the code requires for a specific action-resource pair, often with a mandatory 'reason' or 'justification' field captured from the user.

Compliance or control-mapping documentation (SSP, control matrix, ADR) that cites AU-10 or 'non-repudiation' for a named action, or a dispute/chargeback workflow that retrieves the stored proof of that action.

distinguish.security.auditconfig: the element specifies which events are logged, at what verbosity, and with which fields sanitized, rather than the obligation to prove that a particular action happened.
distinguish.security.evidence: the element is the concrete proof artifact itself (a signature, hash, timestamp or audit-trail entry), not the requirement that such proof exist.
