distinguish.security.needtoknow: the declared purpose is a precondition an actor must state before being granted access, rather than a justification attached to proving an action after it occurs.
distinguish.security.retentionpolicy: the concern is how long the proof or logs are kept and how they are disposed of.

types.title: Actor
types.description: A named principal (a human user population, service account, automated system, or external party) that is the subject of authentication and authorization decisions, typed by category and optionally assigned a trust level. It represents who acts, as distinct from the permission bundle it holds or the authority it receives temporarily. Use Role instead when the element is a named bundle of permissions that many principals can be assigned, such as 'admin' or 'editor', rather than the principal itself. Use Delegation instead when the element records a transfer of authority from one principal to another, with a scope or expiry, rather than the principal that delegates or receives it. Use AuthenticationConfig instead when the element describes how principals prove identity, such as the provider, MFA or session timeout, rather than who is being identified. Use Threat instead when the element models an adversary or attack scenario with a likelihood and impact, rather than a legitimate principal that the system recognises and authorizes.
evidence: A principal or user-context class (e.g. UserPrincipal, ServiceIdentity) populated from a verified token and passed to authorization checks.
Declared service accounts or machine identities in configuration, such as a Kubernetes ServiceAccount, cloud IAM users or roles for workloads, or OAuth client_credentials client registrations.
Branching in authorization code on the principal's kind or trust level, such as `if principal.type == 'service'` or checks on an `is_internal` or `partner` flag.

distinguish.security.role: the element is a named bundle of permissions that many principals can be assigned, such as 'admin' or 'editor', rather than the principal itself.
distinguish.security.delegation: the element records a transfer of authority from one principal to another, with a scope or expiry, rather than the principal that delegates or receives it.
distinguish.security.authenticationconfig: the element describes how principals prove identity, such as the provider, MFA or session timeout, rather than who is being identified.
distinguish.security.threat: the element models an adversary or attack scenario with a likelihood and impact, rather than a legitimate principal that the system recognises and authorizes.

types.title: AuditConfig
types.description: A logging configuration that determines which security-relevant events on protected resources or operations are written to an audit trail, at what verbosity, and which request elements (payload, headers) are captured or sanitized before recording. It covers audit record generation and content only. How long records are kept and how they are disposed of belong to RetentionPolicy. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the code or config specifies how long audit or access records are kept, where they are archived, or how they are securely deleted, rather than what is captured. Use AccountabilityRequirement instead when the artifact states an obligation that a party must be able to prove an action occurred (non-repudiation, challengeability), independent of the logging mechanism. Use Evidence instead when the symbol is a produced artifact, such as a log entry, signature, hash or timestamp, rather than the configuration that causes such artifacts to be generated. Use PolicyAction instead when logging is a one-off enforcement response (type 'log' or 'alert') fired by a specific policy rule match, rather than a standing capture configuration for a resource or operation.
evidence: Audit middleware, interceptor or filter registered on a router or service, configured with options such as level, includeBody/includeHeaders and a redact or mask field list.
Decorators or annotations such as @Audited, @Auditable or auditlog.register(Model) attached to handlers or entities, optionally with parameters controlling captured detail.
A configuration block named audit/auditLog (YAML, JSON, env vars) with keys like enabled, level, logRequestBody and sensitiveFields, distinct from general application logging settings.

distinguish.security.retentionpolicy: the code or config specifies how long audit or access records are kept, where they are archived, or how they are securely deleted, rather than what is captured.
distinguish.security.accountabilityrequirement: the artifact states an obligation that a party must be able to prove an action occurred (non-repudiation, challengeability), independent of the logging mechanism.
distinguish.security.evidence: the symbol is a produced artifact, such as a log entry, signature, hash or timestamp, rather than the configuration that causes such artifacts to be generated.
distinguish.security.policyaction: logging is a one-off enforcement response (type 'log' or 'alert') fired by a specific policy rule match, rather than a standing capture configuration for a resource or operation.

types.title: AuthenticationConfig
types.description: A configuration element that fixes, for one application or service, the mechanism by which principals prove their identity: the authentication protocol or identity provider, whether a second factor is required, how long an authenticated session remains valid, and which credential policy applies. It describes identity verification only, not what an authenticated principal may do afterwards. Use PasswordPolicy instead when the element only specifies credential complexity, rotation, reuse or lockout rules rather than the provider, MFA and session settings of the login mechanism. Use Actor instead when the element is the principal being authenticated (user, service account, external system) rather than the mechanism that verifies it. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the element is a prioritized set of rules deciding access to targeted resources after identity is established, rather than how identity is established. Use Permission instead when the code checks whether an already-identified principal may perform an action on a resource (authorization) rather than verifying who the principal is.
evidence: Authentication middleware or framework setup, e.g. passport.use(new OIDCStrategy(...)), Spring Security oauth2Login()/saml2Login(), or NextAuth providers array, with issuer, client ID and callback URLs.
Configuration files or environment variables declaring identity-provider settings such as OIDC_ISSUER_URL, SAML metadata URL, LDAP bind DN, or JWT issuer/audience and signing keys.
Session or token lifetime settings alongside MFA enforcement, e.g. SESSION_MAX_AGE, JWT expiresIn, refresh-token TTL, or an 'mfa: required' / TOTP or WebAuthn enrollment flag in auth config.

distinguish.security.passwordpolicy: the element only specifies credential complexity, rotation, reuse or lockout rules rather than the provider, MFA and session settings of the login mechanism.
distinguish.security.actor: the element is the principal being authenticated (user, service account, external system) rather than the mechanism that verifies it.
distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the element is a prioritized set of rules deciding access to targeted resources after identity is established, rather than how identity is established.
distinguish.security.permission: the code checks whether an already-identified principal may perform an action on a resource (authorization) rather than verifying who the principal is.

types.title: BindingOfDuty
types.description: A procedural access constraint requiring that the actor who performs one step of a multi-step task or workflow also performs its designated follow-on steps, so that any attempt by a different actor to continue or complete that task instance is rejected. Use SeparationOfDuty instead when the rule requires that two steps be performed by different actors or roles, rather than by the same actor. Use AccessCondition instead when the check is a standalone predicate on a single request (e.g. resource.ownerId eq currentUser) with no link to a task instance the actor started. Use NeedToKnow instead when access is restricted according to the actor's declared purpose rather than its participation in an earlier workflow step. Use PolicyRule instead when the logic is a general condition-plus-effect rule in a policy rather than a task-continuity obligation tied to workflow steps.
evidence: a workflow or state-machine transition guard that compares the stored initiator, claimant or assignee of a task instance (e.g. startedBy, claimedBy) with the current user id and throws or returns 403 when they differ
BPMN/Camunda or similar workflow configuration that assigns a later user task to the process initiator (e.g. assignee="${initiator}") or locks a claimed task to a single user until completion
a dedicated exception or error message such as 'Only the user who started this request may submit it' or a class named like TaskOwnershipViolation or SameUserRequired raised in multi-step flows

distinguish.security.separationofduty: the rule requires that two steps be performed by different actors or roles, rather than by the same actor.
distinguish.security.accesscondition: the check is a standalone predicate on a single request (e.g. resource.ownerId eq currentUser) with no link to a task instance the actor started.
distinguish.security.needtoknow: access is restricted according to the actor's declared purpose rather than its participation in an earlier workflow step.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the logic is a general condition-plus-effect rule in a policy rather than a task-continuity obligation tied to workflow steps.

types.title: Condition
types.description: A named, reusable boolean expression over request context (time, location, subject attributes, environment or resource state) that is defined once and referenced by one or more PolicyRules or SecurityPolicies to decide whether they apply. It may be a free-form expression or a composition of AccessCondition predicates. Use AccessCondition instead when the predicate is a single concrete field + operator + value comparison written inline in one rule's condition chain rather than a named expression reused across rules. Use PolicyRule instead when the element carries an effect (permit/deny) and enforcement outcome, not just the applicability test. Use InformationRight instead when the constraint expression is bound to a specific actor and the operations they may perform on an InformationEntity. Use PolicyAction instead when the element describes what happens after a match (deny, alert, mask, redirect) rather than the test that produces the match.
evidence: A named predicate function or helper rule (e.g. isBusinessHours(ctx), fromTrustedNetwork(req), rego `allow_if_mfa` helper) referenced by several authorization rules
A Condition block in a policy document (AWS IAM `Condition`, Azure ABAC condition, Cedar `when` clause) defined once and reused by multiple statements
A Spring Security SpEL expression or CEL/OPA expression string stored in config and referenced by name from @PreAuthorize annotations or policy rule entries

distinguish.security.accesscondition: the predicate is a single concrete field + operator + value comparison written inline in one rule's condition chain rather than a named expression reused across rules.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the element carries an effect (permit/deny) and enforcement outcome, not just the applicability test.
distinguish.security.informationright: the constraint expression is bound to a specific actor and the operations they may perform on an InformationEntity.
distinguish.security.policyaction: the element describes what happens after a match (deny, alert, mask, redirect) rather than the test that produces the match.

types.title: Countermeasure
types.description: A security control or mitigation mechanism, recorded against one or more identified Threats, that reduces their likelihood or impact and is characterised by control class, implementation status and assessed effectiveness. It is the threat-mitigation view of a control; the concrete configuration that realises it (password rules, auth settings, rate limits) is modelled by other types that realize or mandate it. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the element is a named, prioritised set of evaluation rules that produces access-control decisions for a target, rather than a mitigation linked to a threat. Use PolicyAction instead when the element is the runtime response (deny, alert, mask, quarantine) executed when a specific policy rule fires, not the standing control that the response helps realise. Use PasswordPolicy instead when the element is the concrete credential complexity, rotation and lockout parameters; model the anti-brute-force mitigation those parameters deliver as a Countermeasure. Use Threat instead when the element describes what could go wrong (attacker, vulnerability, likelihood, impact) rather than the measure taken against it.
evidence: a threat-model artifact (STRIDE/LINDDUN table, OWASP Threat Dragon or MS TMT file) whose 'mitigation' or 'countermeasure' entries name a control against a listed threat
security middleware or filters registered globally (e.g. helmet, CSRF token filter, input sanitiser, WAF rule set) with comments or config referencing a CWE, OWASP Top 10 item or NIST control ID
a control-implementation record such as an OSCAL component-definition, system security plan or compliance matrix mapping control IDs (e.g. SC-8, SI-10) to an implementation status

distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the element is a named, prioritised set of evaluation rules that produces access-control decisions for a target, rather than a mitigation linked to a threat
distinguish.security.policyaction: the element is the runtime response (deny, alert, mask, quarantine) executed when a specific policy rule fires, not the standing control that the response helps realise
distinguish.security.passwordpolicy: the element is the concrete credential complexity, rotation and lockout parameters; model the anti-brute-force mitigation those parameters deliver as a Countermeasure
distinguish.security.threat: the element describes what could go wrong (attacker, vulnerability, likelihood, impact) rather than the measure taken against it

types.title: DataClassification
types.description: A labelled data-sensitivity tier that assigns a classification level to data and states the minimum protection obligations, such as encryption, that any data carrying that label must meet. It is the label and its handling rules, not the data asset, field or store being labelled. Use InformationEntity instead when the element is the named information asset (e.g. customer PII, payment records) that receives a classification, rather than the classification tier and its handling rules. Use FieldAccessControl instead when the element specifies how one particular field is masked, redacted or tokenized for unauthorized principals, rather than a sensitivity tier applied across many fields. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the element defines how long data is kept and how it is disposed of, even if that period is selected by classification level. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the element is a prioritized set of evaluation rules producing access decisions, rather than a sensitivity label those rules may reference.
evidence: an enum or constant set of sensitivity labels (e.g. PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED) referenced by annotations, schema tags or column metadata such as @Sensitive(level=...) or x-data-classification
a configuration map or policy file keyed by classification label that sets handling requirements, e.g. 'restricted: encrypt at-rest with KMS key, TLS required, no export'
a data-handling or data-classification policy document or data-catalog taxonomy that defines each sensitivity tier and its required controls

distinguish.security.informationentity: the element is the named information asset (e.g. customer PII, payment records) that receives a classification, rather than the classification tier and its handling rules.
distinguish.security.fieldaccesscontrol: the element specifies how one particular field is masked, redacted or tokenized for unauthorized principals, rather than a sensitivity tier applied across many fields.
distinguish.security.retentionpolicy: the element defines how long data is kept and how it is disposed of, even if that period is selected by classification level.
distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the element is a prioritized set of evaluation rules producing access decisions, rather than a sensitivity label those rules may reference.

types.title: Delegation
types.description: An authority grant record in which one named actor (the delegator) transfers some or all of its own permissions or role to another actor (the delegatee), qualified by a delegation type and optionally an expiry. It differs from a role assignment or a standing permission in that the authority is derived from, and revocable by, the delegating actor rather than granted directly by administration. Use Role instead when the authority is a standing, administratively assigned collection of permissions rather than one actor passing its own authority to another. Use Permission instead when you are modelling the atomic action-on-resource grant itself, not the act of handing it from one actor to another. Use InformationRight instead when the grant is an ABAC rule giving an actor operations on an InformationEntity under a constraint expression, with no delegating party. Use Actor instead when the symbol represents the principal (user, service account) itself rather than the transfer of authority between principals.
evidence: A persisted entity or table such as Delegation, ProxyAssignment or ActingAs with columns like delegator_id, delegatee_id, scope and expires_at
An OAuth 2.0 token-exchange or impersonation flow (e.g. RFC 8693 'act' claim, 'on_behalf_of' or 'impersonate' endpoint) that issues a token for one principal acting for another
Authorization middleware that, when checking permissions, merges in roles from active, unexpired delegation records granted to the current user and logs the delegation in the audit trail

distinguish.security.role: the authority is a standing, administratively assigned collection of permissions rather than one actor passing its own authority to another.
distinguish.security.permission: you are modelling the atomic action-on-resource grant itself, not the act of handing it from one actor to another.
distinguish.security.informationright: the grant is an ABAC rule giving an actor operations on an InformationEntity under a constraint expression, with no delegating party.
distinguish.security.actor: the symbol represents the principal (user, service account) itself rather than the transfer of authority between principals.

types.title: Evidence
types.description: A kind of proof artifact — log record, digital signature, trusted timestamp, hash, certificate or audit trail — produced or retained by the system so that a specific action or event can later be verified as having occurred and attributed to an actor. It is the artifact itself as a modelled category, not the obligation to produce it or the logging configuration that emits it. Use AuditConfig instead when the code configures which events are logged, verbosity, payload inclusion or field sanitisation rather than defining a specific proof artifact and its origin. Use AccountabilityRequirement instead when the element states who must prove an action took place and whether that proof is challengeable, rather than the artifact that constitutes the proof. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the concern is how long evidence or logs are kept, where they are archived and how they are destroyed. Use Countermeasure instead when the element is a control such as signing middleware or a tamper-detection mechanism that mitigates a threat, rather than the record it produces.
evidence: code that computes and persists a digital signature or HMAC over a transaction or request payload alongside the record (e.g. a signature column, JWS detached signature, or signed receipt object)
an append-only or hash-chained audit trail table, WORM bucket or ledger write (e.g. an audit_events table with previous_hash, AWS QLDB, S3 Object Lock) recording actor, action and timestamp
calls to an RFC 3161 timestamping authority or certificate-based signing service (e.g. TSA client, KMS Sign API, X.509 cert attached to a document approval)

distinguish.security.auditconfig: the code configures which events are logged, verbosity, payload inclusion or field sanitisation rather than defining a specific proof artifact and its origin
distinguish.security.accountabilityrequirement: the element states who must prove an action took place and whether that proof is challengeable, rather than the artifact that constitutes the proof
distinguish.security.retentionpolicy: the concern is how long evidence or logs are kept, where they are archived and how they are destroyed
distinguish.security.countermeasure: the element is a control such as signing middleware or a tamper-detection mechanism that mitigates a threat, rather than the record it produces

types.title: FieldAccessControl
types.description: A field-level protection rule bound to one named field (property, column or attribute) of a SecureResource. It states how that field's value is masked, redacted, hashed, tokenized or truncated when the field is exposed to a principal that lacks the permission to see it in clear. Use ValidationRule instead when the constraint governs which values a field may accept or contain (pattern, range, length), not how its value is hidden from unauthorized readers. Use SecureResource instead when the control applies to the whole resource, endpoint or table and its operations, not to an individual field within it. Use DataClassification instead when the element assigns a sensitivity tier or encryption obligation to data, rather than naming the masking technique for one specific field. Use PolicyAction instead when masking is the generic enforcement response fired by a PolicyRule match, not a standing rule attached to a named field.
evidence: A DTO or serializer field carrying a masking or redaction annotation or type, e.g. @Sensitive, @JsonSerialize(using = MaskingSerializer.class), Pydantic SecretStr, or a custom redact() field transformer.
Response-shaping code that replaces or drops a specific field after a permission check, e.g. `if not user.has_perm('view_ssn'): data['ssn'] = mask(data['ssn'])`.

Declarative column- or field-level masking configuration: a GraphQL @auth or @mask directive on a field, Hasura column permissions, SQL Server `MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = ...)`, or a Snowflake/Postgres masking policy on a column.

distinguish.security.validationrule: the constraint governs which values a field may accept or contain (pattern, range, length), not how its value is hidden from unauthorized readers.
distinguish.security.secureresource: the control applies to the whole resource, endpoint or table and its operations, not to an individual field within it.
distinguish.security.dataclassification: the element assigns a sensitivity tier or encryption obligation to data, rather than naming the masking technique for one specific field.
distinguish.security.policyaction: masking is the generic enforcement response fired by a PolicyRule match, not a standing rule attached to a named field.

types.title: InformationEntity
types.description: A named logical category of information (e.g. customer PII, payment card data, medical records) defined independently of where or how it is stored, which carries a sensitivity classification and is the object to which InformationRights grant actors access. It names *what* the data is, not the endpoint, table or field that holds it. Use SecureResource instead when the protected thing is a concrete technical artefact (an API endpoint, database table, file store, service or UI) with operations performed on it, rather than a storage-independent category of data. Use DataClassification instead when you are modelling the classification scheme itself (levels, encryption obligations) rather than a specific data category that is assigned one of those levels. Use FieldAccessControl instead when the control applies to one named field and its masking or redaction strategy, rather than to a whole logical grouping of data that may span many fields and stores.
evidence: A data inventory, record-of-processing (ROPA) or data-catalog document listing named data categories such as 'Customer PII' or 'Cardholder Data', each with a sensitivity level.
An enum or constant set of data categories (e.g. DataCategory.PII, DataCategory.PHI, DataCategory.PCI) referenced by authorization checks or masking logic across several classes.

Marker annotations or catalog tags (e.g. @PersonalData(category="contact"), BigQuery policy tags, AWS Macie or Purview classifications) applied consistently to fields in multiple models or tables to group them into one asset.

distinguish.security.secureresource: the protected thing is a concrete technical artefact (an API endpoint, database table, file store, service or UI) with operations performed on it, rather than a storage-independent category of data.
distinguish.security.dataclassification: you are modelling the classification scheme itself (levels, encryption obligations) rather than a specific data category that is assigned one of those levels.
distinguish.security.fieldaccesscontrol: the control applies to one named field and its masking or redaction strategy, rather than to a whole logical grouping of data that may span many fields and stores.

types.title: InformationRight
types.description: An access grant that authorizes one specific actor to perform a listed set of operations on a single InformationEntity. The grant applies only while an attribute-based constraint expression evaluates to true at decision time. It differs from a role-assigned Permission because it names the grantee directly and carries its own qualifying condition. Use Permission instead when the grant is a reusable resource+action entitlement assigned to Roles rather than to a named actor, and has no per-grant constraint expression. Use Delegation instead when authority is transferred from one actor (delegator) to another (delegatee), possibly time-bounded, rather than granted directly on an information asset. Use NeedToKnow instead when access is gated by the actor declaring a purpose or justification rather than by an attribute-based boolean constraint. Use AccessCondition instead when the element is only the field/operator/value predicate itself, not the grant binding an actor and operations to an information asset.
evidence: An ABAC policy line naming a concrete subject, data asset, actions and condition, e.g. Casbin `p, billing-svc, customer_pii, read, r.sub.region == r.obj.region`
A cloud IAM or KMS policy statement whose Principal is a specific user or service, whose Resource is a named data store or dataset, and which has an Action list and a Condition block
An OPA/Rego or Cedar `permit` rule keyed on a specific principal id and data category, with a `when`/`if` clause comparing subject attributes to resource attributes

distinguish.security.permission: the grant is a reusable resource+action entitlement assigned to Roles rather than to a named actor, and has no per-grant constraint expression
distinguish.security.delegation: authority is transferred from one actor (delegator) to another (delegatee), possibly time-bounded, rather than granted directly on an information asset
distinguish.security.needtoknow: access is gated by the actor declaring a purpose or justification rather than by an attribute-based boolean constraint
distinguish.security.accesscondition: the element is only the field/operator/value predicate itself, not the grant binding an actor and operations to an information asset

types.title: NeedToKnow
types.description: A procedural access constraint that limits access to a named resource to actors whose declared business or operational purpose matches a stated objective, optionally requiring the actor to submit an explicit justification before access is granted. It gates access by purpose, not by identity, role or attribute match alone. Use InformationRight instead when the rule grants specific operations on an information entity to a named actor under a constraint expression, with no purpose declaration involved. Use AccountabilityRequirement instead when the purpose declaration is recorded as evidence that an action occurred, and is not checked as a gate before access. Use AccessCondition instead when the check is a generic field/operator/value predicate on request context inside a PolicyRule chain, rather than a purpose-of-use restriction. Use Permission instead when the element is an atomic action grant on a resource assigned to roles, with no justification or purpose requirement.
evidence: Middleware or an interceptor that rejects requests to a sensitive endpoint when a purpose or reason field (e.g. X-Access-Reason, purposeOfUse) is missing or not in an allowed set.
A UI dialog or 'break-glass' prompt that forces the user to enter or select a reason before showing a protected record such as a patient chart or customer PII.
A configuration map from resources to permitted purpose codes (e.g. HIPAA TREAT/PAYMENT/OPS), together with a denial message shown when the stated purpose does not match.

distinguish.security.informationright: the rule grants specific operations on an information entity to a named actor under a constraint expression, with no purpose declaration involved.
distinguish.security.accountabilityrequirement: the purpose declaration is recorded as evidence that an action occurred, and is not checked as a gate before access.
distinguish.security.accesscondition: the check is a generic field/operator/value predicate on request context inside a PolicyRule chain, rather than a purpose-of-use restriction.
distinguish.security.permission: the element is an atomic action grant on a resource assigned to roles, with no justification or purpose requirement.

types.title: PasswordPolicy
types.description: A credential rule set that fixes the length bounds, required character classes, reuse history, expiry interval and failed-attempt lockout for memorized secrets (passwords or passphrases) accepted by an authenticator. It covers only the rules a password must satisfy and how repeated failures are handled, not how the principal is authenticated overall. Use AuthenticationConfig instead when the symbol configures the identity provider, MFA, session timeout or verification level, of which password rules are at most one referenced part. Use ValidationRule instead when a regex, length or range check validates an ordinary data field rather than the composition of a login credential. Use Countermeasure instead when the code implements a general brute-force or credential-stuffing mitigation (IP throttling, CAPTCHA, breached-password screening) not expressed as password composition or account lockout parameters.
evidence: Framework password option blocks such as Django AUTH_PASSWORD_VALIDATORS (MinimumLengthValidator), ASP.NET Identity PasswordOptions/LockoutOptions, or Spring Security password constraint beans.

Identity-provider or infrastructure declarations such as a Keycloak realm passwordPolicy string ('length(12) and upperCase(1) and passwordHistory(5)'), an AWS Cognito PasswordPolicy block, or a Terraform aws_iam_account_password_policy resource.

A password-change or registration routine that tests character-class regexes, compares the new hash against stored previous hashes, and returns messages like 'Password must contain a special character', or a failed-login counter that sets a locked-until timestamp.

distinguish.security.authenticationconfig: the symbol configures the identity provider, MFA, session timeout or verification level, of which password rules are at most one referenced part.
distinguish.security.validationrule: a regex, length or range check validates an ordinary data field rather than the composition of a login credential.
distinguish.security.countermeasure: the code implements a general brute-force or credential-stuffing mitigation (IP throttling, CAPTCHA, breached-password screening) not expressed as password composition or account lockout parameters.

types.title: Permission
types.description: An atomic authorization grant that pairs one action with one named resource at a stated access scope, independent of any particular principal, and is assigned to Roles and checked at enforcement points such as routes, API operations and UI components. It names what may be done. Who holds it, and under what runtime conditions, is captured elsewhere. Use ResourceOperation instead when the symbol declares which operations a SecureResource supports, along with that operation's conditions, rate limits and audit bindings, rather than a grantable entitlement that is assigned to roles. Use Role instead when the symbol is a named bundle of permissions with a privilege level or inheritance, such as 'admin' or 'editor', rather than a single action-on-resource grant. Use InformationRight instead when the grant is bound to a specific actor on an InformationEntity and is qualified by a constraint expression (ABAC), rather than being an actor-independent entitlement handed out via roles. Use PolicyRule instead when the symbol evaluates a condition and yields a permit or deny effect at decision time, rather than naming a static entitlement that the check looks up.
evidence: Permission identifier constants or enum members such as 'orders:read' or 'INVOICE_DELETE', defined in a central permissions file or seeded into a permissions table by migrations or fixtures.

Enforcement annotations or guards that take a permission name, such as @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('report.export')"), @RequiresPermission, a requirePermission('user.update') middleware, or a CASL can('update','Article') rule.
OAuth scope or role-to-permission mapping entries, for example OpenAPI securitySchemes scopes or a YAML/JSON policy file listing the permissions granted to each role.

distinguish.security.resourceoperation: the symbol declares which operations a SecureResource supports, along with that operation's conditions, rate limits and audit bindings, rather than a grantable entitlement that is assigned to roles.
distinguish.security.role: the symbol is a named bundle of permissions with a privilege level or inheritance, such as 'admin' or 'editor', rather than a single action-on-resource grant.
distinguish.security.informationright: the grant is bound to a specific actor on an InformationEntity and is qualified by a constraint expression (ABAC), rather than being an actor-independent entitlement handed out via roles.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the symbol evaluates a condition and yields a permit or deny effect at decision time, rather than naming a static entitlement that the check looks up.

types.title: PolicyAction
types.description: A response step that the enforcement point carries out when a PolicyRule or Condition matches, such as blocking, redirecting, challenging, masking, quarantining, or notifying. It is parameterised by a type and its configuration, and corresponds to an obligation or advice attached to a policy decision rather than to the decision itself. Use PolicyRule instead when the element is the condition-plus-effect unit that yields the permit/deny decision, not the side-effect or response carried out after the decision. Use Countermeasure instead when the element is a standing control or mitigation assessed against a threat, with effectiveness and implementation status, rather than a per-match runtime response. Use AuditConfig instead when the element configures which events are logged and at what verbosity system-wide, rather than a single 'log' or 'alert' step fired by a rule match. Use FieldAccessControl instead when masking or redaction is declared statically for a named data field, independent of any policy rule firing.
evidence: A WAF or gateway rule config whose action field is set to a verb such as block, captcha, challenge, redirect, or count (e.g. AWS WAF Action, Cloudflare firewall action, Envoy RBAC action).
A policy-decision handler that switches on the decision or obligation ID and dispatches to a 403 response, a step-up MFA challenge, a redirect, or a notification sender.
An OPA/Rego or Cedar policy output that returns obligations or advice objects alongside allow/deny (e.g. {"action":"notify","recipient":...}), consumed by enforcement middleware.

distinguish.security.policyrule: the element is the condition-plus-effect unit that yields the permit/deny decision, not the side-effect or response carried out after the decision.
distinguish.security.countermeasure: the element is a standing control or mitigation assessed against a threat, with effectiveness and implementation status, rather than a per-match runtime response.
distinguish.security.auditconfig: the element configures which events are logged and at what verbosity system-wide, rather than a single 'log' or 'alert' step fired by a rule match.
distinguish.security.fieldaccesscontrol: masking or redaction is declared statically for a named data field, independent of any policy rule firing.

types.title: PolicyRule
types.description: A single evaluation unit inside a security policy that pairs one condition predicate over the request context with a decision effect (permit or deny, or indeterminate / not-applicable where the source engine records those outcomes). It may also trigger obligation actions when the condition matches. It is the smallest construct that both tests a condition and yields an access decision. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the element is the named, prioritized container with a target that groups and orders several rules, rather than one condition-plus-effect pair. Use AccessCondition instead when the element is only a field/operator/value predicate that yields true or false and carries no permit/deny effect of its own. Use PolicyAction instead when the element is the response executed after a rule matches (log, alert, redirect, rate-limit, mask), not the decision itself. Use Permission instead when the element is a static grant of an action on a resource assigned to a role, with no runtime condition evaluated to produce a decision.
evidence: A statement in a policy language file with an explicit effect and condition, such as an AWS IAM Statement with "Effect": "Deny" and a Condition block, a Cedar `permit(...) when { ... };` clause, or an OPA Rego `deny[msg] { ... }` rule.

An entry in a rules array of a policy config or Casbin policy file whose fields include a match expression and an effect value (e.g. `p, alice, /reports, GET, allow`, or `{condition: ..., effect: 'deny'}`).
A branch in a policy-evaluator or authorization middleware that tests a predicate on user, resource or request attributes and returns an ALLOW or DENY decision, often with a denial reason string.

distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the element is the named, prioritized container with a target that groups and orders several rules, rather than one condition-plus-effect pair
distinguish.security.accesscondition: the element is only a field/operator/value predicate that yields true or false and carries no permit/deny effect of its own
distinguish.security.policyaction: the element is the response executed after a rule matches (log, alert, redirect, rate-limit, mask), not the decision itself
distinguish.security.permission: the element is a static grant of an action on a resource assigned to a role, with no runtime condition evaluated to produce a decision

types.title: ResourceOperation
types.description: An action declared on a single SecureResource (create, read, approve, export, etc.) that the authorization layer can permit or refuse. It carries the access conditions, rate limits and audit settings that apply whenever an actor invokes that action on that resource, and so forms the verb in a subject-verb-object access decision. Use Permission instead when the element is the grant authorizing a role or actor to perform an action, i.e. who may do it, rather than the action as exposed and guarded on the resource. Use SecureResource instead when the element is the protected API, table, file or service itself rather than one of the actions that can be performed on it. Use PolicyAction instead when the element is the enforcement response a policy rule produces (deny, log, redirect, mask), not the operation an actor requests. Use AccessCondition instead when the element is the field-operator-value predicate that must hold before the operation is allowed, rather than the operation it gates.
evidence: An authorization check naming both a resource type and an action verb, e.g. @PreAuthorize("hasPermission(#id, 'Invoice', 'approve')") or authorize(user, 'export', report).
A per-resource list of actions in an authorization schema or policy file, e.g. an Oso/Cedar/OpenFGA resource block with actions = ["read", "update", "share"].
A controller handler for one verb on one resource wrapped with its own guard, rate-limit and audit-log middleware, e.g. router.post('/orders/:id/approve', requireRole, rateLimit, auditLog, handler).

distinguish.security.permission: the element is the grant authorizing a role or actor to perform an action, i.e. who may do it, rather than the action as exposed and guarded on the resource.
distinguish.security.secureresource: the element is the protected API, table, file or service itself rather than one of the actions that can be performed on it.
distinguish.security.policyaction: the element is the enforcement response a policy rule produces (deny, log, redirect, mask), not the operation an actor requests.
distinguish.security.accesscondition: the element is the field-operator-value predicate that must hold before the operation is allowed, rather than the operation it gates.

types.title: RetentionPolicy
types.description: A data-lifecycle rule for one category of security-relevant data (audit logs, access records, evidence, cryptographic keys) that sets the minimum time the data must be kept, where it is kept, and how it is disposed of once that period ends. Use AuditConfig instead when the element decides which security events are captured, at what verbosity, and which fields are sanitized, rather than how long captured records are kept or how they are destroyed. Use Evidence instead when the element is the retained artifact itself (a log stream, signature, hash or audit trail), not the rule that governs how long it is kept. Use DataClassification instead when the element assigns a sensitivity tier or encryption obligation to data, rather than a retention duration and disposal method. Use AccountabilityRequirement instead when the element states who must prove that an action occurred and whether that proof can be challenged, independent of how long the proof is stored.
evidence: Log-store retention settings scoped to audit or security streams, such as CloudWatch retentionInDays on an audit log group, an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch ILM policy with a delete phase, or Loki retention_period.
An S3, GCS or Azure Blob lifecycle rule on an audit or evidence bucket with expiration or transition-to-archive days, or an object-lock/WORM retention configuration.
A scheduled job or cron task that purges, crypto-shreds or archives audit, access-log or key records older than a configured age, often citing a compliance period such as '7 years' or 'P90D'.

distinguish.security.auditconfig: the element decides which security events are captured, at what verbosity, and which fields are sanitized, rather than how long captured records are kept or how they are destroyed.
distinguish.security.evidence: the element is the retained artifact itself (a log stream, signature, hash or audit trail), not the rule that governs how long it is kept.
distinguish.security.dataclassification: the element assigns a sensitivity tier or encryption obligation to data, rather than a retention duration and disposal method.
distinguish.security.accountabilityrequirement: the element states who must prove that an action occurred and whether that proof can be challenged, independent of how long the proof is stored.

types.title: Role
types.description: A named, assignable grouping of Permissions that actors receive by being assigned to it, rather than by individual grants. It optionally inherits all permissions of a single parent role and carries a privilege tier. Use Actor instead when the element is the principal itself (a user, service account or external system) that holds roles, not the grouping it is assigned to. Use Permission instead when the element is a single action-on-resource grant (e.g. 'orders:delete') rather than a named bundle of such grants. Use Delegation instead when authority is transferred from one specific actor to another, usually time-bounded or revocable, rather than held through standing role membership. Use InformationRight instead when access is granted directly to a named actor on an InformationEntity under a constraint expression, with no intermediate role.
evidence: An enum, constant set or database 'roles' table of role names (e.g. ADMIN, EDITOR, VIEWER) referenced by user-to-role assignment code.
Authorization guards keyed on a role name, such as @RolesAllowed("admin"), @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), requireRole('editor') middleware, or a route/navigation guard checking user.roles.

A configuration or manifest mapping a role name to a permission list and optional parent, e.g. roles.yaml with 'permissions:' and 'inherits:' keys, Keycloak realm/composite roles, or Kubernetes Role/ClusterRole objects.

distinguish.security.actor: the element is the principal itself (a user, service account or external system) that holds roles, not the grouping it is assigned to.
distinguish.security.permission: the element is a single action-on-resource grant (e.g. 'orders:delete') rather than a named bundle of such grants.
distinguish.security.delegation: authority is transferred from one specific actor to another, usually time-bounded or revocable, rather than held through standing role membership.
distinguish.security.informationright: access is granted directly to a named actor on an InformationEntity under a constraint expression, with no intermediate role.

types.title: SecureResource
types.description: A protected object in an access control model — an API, database, file, service, UI area or stream — named as the target of authorization decisions and owning the set of ResourceOperations permitted on it and any FieldAccessControls over its fields. It is the 'object' of a subject-action-object triple, not the grant, rule or operation applied to it. Use InformationEntity instead when the thing protected is a logical information asset (e.g. customer PII) governed by InformationRight grants and classification, independent of the system resource that stores or exposes it. Use ResourceOperation instead when the element is a specific verb (read, approve, export) permitted on the resource rather than the resource itself. Use Permission instead when the element is a grant of an action on a resource assigned to a role, rather than the resource being protected. Use FieldAccessControl instead when the restriction applies to a single field's masking or redaction inside a resource rather than to the resource as a whole.
evidence: A route group, controller or API path prefix wrapped by an authorization guard or middleware (e.g. @PreAuthorize, router.use(requireAuth), [Authorize]) that names the protected resource

A resource identifier string used as the object argument in permission checks (e.g. can(user, 'update', 'invoice'), enforcer.enforce(sub, 'orders', act)) or as a resource entry in a Casbin/OPA/IAM policy file
A database table, bucket or topic declared in an IAM/RLS/ACL configuration (e.g. Postgres row-level security policy, S3 bucket policy, Kafka ACL) restricting which principals may operate on it

distinguish.security.informationentity: the thing protected is a logical information asset (e.g. customer PII) governed by InformationRight grants and classification, independent of the system resource that stores or exposes it
distinguish.security.resourceoperation: the element is a specific verb (read, approve, export) permitted on the resource rather than the resource itself
distinguish.security.permission: the element is a grant of an action on a resource assigned to a role, rather than the resource being protected
distinguish.security.fieldaccesscontrol: the restriction applies to a single field's masking or redaction inside a resource rather than to the resource as a whole

types.title: SecurityConstraints
types.description: An application-scoped container that groups the procedural, workflow-level access constraints (SeparationOfDuty, BindingOfDuty and NeedToKnow rules) applied within a SecurityModel. It holds no predicate or decision logic of its own; its content is the set of duty and purpose constraints it aggregates. Use SeparationOfDuty instead when modelling one specific rule that two tasks or roles must be held by different actors, rather than the collection of all such rules for the application. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the artifact is a prioritized set of evaluable rules with permit/deny effects targeting endpoints, data or roles, rather than a grouping of duty and need-to-know constraints. Use SecurityModel instead when the element is the root security specification for the application, composing authentication, roles, threats, classification and policies, not only the procedural constraints. Use NeedToKnow instead when modelling a single purpose-justification requirement for one resource rather than the grouping container.
evidence: a dedicated configuration block or file (e.g. 'constraints:' or 'duty-rules.yaml') listing separation-of-duty pairs, binding-of-duty tasks and need-to-know resources together
a registry or module (e.g. WorkflowConstraintRegistry, DutyConstraintService) that loads and applies several SoD/BoD/purpose checks to workflow transitions such as request/approve
a documentation section titled e.g. 'Procedural Access Constraints' or 'Segregation of Duties Matrix' enumerating mutually exclusive roles and task-continuity rules for one application

distinguish.security.separationofduty: modelling one specific rule that two tasks or roles must be held by different actors, rather than the collection of all such rules for the application
distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the artifact is a prioritized set of evaluable rules with permit/deny effects targeting endpoints, data or roles, rather than a grouping of duty and need-to-know constraints
distinguish.security.securitymodel: the element is the root security specification for the application, composing authentication, roles, threats, classification and policies, not only the procedural constraints
distinguish.security.needtoknow: modelling a single purpose-justification requirement for one resource rather than the grouping container

types.title: SecurityModel
types.description: A root container element that groups every security element (actors, authentication configuration, roles, permissions, secure resources, policies, constraints, threats, data classification and accountability requirements) defined for exactly one application or bounded context. There is one instance per application; it names that application and its access control paradigm. Use SecurityConstraints instead when the container groups only procedural constraints (SeparationOfDuty, BindingOfDuty, NeedToKnow) and not the whole security posture of the application. Use SecurityPolicy instead when the element is a single prioritized set of evaluation rules targeting particular resources or operations, not the umbrella specification for the application. Use AuthenticationConfig instead when the code or config only sets up identity verification (provider, MFA, session timeout) and does not also cover authorization, threats or policies.
evidence: A top-level security configuration entry point for one application (e.g. a Spring class annotated @EnableWebSecurity, a NestJS SecurityModule, or a root security.yaml/policy bundle) that wires together the authentication provider, role/permission definitions and access policies.

A central registry module that exports the application's role, permission and resource-action maps together with the authorization strategy in use (e.g. a Casbin model file declaring RBAC/ABAC, or an OPA bundle manifest scoped to one service).

A per-application security architecture or threat-model document (system security plan, STRIDE worksheet, security.md) that lists actors, protected resources, threats, data classifications and controls under a single version number.

distinguish.security.securityconstraints: the container groups only procedural constraints (SeparationOfDuty, BindingOfDuty, NeedToKnow) and not the whole security posture of the application.
distinguish.security.securitypolicy: the element is a single prioritized set of evaluation rules targeting particular resources or operations, not the umbrella specification for the application.
distinguish.security.authenticationconfig: the code or config only sets up identity verification (provider, MFA, session timeout) and does not also cover authorization, threats or policies.

types.title: SecurityPolicy
types.description: A named, prioritized container of ordered PolicyRules that together produce an access-control decision for one category of target (endpoint, service, data, user, role or resource). When several policies match, they are evaluated by priority. It corresponds to an XACML Policy, not to a single rule, condition or enforcement action. Use PolicyRule instead when the element is a single condition-plus-effect (permit/deny) evaluation unit rather than a named, prioritized grouping of such units. Use PolicyAction instead when the element is the enforcement response (deny, log, rate-limit, mask, etc.) executed when a rule matches, not the policy that contains the rules. Use SecurityConstraints instead when the element groups procedural SeparationOfDuty, BindingOfDuty or NeedToKnow constraints rather than ordered access-decision rules. Use SecurityModel instead when the element is the application-wide root aggregating authentication, roles, threats and all policies, rather than one targeted policy.
evidence: A named policy file or block (OPA/Rego package, Cedar policy set, XACML <Policy>, Casbin policy, AWS IAM policy document) containing multiple allow/deny rules
A policy registry or middleware that loads named policies with an explicit priority, order or weight and evaluates them in sequence against a request
A configuration entry that pairs a list of rules with a target selector (route pattern, service name, data type) and carries an enabled or disabled flag

distinguish.security.policyrule: the element is a single condition-plus-effect (permit/deny) evaluation unit rather than a named, prioritized grouping of such units
distinguish.security.policyaction: the element is the enforcement response (deny, log, rate-limit, mask, etc.) executed when a rule matches, not the policy that contains the rules
distinguish.security.securityconstraints: the element groups procedural SeparationOfDuty, BindingOfDuty or NeedToKnow constraints rather than ordered access-decision rules
distinguish.security.securitymodel: the element is the application-wide root aggregating authentication, roles, threats and all policies, rather than one targeted policy

types.title: SeparationOfDuty
types.description: A procedural access-control constraint requiring that two or more conflicting tasks or roles in a workflow (e.g., request and approve, initiate and authorize) are held or performed by different actors. It may be static, where the roles are mutually exclusive in assignment, or dynamic, where the same subject is barred from executing a later step on an item it acted on earlier. Use BindingOfDuty instead when the rule requires the same actor who started a task to also complete it, rather than forbidding the same actor from performing both steps. Use PolicyRule instead when the logic is a generic condition-plus-effect evaluation (permit/deny) not specifically about preventing one subject from holding or exercising conflicting duties. Use Role instead when the thing being modelled is the named permission bundle itself rather than the exclusion constraint between bundles. Use NeedToKnow instead when access is restricted by the actor's declared purpose rather than by conflict with another task or role the actor holds.
evidence: An approval handler that rejects the request when approver.id equals the request's createdBy/submittedBy field, often with an error like 'cannot approve your own request'.
A role-assignment validator or config list of mutually exclusive role pairs (e.g., 'conflictingRoles: [payment_creator, payment_approver]') checked when granting roles.

A maker-checker or four-eyes workflow configuration requiring a distinct second user to authorize a step, such as a minimum-distinct-approvers setting or a branch-protection rule that disallows self-approval.

distinguish.security.bindingofduty: the rule requires the same actor who started a task to also complete it, rather than forbidding the same actor from performing both steps.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the logic is a generic condition-plus-effect evaluation (permit/deny) not specifically about preventing one subject from holding or exercising conflicting duties.
distinguish.security.role: the thing being modelled is the named permission bundle itself rather than the exclusion constraint between bundles.
distinguish.security.needtoknow: access is restricted by the actor's declared purpose rather than by conflict with another task or role the actor holds.

types.title: Threat
types.description: A threat-model entry naming a potential adverse event or attack technique (e.g., credential stuffing, SQL injection, privilege escalation) against an identified asset, rated by likelihood and impact. It records what could go wrong and how badly. It does not record the control that prevents it or the principal who carries it out. Use Countermeasure instead when the item is the control, check or mitigation technique that reduces a threat's likelihood or impact, such as input sanitisation, CSRF tokens or a WAF rule, rather than the attack itself. Use Actor instead when the item is the principal or adversary (human, service, external entity) whose identity and trust level are modelled, rather than the adverse event that principal might cause. Use PolicyRule instead when the item is an evaluable condition-plus-effect rule that permits or denies requests, even if it was written in response to a threat. Use ValidationRule instead when the item is a concrete pattern, range or length constraint on a field that blocks malicious input, rather than the injection or tampering risk it guards against.
evidence: A threat-model artefact checked into the repository that lists threat entries with likelihood/impact or risk ratings, such as an OWASP Threat Dragon JSON file, a Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool .tm7 file, or a threat-model.md with a STRIDE table.
Code comments, ADRs or security docs that cite CWE, CAPEC or OWASP Top 10 identifiers (e.g., '// guards against CWE-89 SQL injection') adjacent to the code they protect.
Security test cases or abuse-case specs named after attack scenarios (e.g., test_rejects_sql_injection, it('blocks replayed JWT')) that assert a specific attack fails.

distinguish.security.countermeasure: the item is the control, check or mitigation technique that reduces a threat's likelihood or impact, such as input sanitisation, CSRF tokens or a WAF rule, rather than the attack itself.
distinguish.security.actor: the item is the principal or adversary (human, service, external entity) whose identity and trust level are modelled, rather than the adverse event that principal might cause.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the item is an evaluable condition-plus-effect rule that permits or denies requests, even if it was written in response to a threat.
distinguish.security.validationrule: the item is a concrete pattern, range or length constraint on a field that blocks malicious input, rather than the injection or tampering risk it guards against.

types.title: ValidationRule
types.description: A single input-validation constraint (regex pattern, numeric range, length limit, allowed-value list or custom check) that the value of a protected field or request attribute must satisfy, with a violation message and severity. It accepts or rejects the value itself and does not decide who may access it. Use AccessCondition instead when the predicate tests a request-context attribute (user, role, time, IP) to decide whether the request is authorized, rather than checking that a supplied value is well-formed. Use FieldAccessControl instead when the concern is how a field's value is masked, redacted or hidden from unauthorized principals, rather than which values are acceptable. Use PolicyRule instead when the unit produces a permit/deny decision with optional obligations, rather than a pass/fail check with a violation message. Use PasswordPolicy instead when the constraints are the complete credential complexity, rotation and lockout regime, rather than one individual check that such a policy might use.
evidence: Bean Validation, Pydantic, Joi or Zod constraints such as @Pattern, @Size, constr(regex=...) or .max() declared on security-sensitive DTO fields like email, account number, token or redirect URL.
Input-sanitization middleware or allowlist regexes that reject a request with HTTP 400/422 and a specific error message when a parameter fails the check.

A validator function or schema entry named for the check (e.g. validateIban, SAFE_FILENAME_RE) referenced from an access-control or field-protection layer, with configurable severity or logging on failure.

distinguish.security.accesscondition: the predicate tests a request-context attribute (user, role, time, IP) to decide whether the request is authorized, rather than checking that a supplied value is well-formed.
distinguish.security.fieldaccesscontrol: the concern is how a field's value is masked, redacted or hidden from unauthorized principals, rather than which values are acceptable.
distinguish.security.policyrule: the unit produces a permit/deny decision with optional obligations, rather than a pass/fail check with a violation message.
distinguish.security.passwordpolicy: the constraints are the complete credential complexity, rotation and lockout regime, rather than one individual check that such a policy might use.

layers.name: Application Layer
layers.scope: Models the application architecture: application components (deployable modules, classes and services), the application functions and processes that describe their internal behaviour, the application services and interfaces through which that behaviour is exposed, application events and interactions, collaborations between components, and the data objects they process (ArchiMate 3.2 application layer). This is the default home for ordinary application code structure; more specific layers apply only when a symbol is itself an API contract, a data schema, a persistence object, a UI element, telemetry, security logic or a test asset. Modelling rules: components and collaborations are assigned to the functions, processes and interactions they perform (assigned-to), and a collaboration aggregates its components and nested collaborations. A component provides the interfaces its own code declares and is assigned to an interface it only handles; an interface is assigned to the services it offers. Functions, processes and interactions realize application services; a component may realize one directly, as a shortcut through the behaviour assigned to it. Services serve the components, functions, processes and interactions that use them. Functions, processes, interactions, events and services access data objects, and so do components, unlike in the business layer, because a component is code that holds and passes data; interfaces and collaborations do not. Functions, components and events also access the data-model object schemas and schema definitions they read and write, such as entity classes, directly rather than through a data object. Components, functions and services likewise access the data-store collections and views they read and write. Events trigger processes, interactions and functions (unlike a business function, an application function can be an event handler), and behaviour raises events. A hand-off between behaviours is flows-to; depends-on means one element needs another to work, and is never used where assigned-to, accesses, serves or triggers says it. Across layers, application processes and functions realize the business processes and functions they automate, and application services realize business services and product features and capabilities and, with the behaviour that realizes them, carry the link to motivation (realize goals, satisfy requirements and constraints, deliver value).

types.title: ApplicationCollaboration
types.description: An active structure element that names a grouping of two or more application components (or nested collaborations) which jointly perform collective behaviour. It is a logical or configured grouping of independently deployable parts, not a deployable unit or behaviour in its own right. Use ApplicationComponent instead when the symbol is a single modular, deployable unit, even if it internally composes sub-modules or calls other services. Use ApplicationInteraction instead when the symbol describes the joint behaviour itself, such as a message exchange, saga step sequence or protocol between components, rather than the group of participants. Use ApplicationProcess instead when the symbol is an ordered sequence of steps that achieves a result, even if those steps span several components. Use ApplicationService instead when the symbol is the externally exposed functionality the group offers rather than the group of participating components.
evidence: a saga or choreography definition (e.g. Temporal/Camunda workflow config, event-flow manifest) that enumerates several named participating services under one collective name
a docker-compose file, Helm umbrella chart or Kubernetes namespace that groups multiple separately built services as one named subsystem delivering a shared capability
an architecture document, ADR or C4 diagram boundary that names a set of cooperating services (e.g. 'checkout subsystem: cart, pricing, payment') as a unit

distinguish.application.applicationcomponent: the symbol is a single modular, deployable unit, even if it internally composes sub-modules or calls other services
distinguish.application.applicationinteraction: the symbol describes the joint behaviour itself, such as a message exchange, saga step sequence or protocol between components, rather than the group of participants
distinguish.application.applicationprocess: the symbol is an ordered sequence of steps that achieves a result, even if those steps span several components
distinguish.application.applicationservice: the symbol is the externally exposed functionality the group offers rather than the group of participating components

types.title: ApplicationComponent
types.description: An active structural application element that encapsulates a cohesive set of application behaviour and data behind its interfaces and can be built, deployed, or replaced as a unit, such as a service, module, package, or dependency-injected class with its own responsibility. It is the thing that performs behaviour, not the behaviour itself. Use ApplicationFunction instead when the symbol is a unit of behaviour, such as a method, function, or handler body, that a component performs, rather than the structural unit that owns that behaviour. Use ApplicationInterface instead when the symbol is only the access point through which a component's services are reached, such as a controller endpoint set, client stub, or exported port, rather than the implementing unit. Use ApplicationCollaboration instead when the symbol represents a grouping of several components that work together, such as a system-of-services or a composite deployment, rather than a single replaceable unit. Use DataObject instead when the symbol is a passive data structure, such as a DTO, record, or entity without behaviour of its own, that components read or write.
evidence: a module, package, or service directory with its own build manifest or deployment descriptor (package.json, pom.xml, go.mod, Dockerfile, Kubernetes Deployment)
a class annotated or registered as a managed component in a DI container (@Component, @Service, @Injectable, Module providers) whose instances are injected into other classes
an entry in docker-compose, Helm charts, or an architecture/service catalogue (e.g. Backstage catalog-info.yaml) naming the unit as a separately deployable service or library

distinguish.application.applicationfunction: the symbol is a unit of behaviour, such as a method, function, or handler body, that a component performs, rather than the structural unit that owns that behaviour
distinguish.application.applicationinterface: the symbol is only the access point through which a component's services are reached, such as a controller endpoint set, client stub, or exported port, rather than the implementing unit
distinguish.application.applicationcollaboration: the symbol represents a grouping of several components that work together, such as a system-of-services or a composite deployment, rather than a single replaceable unit
distinguish.application.dataobject: the symbol is a passive data structure, such as a DTO, record, or entity without behaviour of its own, that components read or write

types.title: ApplicationEvent
types.description: An application behavior element representing a named, instantaneous occurrence of a state change that an application component emits or receives, and that triggers or is consumed by other application behavior. It has no duration and performs no work itself; reacting is done by processes, functions or interactions. Use DataObject instead when the symbol is a data structure that components read, store or transform, and it is never published, emitted or subscribed to as a notification of something that happened. Use ApplicationProcess instead when the symbol is the handler, listener body or workflow that runs in response to the event, or that produces it, rather than the occurrence itself. Use ApplicationService instead when the symbol is an exposed capability that consumers invoke or subscribe to, such as an event stream offered as a service, rather than one specific kind of occurrence. Use ApplicationInteraction instead when the symbol describes the joint publish-subscribe or messaging behavior between two or more components rather than a single event type exchanged within it.
evidence: A class or record named in the past tense (e.g. OrderPlaced, UserRegisteredEvent) that extends a framework event base type such as Spring ApplicationEvent or a DomainEvent marker, and is passed to a publisher (eventPublisher.publish, mediator.Publish, bus.emit).
A string or constant event or topic name used in both an emit or publish call and a subscription (emitter.on('invoice.paid'), @EventListener, @KafkaListener(topics=...), RabbitMQ routing key).
A message entry in an AsyncAPI document, event catalog or CloudEvents type registry that declares the event's name and payload and lists its producers and consumers.

distinguish.application.dataobject: the symbol is a data structure that components read, store or transform, and it is never published, emitted or subscribed to as a notification of something that happened.
distinguish.application.applicationprocess: the symbol is the handler, listener body or workflow that runs in response to the event, or that produces it, rather than the occurrence itself.
distinguish.application.applicationservice: the symbol is an exposed capability that consumers invoke or subscribe to, such as an event stream offered as a service, rather than one specific kind of occurrence.
distinguish.application.applicationinteraction: the symbol describes the joint publish-subscribe or messaging behavior between two or more components rather than a single event type exchanged within it.

types.title: ApplicationFunction
types.description: A unit of automated behavior performed by a single application component, grouped by the kind of work or capability it covers rather than by execution order or trigger, and invoked from inside the system rather than offered as a contract to external consumers. It may be an event handler that an ApplicationEvent triggers, such as a message listener or subscriber callback. Use ApplicationProcess instead when the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps leading to a defined operational result, such as a workflow, saga, pipeline or multi-step job, rather than a capability grouping with no inherent order. Use ApplicationService instead when the behavior is the externally visible, consumer-facing offering, such as a public service-layer method or endpoint-backed capability. The function is the internal behavior that realizes it. Use ApplicationInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more components, such as a request-reply exchange or a publish-subscribe handshake, rather than by one component alone. Use ApplicationComponent instead when the symbol is the deployable or replaceable structural unit, such as a module, package or service class, that owns behavior, rather than the behavior itself.
evidence: A class or module of internal, unexported or package-private methods grouped around one concern (e.g. PricingCalculator.computeDiscount, TaxRules.apply) whose callers are other classes in the same codebase rather than route handlers or external clients.

A domain or utility function, such as validation, scoring, matching or transformation logic, that is reused by several workflows or service methods and is not registered on any HTTP router, message listener or public API surface.

A stored procedure, rule-engine rule or helper invoked through an internal call graph, documented as 'computes', 'validates' or 'derives' something, with no ordering of steps and no direct external trigger.

distinguish.application.applicationprocess: the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps leading to a defined operational result, such as a workflow, saga, pipeline or multi-step job, rather than a capability grouping with no inherent order.
distinguish.application.applicationservice: the behavior is the externally visible, consumer-facing offering, such as a public service-layer method or endpoint-backed capability. The function is the internal behavior that realizes it.
distinguish.application.applicationinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more components, such as a request-reply exchange or a publish-subscribe handshake, rather than by one component alone.
distinguish.application.applicationcomponent: the symbol is the deployable or replaceable structural unit, such as a module, package or service class, that owns behavior, rather than the behavior itself.

types.title: ApplicationInteraction
types.description: A unit of application behaviour performed jointly by two or more application components acting as a collaboration, which no single participant completes alone, such as a saga, a multi-service choreography or a handshake protocol spanning both sides of an exchange. Use ApplicationProcess instead when the ordered sequence of steps is executed by a single application component, even if it calls other components as dependencies. Use ApplicationCollaboration instead when the symbol represents the structural grouping of cooperating components rather than the behaviour they jointly perform. Use ApplicationService instead when the symbol is the externally exposed, consumer-facing behaviour offered to callers rather than the internal joint behaviour that realizes it. Use ApplicationEvent instead when the symbol is the message, notification or state change exchanged between participants rather than the cooperative behaviour that produces and handles it.
evidence: a saga or choreography definition (e.g. Temporal/Camunda workflow, Axon saga, Step Functions state machine) whose steps invoke and compensate operations in several distinct services

a matched producer and consumer pair across separate deployable modules bound to the same topic, queue or RPC contract and documented as one flow (e.g. an AsyncAPI channel or sequence diagram naming multiple services)
a coordinator implementing a multi-party protocol such as two-phase commit, distributed lock negotiation or a client-server handshake where both sides' logic is required to complete the exchange

distinguish.application.applicationprocess: the ordered sequence of steps is executed by a single application component, even if it calls other components as dependencies.
distinguish.application.applicationcollaboration: the symbol represents the structural grouping of cooperating components rather than the behaviour they jointly perform.
distinguish.application.applicationservice: the symbol is the externally exposed, consumer-facing behaviour offered to callers rather than the internal joint behaviour that realizes it.
distinguish.application.applicationevent: the symbol is the message, notification or state change exchanged between participants rather than the cooperative behaviour that produces and handles it.

types.title: ApplicationInterface
types.description: An active-structure access point owned by an application component or collaboration, such as a mounted controller, gRPC server binding, GraphQL endpoint or message-channel listener, through which that component's application services are reachable by users or other components over a specific application-level protocol. It is the channel itself, not the behaviour offered through it and not the formal contract document describing it. Use ApplicationService instead when the element describes the externally visible behaviour or functionality offered, such as 'order placement', independent of the endpoint, protocol or channel through which it is reached. Use ApplicationComponent instead when the symbol is the deployable or replaceable module, service or package as a whole, rather than one of the access points it provides. Use ApplicationInteraction instead when the symbol represents joint behaviour carried out by two or more components exchanging messages, rather than the single access point one component offers. Use ApplicationFunction instead when the symbol is internal handler or business logic invoked behind the endpoint, rather than the endpoint binding or adapter itself.
evidence: A controller or router class that groups route handlers under a base path and is mounted on a web server, such as a Spring @RestController with @RequestMapping("/orders"), an Express Router passed to app.use('/orders', ...), or a FastAPI APIRouter included in the app.
