A gRPC servicer or GraphQL schema/resolver set registered on a server at startup, such as add_OrderServiceServicer_to_server(...) or an Apollo server exposing /graphql.

A message or socket entry point bound to a named channel in code or config, such as a @RabbitListener(queues="orders") consumer, an AMQP queue binding in application.yml, or a WebSocket endpoint handler (@ServerEndpoint, socket.io namespace).

distinguish.application.applicationservice: the element describes the externally visible behaviour or functionality offered, such as 'order placement', independent of the endpoint, protocol or channel through which it is reached.
distinguish.application.applicationcomponent: the symbol is the deployable or replaceable module, service or package as a whole, rather than one of the access points it provides.
distinguish.application.applicationinteraction: the symbol represents joint behaviour carried out by two or more components exchanging messages, rather than the single access point one component offers.
distinguish.application.applicationfunction: the symbol is internal handler or business logic invoked behind the endpoint, rather than the endpoint binding or adapter itself.

types.title: ApplicationProcess
types.description: An internal behaviour element of an application component consisting of a fixed, ordered series of steps (calls, transformations, state transitions) that runs from a start trigger to a defined end result. What sets it apart is that the sequence and the outcome are explicit, as in a workflow, saga, pipeline or multi-step orchestration method, rather than a grouping of related capabilities. Use ApplicationFunction instead when the behaviour is a cohesive grouping of capability, such as a module of related operations or a single-purpose routine, with no meaningful step order or defined end-to-end outcome. Use ApplicationService instead when the symbol is the externally consumable entry point or contract (a service method or endpoint offered to consumers) rather than the internal step sequence that fulfils it. Use ApplicationInteraction instead when the ordered behaviour is jointly performed by two or more components, for example a choreographed exchange, and cannot be attributed to a single component. Use ApplicationEvent instead when the symbol represents the occurrence or state change that starts or ends the sequence (an event class or message type), not the steps themselves.
evidence: A workflow, saga or state-machine definition (e.g. Temporal/Camunda/Step Functions workflow, Spring State Machine, a Saga class) declaring ordered steps or states with transitions

An orchestration method that calls several functions or services in a fixed sequence with intermediate results passed between steps and a final result or status returned (e.g. processOrder(): validate → reserve → charge → ship)

A pipeline or job definition (ETL job, batch Step/Job configuration, chain of handlers/middleware registered in order) that is started by a trigger such as a scheduled job, a message consumer or an event handler

distinguish.application.applicationfunction: the behaviour is a cohesive grouping of capability, such as a module of related operations or a single-purpose routine, with no meaningful step order or defined end-to-end outcome
distinguish.application.applicationservice: the symbol is the externally consumable entry point or contract (a service method or endpoint offered to consumers) rather than the internal step sequence that fulfils it
distinguish.application.applicationinteraction: the ordered behaviour is jointly performed by two or more components, for example a choreographed exchange, and cannot be attributed to a single component
distinguish.application.applicationevent: the symbol represents the occurrence or state change that starts or ends the sequence (an event class or message type), not the steps themselves

types.title: ApplicationService
types.description: An externally visible unit of application behavior that a component, function, process or interaction makes available to consumers (users, business processes, or other components) as a named set of operations, defined by what it offers rather than how it is implemented or accessed. Use ApplicationFunction instead when the behavior is internal to a component, such as a private helper, mapper or validation routine, and is not offered as a named capability to callers outside that component. Use ApplicationInterface instead when the symbol is the access point or binding through which a service is reached, such as an HTTP controller, gRPC endpoint, WebSocket handler or message listener, carrying a specific protocol. Use ApplicationComponent instead when the symbol is the deployable or replaceable structural unit (module, package, microservice, class as a unit of deployment) that performs or realizes behavior, rather than the behavior it exposes. Use ApplicationProcess instead when the symbol is an ordered sequence of steps, such as a saga, workflow or orchestrator method, that achieves a result rather than an offered capability.
evidence: A service interface or abstract contract, such as IOrderService or a gRPC 'service' block in a .proto file, whose operations are injected into or called from controllers, handlers or other modules
A class annotated @Service, @Injectable or registered in a DI container whose public methods are invoked across module or component boundaries rather than only within its own package

A queue consumer, scheduled batch job or event subscriber documented or configured to fulfil requests from other systems under a named capability, for example a 'payment-processing' worker bound in messaging or cron configuration

distinguish.application.applicationfunction: the behavior is internal to a component, such as a private helper, mapper or validation routine, and is not offered as a named capability to callers outside that component
distinguish.application.applicationinterface: the symbol is the access point or binding through which a service is reached, such as an HTTP controller, gRPC endpoint, WebSocket handler or message listener, carrying a specific protocol
distinguish.application.applicationcomponent: the symbol is the deployable or replaceable structural unit (module, package, microservice, class as a unit of deployment) that performs or realizes behavior, rather than the behavior it exposes
distinguish.application.applicationprocess: the symbol is an ordered sequence of steps, such as a saga, workflow or orchestrator method, that achieves a result rather than an offered capability

types.title: DataObject
types.description: A passive application element: a code-level data structure (class, record, struct, type alias or message payload) whose purpose is to hold state that application components, functions and services create, read, transform or pass along, and which performs no application behavior beyond trivial accessors, constructors or self-validation. Use ApplicationComponent instead when the class encapsulates substantive behavior or dependencies (injected collaborators, business logic, I/O) and acts as a modular, replaceable unit rather than as a carrier of state. Use ApplicationEvent instead when the structure represents the occurrence of a state change that is published or dispatched to trigger reactive behavior, rather than data that is merely accessed; an event class's separate payload type remains a data object. Use ApplicationInterface instead when the type defines an access point (method contract, endpoint binding, client stub) through which a service is invoked, rather than the data exchanged through it. Use data-model ObjectSchema instead when the structure is a persisted entity or ORM model, or its shape is published as a schema (a JSON Schema, an OpenAPI component, a validation model that serializes to one); the object schema may then realize the data object.
evidence: A class, record, struct or dataclass consisting mainly of fields with getters/setters or immutable properties (e.g. Python @dataclass, Java record, Lombok @Data, C# record, TypeScript interface or type alias) and no injected dependencies.
The type appears as a parameter or return type in signatures of service, handler or function methods, e.g. names ending in Dto, Command, Request, Result, Model or ValueObject.

Instances are constructed, mapped (e.g. via a mapper or serializer) and mutated by other classes, while the type itself carries no ORM table mapping, OpenAPI schema annotation or UI binding that would place it in a more specific layer.

distinguish.application.applicationcomponent: the class encapsulates substantive behavior or dependencies (injected collaborators, business logic, I/O) and acts as a modular, replaceable unit rather than as a carrier of state.
distinguish.application.applicationevent: the structure represents the occurrence of a state change that is published or dispatched to trigger reactive behavior, rather than data that is merely accessed; an event class's separate payload type remains a data object.
distinguish.application.applicationinterface: the type defines an access point (method contract, endpoint binding, client stub) through which a service is invoked, rather than the data exchanged through it.

layers.name: Technology Layer
layers.scope: Models the infrastructure and platform the application runs on: nodes and devices, system software and runtimes, frameworks, communication networks and paths, technology services, interfaces, functions and processes, and the artifacts that are deployed to them (ArchiMate 3.2 technology layer). Package manifests, container images, deployment descriptors and infrastructure-as-code are the usual evidence. Modelling rules: nodes compose their devices, system software, interfaces and the artifacts deployed to them; nodes and system software are assigned to the functions and processes they perform, and a collaboration aggregates the nodes, system software and nested collaborations that cooperate in it and is assigned to its interactions. System software provides the interfaces it declares; an interface is assigned to the technology services it offers and serves the behaviour that uses it. Functions, processes and interactions realize technology services, and a node, system software, collaboration, path or network may realize one directly; a hand-off between behaviours is flows-to; events trigger behaviour, behaviour and services raise events, and structure does not trigger. Artifacts are passive: behaviour and system software access them, and they realize the system software they install and the application components they package, such as a container image. A communication network realizes the paths over it, and networks and paths connect the nodes and devices on them; other elements reach a network through the node they run on. Technology services serve nodes, other services and the application (components, services and functions); a node, device or system software may serve an application component directly as a shortcut for hosting it. Technology reaches the business layer through the application layer. Services carry the link to motivation: they realize goals and software capabilities and satisfy requirements; structure satisfies requirements, constraints and principles. Other layers reach technology in two ways: platform services serve the API, UX, APM, navigation and data-store elements that use them, and an element built on or run by a software product depends on that system software (a data-store database also depends on its node).

types.title: Artifact
types.description: A passive, physical unit of data, such as a file, container image, package, archive, script or configuration document, that is produced by a build or authoring process and is stored, deployed onto, or read by nodes and system software. It is identified by a name or path, can usually be versioned or hashed, and performs no behavior itself. Use Node instead when the thing is the running execution environment, such as a container instance, VM or cluster, rather than the image, package or file that is deployed onto it. Use SystemSoftware instead when the thing is the installed platform software providing an execution or storage environment, such as a PostgreSQL engine, Docker daemon or Kafka broker, rather than a distributable binary, image or config file of it. Use TechnologyProcess instead when the subject is the sequence of steps executed, such as a build, deploy or backup job, rather than the pipeline definition file or the outputs it produces. Use TechnologyService instead when the subject is the externally exposed infrastructure capability, such as object storage or a message queue, rather than the deployable unit that realizes it.
evidence: a Dockerfile, or an image reference with registry/name:tag in a docker-compose, Kubernetes or Helm manifest, that is built and pushed or pulled for deployment
a build output declared in a manifest or build script, such as a package.json 'main'/'bin', Maven <packaging>jar</packaging>, a setup.py wheel, or a Gradle task producing a .war/.zip

a configuration or deployment file copied into an image or mounted at runtime, such as application.yaml, nginx.conf, a Kubernetes ConfigMap, a .env template, or a Terraform module consumed by a deployment

distinguish.technology.node: the thing is the running execution environment, such as a container instance, VM or cluster, rather than the image, package or file that is deployed onto it
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the thing is the installed platform software providing an execution or storage environment, such as a PostgreSQL engine, Docker daemon or Kafka broker, rather than a distributable binary, image or config file of it
distinguish.technology.technologyprocess: the subject is the sequence of steps executed, such as a build, deploy or backup job, rather than the pipeline definition file or the outputs it produces
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the subject is the externally exposed infrastructure capability, such as object storage or a message queue, rather than the deployable unit that realizes it

types.title: CommunicationNetwork
types.description: A technology active structure element representing a physical or virtual network infrastructure, such as a LAN, VPC, subnet, overlay, VPN or the public internet, that carries, routes and delivers data among any number of attached nodes and devices. It is identified by an address space or network membership rather than by a specific pair of endpoints. Use Path instead when the element is a logical communication channel between specific named nodes (e.g. service A calls database B over TCP) rather than the shared network infrastructure the traffic travels over. Use Device instead when the element is a physical network appliance such as a router, switch or firewall box (deviceType network-device) rather than the network it forms or joins. Use Node instead when the element is a computational resource that hosts software, such as a VM, container or cluster attached to the network, rather than the network itself. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is a consumable networking capability offered through an interface, such as managed DNS, a load-balancing service or a CDN, rather than the connectivity fabric.
evidence: An infrastructure-as-code resource that declares a network or address space, such as Terraform aws_vpc, aws_subnet, google_compute_network or azurerm_virtual_network, with a cidr_block or address_prefixes value.
A top-level `networks:` entry in a docker-compose file, or a `docker network create` command, that services attach to by name.
A VPN or overlay configuration such as a WireGuard [Interface]/[Peer] file, an OpenVPN .conf, or a CNI plugin config (Calico, Flannel) that defines a network range shared by multiple hosts.

distinguish.technology.path: the element is a logical communication channel between specific named nodes (e.g. service A calls database B over TCP) rather than the shared network infrastructure the traffic travels over.
distinguish.technology.device: the element is a physical network appliance such as a router, switch or firewall box (deviceType network-device) rather than the network it forms or joins.
distinguish.technology.node: the element is a computational resource that hosts software, such as a VM, container or cluster attached to the network, rather than the network itself.
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is a consumable networking capability offered through an interface, such as managed DNS, a load-balancing service or a CDN, rather than the connectivity fabric.

types.title: Device
types.description: A physical, tangible piece of hardware with its own processing or storage capability (such as a server chassis, workstation, router, storage array, phone, or embedded board) onto which system software and artifacts are installed or deployed. Virtual or logical compute resources and the software running on the hardware are excluded. Use Node instead when the resource is virtual or logical (a VM, container, Kubernetes cluster, or cloud instance whose hardware is not identified), or when hardware and its system software are modelled together as one hosting unit. Use SystemSoftware instead when the element is the operating system, firmware runtime, DBMS, or other platform software installed on the hardware rather than the hardware itself. Use CommunicationNetwork instead when the element is the LAN, WAN, VPN, or wireless segment that connects devices, rather than an individual router, switch, or access point. Use TechnologyCollaboration instead when the element is an aggregate of several devices or nodes acting together, such as a rack of servers forming a cluster.
evidence: Hardware inventory or provisioning records (Ansible inventory host_vars, MAAS/Tinkerbell/Ironic hardware entries, CMDB exports) listing a serial number, MAC address, rack location, or hardware model for a named machine.
IoT device registry declarations such as Terraform aws_iot_thing or azurerm_iothub device resources, Azure IoT device twins, or device provisioning certificates bound to a physical unit.

Firmware or OS build configuration that targets a specific physical board or handset, e.g. platformio.ini 'board = esp32dev', a Yocto MACHINE setting, a device tree file, or an MDM enrollment profile for mobile devices.

distinguish.technology.node: the resource is virtual or logical (a VM, container, Kubernetes cluster, or cloud instance whose hardware is not identified), or when hardware and its system software are modelled together as one hosting unit.
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the element is the operating system, firmware runtime, DBMS, or other platform software installed on the hardware rather than the hardware itself.
distinguish.technology.communicationnetwork: the element is the LAN, WAN, VPN, or wireless segment that connects devices, rather than an individual router, switch, or access point.
distinguish.technology.technologycollaboration: the element is an aggregate of several devices or nodes acting together, such as a rack of servers forming a cluster.

types.title: Node
types.description: A computational resource, physical or virtualized, that acts as a deployment target on which system software runs and artifacts are deployed for execution, such as a virtual machine, a running container instance, a Kubernetes cluster, or a provisioned server host. It is identified by being the place where something is hosted, not by its hardware form or by the platform software installed on it. Use Device instead when the element is a specific piece of physical hardware (server chassis, workstation, phone, IoT sensor, storage appliance) described by its hardware form rather than by its role as a hosting environment. Use SystemSoftware instead when the element is the platform software itself (operating system, container runtime such as containerd or Docker Engine, DBMS, message broker) rather than the machine or instance it runs on. Use TechnologyCollaboration instead when the element is an aggregate of separately modelled nodes or devices that jointly perform behaviour (a replica set, a cache cluster, a service mesh) and each member is modelled in its own right. Use Artifact instead when the element is the deployable package or image (container image, JAR, Helm chart, VM image) rather than the running instance or host that executes it.
evidence: Infrastructure-as-code resources that provision compute, such as Terraform aws_instance, google_compute_instance, azurerm_linux_virtual_machine, or aws_eks_cluster blocks
A services entry in docker-compose.yml, or a Kubernetes Pod/Deployment/StatefulSet spec, that names the container instance on which an image is run
A deployment target listed in an Ansible inventory, Helm/kubectl context, or CI deploy step (hostnames, cluster names, environment hosts) to which build outputs are shipped

distinguish.technology.device: the element is a specific piece of physical hardware (server chassis, workstation, phone, IoT sensor, storage appliance) described by its hardware form rather than by its role as a hosting environment
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the element is the platform software itself (operating system, container runtime such as containerd or Docker Engine, DBMS, message broker) rather than the machine or instance it runs on
distinguish.technology.technologycollaboration: the element is an aggregate of separately modelled nodes or devices that jointly perform behaviour (a replica set, a cache cluster, a service mesh) and each member is modelled in its own right
distinguish.technology.artifact: the element is the deployable package or image (container image, JAR, Helm chart, VM image) rather than the running instance or host that executes it

types.title: Path
types.description: A logical communication link between two or more specific nodes or devices over which they exchange data, independent of the physical medium that carries it, such as a service-to-database connection, a VPN tunnel between two sites, or a queue channel between a producer host and a consumer host. Use CommunicationNetwork instead when the element is the shared transmission medium or address space (LAN, VPC, subnet, VPN as a whole) connecting many nodes, rather than a particular link between identified endpoints. Use TechnologyInterface instead when the element is the access point on one node (a listening port, endpoint or protocol binding) through which a service is offered, not the link between two nodes. Use TechnologyInteraction instead when the element is the collective behavior exchanged over the link (handshake, replication protocol, failover exchange), not the channel itself. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is an infrastructure capability offered to consumers, such as a managed messaging or load-balancing service, rather than a point-to-point data channel.
evidence: a connection string or endpoint URL in configuration that names another deployed host and port, e.g. DATABASE_URL=postgres://orders-db:5432 or a gRPC target address in an environment file

an infrastructure-as-code resource that links two specific endpoints, e.g. a Terraform aws_vpc_peering_connection, an IPsec VPN tunnel, or a security-group/NetworkPolicy rule allowing traffic from workload A to workload B on a given port
a docker-compose depends_on/links entry or a service-mesh route (Istio VirtualService, DestinationRule) that directs traffic from one named service to another

distinguish.technology.communicationnetwork: the element is the shared transmission medium or address space (LAN, VPC, subnet, VPN as a whole) connecting many nodes, rather than a particular link between identified endpoints
distinguish.technology.technologyinterface: the element is the access point on one node (a listening port, endpoint or protocol binding) through which a service is offered, not the link between two nodes
distinguish.technology.technologyinteraction: the element is the collective behavior exchanged over the link (handshake, replication protocol, failover exchange), not the channel itself
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is an infrastructure capability offered to consumers, such as a managed messaging or load-balancing service, rather than a point-to-point data channel

types.title: SystemSoftware
types.description: A third-party or platform software product, such as an operating system, language runtime, database engine, message broker, cache server or container runtime, that is installed or run on a node or device to host, execute or store other software and data. It is configured and versioned by the team, but its code is not written by them. Use Node instead when the element is the computational host itself (VM, container instance, Kubernetes cluster) that runs software, rather than the software product running on it. Use Artifact instead when the element is the deployable file or package (a container image tag, installer, binary, config file) rather than the running platform software it delivers. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is the capability consumed through an interface (e.g. a managed database or queueing offered by a cloud provider) rather than the specific software product that provides it. Use Device instead when the element is physical hardware rather than software installed on it.
evidence: A docker-compose service or Kubernetes container spec whose image is a vendor platform product, e.g. image: postgres:15, redis:7-alpine, rabbitmq:3-management, nginx:1.25
A runtime or OS pin such as a Dockerfile 'FROM node:20-alpine' or 'FROM ubuntu:22.04', an .nvmrc/.python-version file, or an 'engines' field in package.json
A connection URL, driver dependency or Helm chart dependency naming an engine, e.g. DATABASE_URL=postgres://..., spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers, or a bitnami/kafka chart in Chart.yaml

distinguish.technology.node: the element is the computational host itself (VM, container instance, Kubernetes cluster) that runs software, rather than the software product running on it
distinguish.technology.artifact: the element is the deployable file or package (a container image tag, installer, binary, config file) rather than the running platform software it delivers
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is the capability consumed through an interface (e.g. a managed database or queueing offered by a cloud provider) rather than the specific software product that provides it
distinguish.technology.device: the element is physical hardware rather than software installed on it

types.title: TechnologyCollaboration
types.description: An aggregate of two or more technology active structure elements (nodes, devices or system software instances) that are configured to cooperate as peers and jointly perform behavior none performs alone. Examples are a replicated database ensemble, a consensus cluster, a sharded cache cluster or a service mesh. It is identified by explicit peer membership or coordination configuration, not merely by co-location or shared hosting. Use Node instead when the thing is a single hosting resource, or a cluster managed and addressed as one computational unit (e.g. a Kubernetes cluster as a deployment target), rather than a grouping of individually modelled cooperating members. Use TechnologyInteraction instead when the element is the joint behavior itself (a failover protocol, leader election, distributed commit) rather than the group of elements that performs it. Use SystemSoftware instead when a single installed software product or instance is meant (e.g. one Redis or PostgreSQL server) with no modelled peer membership. Use CommunicationNetwork instead when the element only transports data between members and performs no collective processing itself.
evidence: A StatefulSet, Helm chart or docker-compose file declaring multiple replicas of the same server with peer discovery settings, such as Kafka/ZooKeeper ensembles, etcd initial-cluster, Redis cluster-enabled yes or Elasticsearch discovery.seed_hosts.

Infrastructure-as-code resources that define a multi-member cooperative group, such as aws_elasticache_replication_group, aws_rds_cluster, aws_msk_cluster or a Patroni/Galera cluster configuration listing member addresses.
Service mesh configuration grouping workloads into one mesh, such as Istio IstioOperator/MeshConfig, Linkerd injection annotations across namespaces, or Consul Connect service definitions.

distinguish.technology.node: the thing is a single hosting resource, or a cluster managed and addressed as one computational unit (e.g. a Kubernetes cluster as a deployment target), rather than a grouping of individually modelled cooperating members.
distinguish.technology.technologyinteraction: the element is the joint behavior itself (a failover protocol, leader election, distributed commit) rather than the group of elements that performs it.
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: a single installed software product or instance is meant (e.g. one Redis or PostgreSQL server) with no modelled peer membership.
distinguish.technology.communicationnetwork: the element only transports data between members and performs no collective processing itself.

types.title: TechnologyEvent
types.description: A technology behavior element that denotes a discrete, instantaneous state change in infrastructure or platform software, such as an alert firing, a node or container failing, a scheduled trigger elapsing, or a deployment completing, that starts or results from technology functions, processes or interactions. It has no duration and performs no work itself. Use TechnologyProcess instead when the element is the multi-step job or pipeline that runs (backup job, deployment pipeline) rather than the trigger that starts it or the completion signal it emits. Use TechnologyFunction instead when the element is a continuous automated capability of a node (health checking, log rotation, load balancing) rather than a single occurrence detected or produced by it. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is the exposed monitoring, alerting or scheduling capability (Alertmanager, EventBridge, a cron service) that emits or delivers events, not the event itself. Use Artifact instead when the element is the file that declares the event condition, such as an alert-rule YAML, crontab or CloudWatch alarm template, rather than the state change it describes.
evidence: A named alerting rule or alarm definition, such as a Prometheus rule with alert:, expr: and for: fields, a CloudWatch/Azure Monitor alarm, or a Datadog monitor, that fires on a metric threshold or failure condition.
A schedule trigger that starts infrastructure work, such as a Kubernetes CronJob schedule: field, a crontab line, a CI on: schedule block, or an EventBridge/Cloud Scheduler rule.

A handler subscribed to infrastructure lifecycle notifications, such as a Kubernetes watch on Pod/Node events, the Docker events API, a CI on: deployment_status trigger, a SIGTERM/preStop hook, or a webhook receiving deployment-completed payloads.

distinguish.technology.technologyprocess: the element is the multi-step job or pipeline that runs (backup job, deployment pipeline) rather than the trigger that starts it or the completion signal it emits
distinguish.technology.technologyfunction: the element is a continuous automated capability of a node (health checking, log rotation, load balancing) rather than a single occurrence detected or produced by it
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is the exposed monitoring, alerting or scheduling capability (Alertmanager, EventBridge, a cron service) that emits or delivers events, not the event itself
distinguish.technology.artifact: the element is the file that declares the event condition, such as an alert-rule YAML, crontab or CloudWatch alarm template, rather than the state change it describes

types.title: TechnologyFunction
types.description: An internal technology behavior element grouping automated infrastructure behavior that a single node or system software performs on an ongoing basis, defined by the capability it provides rather than by a sequence of steps or an externally exposed contract, such as data replication, load balancing, health checking, or log rotation. Use TechnologyProcess instead when the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a defined start and end result, such as a CI/CD pipeline, backup job run, or certificate renewal workflow. Use TechnologyService instead when the behavior is the externally visible capability offered to consumers through an interface (e.g. 'managed object storage'), rather than the internal mechanism that delivers it. Use TechnologyInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more collaborating nodes, such as a consensus round, distributed transaction, or cluster failover handshake. Use SystemSoftware instead when the element is the software product or runtime that performs the behavior (e.g. nginx, PostgreSQL), not the behavior itself.
evidence: Infrastructure configuration that enables a named built-in capability of a platform component, such as a PostgreSQL streaming-replication block, an nginx upstream load-balancing block, or a Redis persistence/eviction policy.
A sidecar, daemon, or DaemonSet that runs continuously to perform a housekeeping capability, such as a logrotate config, a Fluent Bit log-shipping agent, or a node-exporter metrics collector.
Kubernetes or cloud resource settings declaring automated platform behavior, such as liveness/readiness probes, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, or an S3 bucket replication or lifecycle rule.

distinguish.technology.technologyprocess: the behavior is an ordered sequence of steps with a defined start and end result, such as a CI/CD pipeline, backup job run, or certificate renewal workflow.
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the behavior is the externally visible capability offered to consumers through an interface (e.g. 'managed object storage'), rather than the internal mechanism that delivers it.
distinguish.technology.technologyinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more collaborating nodes, such as a consensus round, distributed transaction, or cluster failover handshake.
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the element is the software product or runtime that performs the behavior (e.g. nginx, PostgreSQL), not the behavior itself.

types.title: TechnologyInteraction
types.description: A technology behavior element that is performed jointly by two or more technology active structure elements (nodes, devices, or system software) acting as a collaboration, and that none of the participants can complete alone. Examples include a distributed commit, consensus-based leader election, a cluster failover handover, or a replication sync between peers. Use TechnologyFunction instead when the behavior is carried out by a single node or system software on its own, such as local log rotation or one load balancer distributing requests, with no coordination protocol between peers. Use TechnologyProcess instead when the element is an ordered sequence of steps toward a defined result, such as a deployment pipeline or backup job, whose steps need not be jointly performed by multiple collaborating participants. Use TechnologyCollaboration instead when you are modelling the group of cooperating nodes or software itself (the cluster, mesh, or replica set) rather than the joint behavior that group performs. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is the externally visible capability offered to consumers, such as a highly available database service, rather than the internal multi-party coordination that realizes it.
evidence: Configuration or code for a consensus or coordination protocol among peers, such as Raft or etcd peer settings, ZooKeeper quorum configuration, Redis Sentinel monitor/failover settings, or Patroni leader-election config.

A two-phase or XA distributed transaction setup that coordinates prepare/commit across multiple resource managers, for example a JTA/Atomikos transaction manager enlisting both a database and a message broker.

Replication or cluster-membership protocol settings that require multiple instances to exchange state, such as PostgreSQL streaming replication primary_conninfo, Kafka consumer-group rebalance handlers, or Hazelcast/Akka cluster join and gossip configuration.

distinguish.technology.technologyfunction: the behavior is carried out by a single node or system software on its own, such as local log rotation or one load balancer distributing requests, with no coordination protocol between peers.
distinguish.technology.technologyprocess: the element is an ordered sequence of steps toward a defined result, such as a deployment pipeline or backup job, whose steps need not be jointly performed by multiple collaborating participants.
distinguish.technology.technologycollaboration: you are modelling the group of cooperating nodes or software itself (the cluster, mesh, or replica set) rather than the joint behavior that group performs.
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is the externally visible capability offered to consumers, such as a highly available database service, rather than the internal multi-party coordination that realizes it.

types.title: TechnologyInterface
types.description: An access point on a node, device or system software through which a technology service can be consumed. It is identified by a concrete protocol endpoint, such as a listening port, socket, broker listener or endpoint URL, that other technology or application components connect to. Use TechnologyService instead when the element is the infrastructure capability itself (e.g. managed message queuing, object storage) rather than the specific protocol endpoint through which it is reached. Use Path instead when the element is the communication link or route between two or more nodes (e.g. a service-mesh route, a VPN tunnel between sites), not the endpoint at one end of it. Use SystemSoftware instead when the element is the running platform software (e.g. the PostgreSQL engine, the RabbitMQ broker) that exposes the endpoint, rather than the endpoint itself. Use CommunicationNetwork instead when the element is the network segment (LAN, VPC subnet, VPN) that carries traffic, rather than an addressable listener on a node attached to it.
evidence: A port or listener declaration exposing a protocol endpoint, such as Dockerfile EXPOSE, a containerPort or Kubernetes Service port entry, or an aws_lb_listener resource in Terraform
Platform listener configuration in a broker, database or server config file, e.g. RabbitMQ listeners.tcp, postgresql.conf port/listen_addresses, or an nginx 'listen 443 ssl' directive
An endpoint URL or connection string in environment or application config that consumers use to reach infrastructure, e.g. AMQP_URL=amqp://broker:5672 or REDIS_URL=redis://cache:6379

distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the element is the infrastructure capability itself (e.g. managed message queuing, object storage) rather than the specific protocol endpoint through which it is reached
distinguish.technology.path: the element is the communication link or route between two or more nodes (e.g. a service-mesh route, a VPN tunnel between sites), not the endpoint at one end of it
distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the element is the running platform software (e.g. the PostgreSQL engine, the RabbitMQ broker) that exposes the endpoint, rather than the endpoint itself
distinguish.technology.communicationnetwork: the element is the network segment (LAN, VPC subnet, VPN) that carries traffic, rather than an addressable listener on a node attached to it

types.title: TechnologyProcess
types.description: A technology behavior element that is an ordered sequence of automated infrastructure steps with a defined start (trigger) and a defined end result, performed by a node or system software, such as a CI/CD deployment pipeline, scheduled backup job, certificate renewal workflow, or container rollout sequence. Use TechnologyFunction instead when the behavior is a continuously available capability grouped by what the node can do (e.g. load balancing, replication, log rotation) rather than a sequence of steps with a start, an order and a completion. Use TechnologyInteraction instead when the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more collaborating nodes (e.g. a distributed commit or failover handshake) rather than run as a sequence by a single performer. Use TechnologyEvent instead when the thing modelled is the instantaneous trigger or outcome, such as a cron schedule firing or a deployment-completed signal, rather than the steps executed in response. Use TechnologyService instead when the thing modelled is the externally visible infrastructure capability offered to consumers rather than the internal sequence of steps that realizes it.
evidence: A CI/CD pipeline definition such as .github/workflows/*.yml, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile or azure-pipelines.yml with ordered jobs/stages (build, test, deploy).
A scheduled infrastructure job such as a Kubernetes CronJob manifest, crontab entry or systemd timer that runs a backup, cleanup or certificate-renewal script.
An orchestration workflow such as an Ansible playbook, Argo Workflow/Argo Rollouts spec, Terraform apply runbook or Helm hook sequence that executes named infrastructure steps in order.

distinguish.technology.technologyfunction: the behavior is a continuously available capability grouped by what the node can do (e.g. load balancing, replication, log rotation) rather than a sequence of steps with a start, an order and a completion.
distinguish.technology.technologyinteraction: the behavior can only be performed jointly by two or more collaborating nodes (e.g. a distributed commit or failover handshake) rather than run as a sequence by a single performer.
distinguish.technology.technologyevent: the thing modelled is the instantaneous trigger or outcome, such as a cron schedule firing or a deployment-completed signal, rather than the steps executed in response.
distinguish.technology.technologyservice: the thing modelled is the externally visible infrastructure capability offered to consumers rather than the internal sequence of steps that realizes it.

types.title: TechnologyService
types.description: An externally visible infrastructure capability, such as compute, storage, messaging, database, cache, identity or monitoring, that a node, system software or managed platform offers to application components or other technology elements through a technology interface. It is identified by the capability consumers rely on, not by the product, host or endpoint that delivers it. Use SystemSoftware instead when the element is the specific installed engine or product (e.g. a PostgreSQL 15 server, a Redis binary, a RabbitMQ broker) rather than the capability that consumers use. Use TechnologyInterface instead when the element is the access point itself, such as an endpoint URL, port or protocol binding through which the service is reached. Use TechnologyFunction instead when the behavior is internal to a node and not offered to consumers, such as replication, log rotation or internal load balancing. Use Node instead when the element is the host, VM, container or cluster that provides the computational resource, not the capability exposed from it.
evidence: an infrastructure-as-code resource for a managed backing service (e.g. aws_sqs_queue, aws_db_instance, google_pubsub_topic, azurerm_redis_cache) whose outputs are wired into application configuration

a docker-compose or Helm service entry for a backing service (postgres, redis, kafka, keycloak) whose connection string is injected into application containers via environment variables such as DATABASE_URL or REDIS_URL

a client SDK constructed against an infrastructure endpoint (S3 client, KMS client, OIDC issuer URL, OTLP exporter endpoint) and used by application code to store, publish, authenticate or emit telemetry

distinguish.technology.systemsoftware: the element is the specific installed engine or product (e.g. a PostgreSQL 15 server, a Redis binary, a RabbitMQ broker) rather than the capability that consumers use.
distinguish.technology.technologyinterface: the element is the access point itself, such as an endpoint URL, port or protocol binding through which the service is reached.
distinguish.technology.technologyfunction: the behavior is internal to a node and not offered to consumers, such as replication, log rotation or internal load balancing.
distinguish.technology.node: the element is the host, VM, container or cluster that provides the computational resource, not the capability exposed from it.

layers.name: API Layer
layers.scope: Describes the HTTP API surface the application exposes or consumes: the API document and its servers, paths and operations, parameters, request bodies and responses, media types, headers, links and callbacks, reusable components and schemas, security schemes and webhooks (OpenAPI 3.0). Route handlers, controllers and generated API clients are evidence for elements here; the application behaviour behind an operation belongs to the application layer. Modelling rules: each API object links only to what its OpenAPI 3.0 fields hold, and every nesting in the document tree is composes: the document composes its info, paths, components, servers and tags; paths compose path items, and a path item composes its operations, parameters and servers; an operation composes its parameters, request body, responses map, callbacks and servers; the responses map composes its responses, and a response composes its headers, media types and links; a media type composes its schema, examples and encodings; a server composes its variables, a security scheme its OAuth flows, and components their reusable entries. Reuse through $ref is references, and allOf inheritance is specializes. A rate limit, which OpenAPI does not define, governs the operations, path items and servers it caps, triggers its 429 response, references the headers and security scheme it counts by, and realizes its countermeasure. An operation realizes the application function it exposes and references its application service, and a document realizes its application service; the API reaches the business layer through the application layer. A security scheme realizes the security policy it applies, requires permissions and references the secure resource it protects. API schemas reach data stores and business objects through the data-model schemas that map to them. An operation satisfies requirements and constraints, supports the goals and outcomes it contributes to, and realizes the countermeasures it implements.

types.title: Callback
types.description: An outbound HTTP request contract attached to an operation, in which the API itself calls a consumer-supplied URL. The URL is obtained by evaluating a runtime expression against the triggering request or response, and the full interaction (method, body, expected responses) is described as a PathItem. Use Operation instead when the HTTP interaction is one the API receives and serves on its own paths, rather than a request the API sends to a URL supplied by the consumer. Use Link instead when the relationship describes a follow-up call that the client makes to another operation of this API, using values from a response, rather than a call the API pushes to the client. Use PathItem instead when modelling the set of HTTP methods under a fixed path template of the API, or the inner PathItem that a callback aggregates, rather than the expression-keyed callback wrapper. Use Server instead when the target is a fixed or variable-templated deployment base URL of the API, not a URL resolved per request from a runtime expression.
evidence: A 'callbacks:' map under an operation in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file whose keys are runtime expressions such as '{$request.body#/callbackUrl}'.
A route decorator or annotation declaring callbacks, such as FastAPI's callbacks= router parameter or springdoc/Swagger @Callback, on a subscription or job-submission endpoint.
Handler code that stores a callbackUrl/notifyUrl field from the incoming request and later issues an HTTP POST to it from a background job or event listener using an HTTP client.

distinguish.api.operation: the HTTP interaction is one the API receives and serves on its own paths, rather than a request the API sends to a URL supplied by the consumer.
distinguish.api.link: the relationship describes a follow-up call that the client makes to another operation of this API, using values from a response, rather than a call the API pushes to the client.
distinguish.api.pathitem: modelling the set of HTTP methods under a fixed path template of the API, or the inner PathItem that a callback aggregates, rather than the expression-keyed callback wrapper.
distinguish.api.server: the target is a fixed or variable-templated deployment base URL of the API, not a URL resolved per request from a runtime expression.

types.title: Components
types.description: The single container object within an OpenAPI document that holds named, reusable definitions (schemas, responses, parameters, examples, request bodies, headers, security schemes, links and callbacks), each addressable by a '#/components/<kind>/<name>' $ref pointer. It defines no paths or operations itself; its entries take effect only when referenced. Use OpenAPIDocument instead when the element is the root object carrying openapi, info, paths and servers, of which the components section is only one child. Use Schema instead when the element is an individual data-shape definition, whether inline or stored under components.schemas, rather than the registry that holds it. Use Responses instead when the element is an operation's map of HTTP status codes to Response objects, not the components.responses registry of named reusable responses. Use Paths instead when the element maps URL path templates to PathItem objects that define live API surface, rather than holding unreferenced reusable definitions.
evidence: A top-level 'components:' key in an openapi.yaml/openapi.json with sub-maps such as schemas, securitySchemes, parameters or responses
JSON Reference strings of the form "$ref: '#/components/schemas/User'" or '#/components/responses/NotFound' elsewhere in the spec

Programmatic spec builders populating the section, e.g. springdoc 'new OpenAPI().components(new Components().addSecuritySchemes(...))', NestJS DocumentBuilder().addBearerAuth(), or drf-spectacular/FastAPI registering models under components.schemas

distinguish.api.openapidocument: the element is the root object carrying openapi, info, paths and servers, of which the components section is only one child.
distinguish.api.schema: the element is an individual data-shape definition, whether inline or stored under components.schemas, rather than the registry that holds it.
distinguish.api.responses: the element is an operation's map of HTTP status codes to Response objects, not the components.responses registry of named reusable responses.
distinguish.api.paths: the element maps URL path templates to PathItem objects that define live API surface, rather than holding unreferenced reusable definitions.

types.title: Contact
types.description: A metadata object nested in an API document's Info section that identifies the person or organisation responsible for the exposed API by name, email address and/or URL. It describes who maintains the API contract, not the server it is deployed on or the documentation it links to. Use Info instead when the element carries the API's title, version, description or terms of service rather than only the maintainer's name, email and URL. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the URL points to a guide, wiki or reference material for the API rather than to a support or maintainer contact page. Use License instead when the name and URL identify the legal licence terms under which the API is offered rather than the party to contact.
evidence: An info.contact block with name, email or url keys in an openapi.yaml or openapi.json file.
A framework OpenAPI configuration passing a contact argument, e.g. FastAPI(contact={...}), Springdoc new Contact().name(...).email(...), or a swagger-jsdoc definition.info.contact entry.
An @contact or @Contact annotation or docblock tag in API annotations, such as swag's // @contact.email comment or the MicroProfile @Contact(...) annotation inside @Info.

distinguish.api.info: the element carries the API's title, version, description or terms of service rather than only the maintainer's name, email and URL.
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the URL points to a guide, wiki or reference material for the API rather than to a support or maintainer contact page.
distinguish.api.license: the name and URL identify the legal licence terms under which the API is offered rather than the party to contact.

types.title: Encoding
types.description: A per-property serialization rule inside a request body's MediaType, keyed by a top-level schema property name, that fixes how that property is written as a part of a multipart or application/x-www-form-urlencoded body: its part Content-Type, part headers, and form style/explode/allowReserved behaviour. Use MediaType instead when the element describes the whole body for one MIME type (schema, examples, and the encoding map itself) rather than the rule for one property within it. Use Header instead when the element is an individual header definition (schema, required, description) that a multipart part or response carries, not the part-level serialization rule that lists those headers. Use Schema instead when the element defines the data shape or type of the property (type, format, properties) rather than how that property is serialized onto the wire. Use Parameter instead when the element is a path, query, header or cookie input to the operation rather than a property of a request body.
evidence: An OpenAPI YAML/JSON fragment with an 'encoding:' map under 'requestBody.content.multipart/form-data' or 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded', keyed by property names such as 'profileImage: { contentType: image/png }'.
A springdoc/swagger-core @Encoding(name=..., contentType=...) annotation nested in @Content on a controller method that consumes multipart/form-data, e.g. alongside @RequestPart parameters.

Upload handler code that declares per-field part content types or headers, e.g. FastAPI File/Form fields with media_type, or a multer/busboy field configuration whose field names match properties of the request body schema.

distinguish.api.mediatype: the element describes the whole body for one MIME type (schema, examples, and the encoding map itself) rather than the rule for one property within it.
distinguish.api.header: the element is an individual header definition (schema, required, description) that a multipart part or response carries, not the part-level serialization rule that lists those headers.
distinguish.api.schema: the element defines the data shape or type of the property (type, format, properties) rather than how that property is serialized onto the wire.
distinguish.api.parameter: the element is a path, query, header or cookie input to the operation rather than a property of a request body.

types.title: Example
types.description: A named sample instance of a value, given either inline or by external URL, attached through an `examples` map to a media type, parameter or header, or registered under components.examples for $ref reuse. It illustrates one concrete payload or value. It does not define the shape or constraints of that value. Use Schema instead when the element defines the type, properties and constraints a value must satisfy rather than one concrete sample of it. Use MediaType instead when the element is the MIME-keyed content entry itself; a single inline `example` value on that media type is an attribute of it, not a separate Example. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the URL points to explanatory prose such as a guide or wiki rather than to a sample payload or value. Use Components instead when the element is the reusable registry holding examples rather than one named example entry within it.
evidence: An entry in an `examples:` map under `content.application/json`, a parameter or a header in an openapi.yaml/json file, carrying `summary` and `value` or `externalValue` keys.
A `components.examples` entry referenced elsewhere via `$ref: '#/components/examples/<Name>'`.

Framework annotations that emit named examples, e.g. springdoc `@ExampleObject(name=..., value=...)`, FastAPI `Body(openapi_examples={...})`, NestJS `@ApiBody({ examples: {...} })` or swagger-php `@OA\Examples`.

distinguish.api.schema: the element defines the type, properties and constraints a value must satisfy rather than one concrete sample of it.
distinguish.api.mediatype: the element is the MIME-keyed content entry itself; a single inline `example` value on that media type is an attribute of it, not a separate Example.
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the URL points to explanatory prose such as a guide or wiki rather than to a sample payload or value.
distinguish.api.components: the element is the reusable registry holding examples rather than one named example entry within it.

types.title: ExternalDocumentation
types.description: A metadata object holding a single URL (plus optional descriptive text) that points to documentation hosted outside the OpenAPI document. It attaches through an 'externalDocs' field to the root document, a Tag, an Operation or a Schema. Use Contact instead when the URL or email identifies a person or team to reach for support, not a documentation resource. Use License instead when the URL points to the legal license terms under which the API is offered. Use Info instead when the text is the API's own inline title, description or termsOfService rather than a link to an outside documentation page. Use Example instead when the URL (externalValue) points to a sample payload value rather than to human-readable documentation.
evidence: an 'externalDocs:' block containing a 'url:' key in an openapi.yaml/json file, at root level, under a tag, an operation or a schema
a springdoc/swagger-core @ExternalDocumentation(url=...) or @ExternalDocs annotation on a controller method, OpenAPIDefinition or model class
a NestJS DocumentBuilder().setExternalDoc(description, url) call, or a FastAPI openapi_tags entry with an 'externalDocs' dict

distinguish.api.contact: the URL or email identifies a person or team to reach for support, not a documentation resource.
distinguish.api.license: the URL points to the legal license terms under which the API is offered.
distinguish.api.info: the text is the API's own inline title, description or termsOfService rather than a link to an outside documentation page.
distinguish.api.example: the URL (externalValue) points to a sample payload value rather than to human-readable documentation.

types.title: Header
types.description: A named HTTP header declaration, keyed by header name in a Response's headers map, an Encoding's headers map, or the Components headers registry, that describes the header value's schema, serialization and examples. It carries no 'name' or 'in' field because the name comes from the map key and the location is always header. Use Parameter instead when the header is a client-supplied input to an operation, declared in the operation's or path's parameters list with in: header. Use SecurityScheme instead when the header carries credentials (e.g. Authorization, X-API-Key) and what is being modelled is the authentication mechanism, i.e. an apiKey scheme with in: header or an http bearer scheme. Use RateLimit instead when what is being modelled is the throttling policy itself (request count, window, scope), not the X-RateLimit-* response header that reports it. Use Encoding instead when the intent is to set the MIME type of a multipart part; use Encoding.contentType rather than a Content-Type header, which OpenAPI ignores.
evidence: An OpenAPI YAML/JSON 'headers:' map under a response (e.g. responses.200.headers.X-Request-Id with a schema) or an entry under components.headers.

A springdoc/swagger annotation such as @ApiResponse(headers = @Header(name = "X-Rate-Limit-Remaining", schema = @Schema(type = "integer"))), or a FastAPI/NestJS responses= declaration with a 'headers' dict.
A route handler that sets a fixed response header (e.g. res.setHeader('Location', ...) or response.headers['ETag'] = ...) whose value is documented as part of the response contract.

distinguish.api.parameter: the header is a client-supplied input to an operation, declared in the operation's or path's parameters list with in: header.
distinguish.api.securityscheme: the header carries credentials (e.g. Authorization, X-API-Key) and what is being modelled is the authentication mechanism, i.e. an apiKey scheme with in: header or an http bearer scheme.
distinguish.api.ratelimit: what is being modelled is the throttling policy itself (request count, window, scope), not the X-RateLimit-* response header that reports it.
distinguish.api.encoding: the intent is to set the MIME type of a multipart part; use Encoding.contentType rather than a Content-Type header, which OpenAPI ignores.

types.title: Info
types.description: A single metadata object nested in an OpenAPI document's root 'info' field that records the described API's title, its document version, an optional description and terms-of-service URL, and references to its contact and license. Exactly one exists per OpenAPI document; it describes the API as a whole, not any path, operation or server. Use OpenAPIDocument instead when the element is the root object itself, which holds the 'openapi' spec-version string and the paths, servers, components and security sections, rather than only the descriptive metadata block. Use Contact instead when the element carries only the maintainer's name, email or URL, which Info references through its 'contact' field. Use License instead when the element carries only the license name and license URL, which Info references through its 'license' field. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the element is a link to an external guide or wiki attached to the root document, a tag, an operation or a schema, rather than inline title and version metadata.
evidence: An 'info:' block containing 'title:' and 'version:' keys at the top level of an openapi.yaml or openapi.json file

A framework OpenAPI bootstrap call that sets API metadata, such as FastAPI(title=..., version=..., description=...), NestJS new DocumentBuilder().setTitle().setVersion(), or springdoc new OpenAPI().info(new Info().title(...))
A Java annotation @OpenAPIDefinition(info = @Info(title = ..., version = ...)), or a swagger-jsdoc options object with definition.info.title and definition.info.version

distinguish.api.openapidocument: the element is the root object itself, which holds the 'openapi' spec-version string and the paths, servers, components and security sections, rather than only the descriptive metadata block
distinguish.api.contact: the element carries only the maintainer's name, email or URL, which Info references through its 'contact' field
distinguish.api.license: the element carries only the license name and license URL, which Info references through its 'license' field
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the element is a link to an external guide or wiki attached to the root document, a tag, an operation or a schema, rather than inline title and version metadata

types.title: License
types.description: A metadata object, nested under an API's Info object, that identifies by name the legal license governing use of the API and optionally gives a URL to the full license text. It describes terms of use for the API contract itself, not the license of the implementing source code. Use Info instead when the element is the overall API metadata block (title, version, description, termsOfService) rather than only the license name and URL inside it. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the URL points to guides, wikis or reference docs that explain the API rather than to the legal license terms. Use Contact instead when the information identifies who owns or supports the API (name, email, URL) rather than the legal terms under which it may be used.
evidence: an info.license block with name (e.g. 'Apache 2.0', 'MIT') and url fields in an openapi.yaml/openapi.json file
a framework OpenAPI config call setting license metadata, e.g. springdoc new License().name("Apache 2.0").url(...), FastAPI(license_info={...}) or swagger-jsdoc definition.info.license
an @OpenAPIDefinition(info = @Info(license = @License(name=..., url=...))) or equivalent annotation on an application or config class

distinguish.api.info: the element is the overall API metadata block (title, version, description, termsOfService) rather than only the license name and URL inside it.
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the URL points to guides, wikis or reference docs that explain the API rather than to the legal license terms.
distinguish.api.contact: the information identifies who owns or supports the API (name, email, URL) rather than the legal terms under which it may be used.

types.title: Link
types.description: A response-scoped descriptor that names a target operation, by operationId or operationRef, and maps values from the current response or request (via runtime expressions or literals) onto that operation's parameters or request body. It is a design-time statement of how one call can follow another. It is not a hyperlink carried in the response payload. Use Callback instead when the API itself sends an outbound request to a consumer-supplied URL, rather than describing a follow-up call the consumer may make to an operation in this API. Use Schema instead when the 'links' are runtime data inside the response body (e.g. HAL _links, JSON:API links objects) whose shape is being described, not an OpenAPI Link Object. Use Header instead when the relationship is conveyed by an actual HTTP Link response header (RFC 8288) declared on the response. Use Parameter instead when you are defining the input the target operation accepts, rather than mapping a value from a prior response into that input.
evidence: A 'links:' map under a response in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file whose entries carry operationId or operationRef plus parameters using runtime expressions such as '$response.body#/id'
A springdoc/swagger-core @Link annotation inside @ApiResponse(links = ...), or a swagger-php @OA\Link / NestJS equivalent attached to a response definition
Entries under components.links referenced from responses via $ref '#/components/links/<Name>'

distinguish.api.callback: the API itself sends an outbound request to a consumer-supplied URL, rather than describing a follow-up call the consumer may make to an operation in this API
distinguish.api.schema: the 'links' are runtime data inside the response body (e.g. HAL _links, JSON:API links objects) whose shape is being described, not an OpenAPI Link Object
distinguish.api.header: the relationship is conveyed by an actual HTTP Link response header (RFC 8288) declared on the response
distinguish.api.parameter: you are defining the input the target operation accepts, rather than mapping a value from a prior response into that input

types.title: MediaType
types.description: An entry in the 'content' map of a request body, response, or content-style parameter, keyed by one MIME type or media range (e.g. application/json, text/*), that binds the payload schema, examples, and (for multipart or form-urlencoded bodies) per-property encoding used when the payload has that type. Use Schema instead when the element is the data-shape definition itself (type, properties, items), independent of which MIME type carries it. Use Encoding instead when the element describes serialization of a single property within a multipart or form-urlencoded body rather than the whole payload for a MIME type. Use RequestBody instead when the element is the container holding the description, the required flag and the full content map across all MIME types for an operation's input. Use Response instead when the element is an outcome for a status code, with its description, headers and links, rather than one MIME-typed representation within it.
evidence: An OpenAPI YAML/JSON 'content:' block under a requestBody or response with a key such as 'application/json' or 'multipart/form-data' carrying 'schema:' and 'example(s):'.

A framework annotation declaring a produced or consumed MIME type with a payload schema, e.g. Spring @Content(mediaType="application/json", schema=@Schema(...)) or @Produces/@Consumes on a JAX-RS resource method.
FastAPI/NestJS response declarations naming a MIME type with a model, e.g. responses={200: {"content": {"image/png": {}}}} or @ApiProduces('text/csv') paired with @ApiResponse({type: Dto}).

distinguish.api.schema: the element is the data-shape definition itself (type, properties, items), independent of which MIME type carries it.
distinguish.api.encoding: the element describes serialization of a single property within a multipart or form-urlencoded body rather than the whole payload for a MIME type.
distinguish.api.requestbody: the element is the container holding the description, the required flag and the full content map across all MIME types for an operation's input.
distinguish.api.response: the element is an outcome for a status code, with its description, headers and links, rather than one MIME-typed representation within it.

types.title: OAuthFlow
types.description: A configuration object describing one OAuth 2.0 grant type (implicit, password, clientCredentials or authorizationCode) within an oauth2 security scheme, giving the endpoint URLs that grant uses and the map of scopes it can issue. Its grant type is determined by the OAuthFlows field that holds it, not by a field of its own. Use OAuthFlows instead when the element is the container grouping all grant types for one oauth2 scheme (the 'flows' object) rather than the settings of a single grant. Use SecurityScheme instead when the element declares the authentication mechanism itself (type oauth2, apiKey, http, openIdConnect) and its registry name, rather than the URLs and scopes of one OAuth grant. Use Server instead when the URL is a base address where the API itself is deployed, not an authorization, token or refresh endpoint of an identity provider.
evidence: An entry under components.securitySchemes.<name>.flows.authorizationCode (or implicit/password/clientCredentials) in an openapi.yaml containing authorizationUrl, tokenUrl and scopes keys

A framework security declaration such as FastAPI OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl=...)/OAuth2AuthorizationCodeBearer, springdoc @OAuthFlow(authorizationUrl=..., tokenUrl=..., scopes=@OAuthScope(...)), or NestJS addOAuth2({ flows: { ... } })
A scopes dictionary mapping scope strings (e.g. 'read:users') to descriptions, used in both the spec generator config and route-level scope checks

distinguish.api.oauthflows: the element is the container grouping all grant types for one oauth2 scheme (the 'flows' object) rather than the settings of a single grant.
distinguish.api.securityscheme: the element declares the authentication mechanism itself (type oauth2, apiKey, http, openIdConnect) and its registry name, rather than the URLs and scopes of one OAuth grant.
distinguish.api.server: the URL is a base address where the API itself is deployed, not an authorization, token or refresh endpoint of an identity provider.

types.title: OAuthFlows
types.description: A container object nested in an oauth2-type SecurityScheme that maps each supported OAuth 2.0 grant type (implicit, password, clientCredentials, authorizationCode) to one OAuthFlow configuration. It holds no URLs or scopes of its own; it only selects which grant types the scheme offers. Use OAuthFlow instead when the element carries the authorizationUrl, tokenUrl, refreshUrl or scopes of a single grant type rather than the set of grant-type slots. Use SecurityScheme instead when the element declares the authentication mechanism itself (type, description, name/in, scheme) rather than the flows block inside an oauth2 scheme. Use Components instead when the element is the document-wide registry holding named securitySchemes, not the flows object within one scheme.
evidence: A 'flows:' map with keys such as authorizationCode or clientCredentials under a securitySchemes entry whose type is oauth2 in openapi.yaml or openapi.json
A springdoc/swagger-annotations @OAuthFlows(...) passed as the flows argument of @SecurityScheme(type = SecuritySchemeType.OAUTH2)
A framework flows model instantiated for an OAuth2 scheme, e.g. FastAPI OAuthFlowsModel(password=...) or .NET Swashbuckle new OpenApiOAuthFlows { AuthorizationCode = ... }

distinguish.api.oauthflow: the element carries the authorizationUrl, tokenUrl, refreshUrl or scopes of a single grant type rather than the set of grant-type slots.
distinguish.api.securityscheme: the element declares the authentication mechanism itself (type, description, name/in, scheme) rather than the flows block inside an oauth2 scheme.
distinguish.api.components: the element is the document-wide registry holding named securitySchemes, not the flows object within one scheme.

types.title: OpenAPIDocument
types.description: A root-level API description that declares one OpenAPI version and binds together exactly one Info object, one Paths map, and optionally servers, components, root security requirements, tags and external docs, describing a single API surface. One instance exists per openapi.yaml/json file or per generated spec endpoint, not per path, operation or reusable component. Use Info instead when the element is only the title/version/description/contact/license metadata block, not the whole specification. Use Paths instead when the element is only the map of URL path templates to PathItems inside a document. Use Components instead when the element is the reusable-definitions registry (schemas, responses, securitySchemes, etc.), even if it lives in a separate shared file referenced via $ref. Use PathItem instead when the element describes the operations under one URL path rather than the whole API.
evidence: a file such as openapi.yaml, openapi.json or swagger/v3 spec whose top-level key is 'openapi: 3.0.x' alongside 'info' and 'paths'
framework spec bootstrap code, e.g. FastAPI(title=..., version=...), springdoc OpenAPI bean, swagger-jsdoc definition object, or NSwag/Swashbuckle AddSwaggerGen document registration
an HTTP route serving the generated spec (e.g. GET /openapi.json, /v3/api-docs) or a Swagger UI/Redoc config pointing at that URL, or an openapi-generator input path in build config

distinguish.api.info: the element is only the title/version/description/contact/license metadata block, not the whole specification.
distinguish.api.paths: the element is only the map of URL path templates to PathItems inside a document.
distinguish.api.components: the element is the reusable-definitions registry (schemas, responses, securitySchemes, etc.), even if it lives in a separate shared file referenced via $ref.
distinguish.api.pathitem: the element describes the operations under one URL path rather than the whole API.

types.title: Operation
types.description: An HTTP interaction contract identified by one HTTP method on one URL path template, specifying the parameters, request body, responses and security that apply to that method-path pair. Each route handler, controller action or generated client method bound to a distinct method plus path is one instance. Use PathItem instead when the element groups all methods available under a single URL path template, or carries path-level parameters shared by those methods, rather than describing one method's contract. Use Callback instead when the element is an outbound request the API sends to a consumer-supplied URL resolved from a runtime expression, rather than an endpoint the API itself serves. Use Link instead when the element only describes how values from one operation's response feed the parameters of another operation, rather than defining an endpoint. Use Paths instead when the element is the document-wide map of all path templates, not a single method on a single path.
evidence: A handler function or method registered for a specific HTTP verb and path, e.g. @app.get('/users/{id}'), @GetMapping("/users/{id}"), router.post('/orders', ...), or [HttpDelete("{id}")] on an ASP.NET controller action
An entry under paths.<template>.<get|post|put|delete|patch|head|options|trace> in an openapi.yaml or openapi.json file, typically carrying an operationId
A method in a generated API client, for example from openapi-generator or NSwag, that issues a request with a fixed HTTP method to a fixed path template and is named after an operationId

distinguish.api.pathitem: the element groups all methods available under a single URL path template, or carries path-level parameters shared by those methods, rather than describing one method's contract
distinguish.api.callback: the element is an outbound request the API sends to a consumer-supplied URL resolved from a runtime expression, rather than an endpoint the API itself serves
distinguish.api.link: the element only describes how values from one operation's response feed the parameters of another operation, rather than defining an endpoint
distinguish.api.paths: the element is the document-wide map of all path templates, not a single method on a single path

types.title: Parameter
types.description: A named input to an API operation or path item that is carried outside the request body, in the URL path, the query string, a request header or a cookie. It is identified by the pair (name, in) and constrained by either a schema or a single-entry content map. Use RequestBody instead when the input is carried in the HTTP message body, including form fields of application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data payloads. Use Header instead when the header describes a response header, or a multipart part header under an Encoding, where the name comes from a map key and no 'in' location is given. Use ServerVariable instead when the {placeholder} is substituted in a Server URL (host, base path, tenant) rather than in a Paths key template. Use Schema instead when you are modelling the data type or constraints of the value itself rather than the named input slot that carries it.
evidence: Framework parameter bindings on handler arguments, such as Spring @PathVariable/@RequestParam/@RequestHeader/@CookieValue, FastAPI Path()/Query()/Header()/Cookie(), or ASP.NET [FromRoute]/[FromQuery]/[FromHeader].
Handler code reading req.params.<name>, req.query.<name>, req.get('<Header>') or req.cookies.<name> in an Express/Koa-style route registered on a router.
An entry under a 'parameters:' list in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file, at operation, path-item or components level, containing 'name:' and 'in: path|query|header|cookie'.

distinguish.api.requestbody: the input is carried in the HTTP message body, including form fields of application/x-www-form-urlencoded or multipart/form-data payloads.
distinguish.api.header: the header describes a response header, or a multipart part header under an Encoding, where the name comes from a map key and no 'in' location is given.
