distinguish.api.servervariable: the {placeholder} is substituted in a Server URL (host, base path, tenant) rather than in a Paths key template.
distinguish.api.schema: you are modelling the data type or constraints of the value itself rather than the named input slot that carries it.

types.title: PathItem
types.description: An OpenAPI path-level object that groups the HTTP operations exposed under exactly one URL path template (e.g. /users/{userId}), or under one callback runtime expression. It carries parameters and servers shared by all of those operations. It describes the whole path, not any single method. Use Operation instead when the element is one HTTP method on the path (e.g. GET /users/{userId}) with its own operationId, request body and responses. Use Paths instead when the element is the document-wide map from every path template to its PathItem, not a single path entry. Use Callback instead when the element is the runtime-expression key (e.g. $request.body#/callbackUrl) naming where an asynchronous notification is sent, rather than the PathItem that key maps to. Use Parameter instead when the element is a single named input (path, query, header or cookie), even if it is declared at path level and shared by all operations.
evidence: a key beginning with '/' directly under 'paths:' in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file, whose children are HTTP-method keys (get, post, put, delete) and optionally a shared 'parameters' or 'servers' list
a router chain bound to one path string with several verb handlers, e.g. Express router.route('/users/:id').get(...).put(...).delete(...)
a class-based view bound to a single URL pattern whose methods are named after HTTP verbs, e.g. a Flask MethodView or Django APIView registered at path('users/<int:id>/', ...)

distinguish.api.operation: the element is one HTTP method on the path (e.g. GET /users/{userId}) with its own operationId, request body and responses
distinguish.api.paths: the element is the document-wide map from every path template to its PathItem, not a single path entry
distinguish.api.callback: the element is the runtime-expression key (e.g. $request.body#/callbackUrl) naming where an asynchronous notification is sent, rather than the PathItem that key maps to
distinguish.api.parameter: the element is a single named input (path, query, header or cookie), even if it is declared at path level and shared by all operations

types.title: Paths
types.description: A single container object within one OpenAPI document that maps each relative URL path template (a key beginning with '/', e.g. /users/{id}) to exactly one PathItem, representing the complete set of endpoints the document exposes. There is one per OpenAPI document, and it does not itself carry operations, servers or metadata. Use PathItem instead when the symbol represents one specific URL path pattern and the HTTP methods available on it, rather than the whole collection of paths. Use OpenAPIDocument instead when the symbol is the root specification object carrying openapi version, info, servers, components and security in addition to the paths map. Use Operation instead when the symbol is a single HTTP method handler bound to a path, with its own parameters, request body and responses. Use Components instead when the map holds reusable named definitions (schemas, responses, parameters, etc.) referenced via $ref rather than routable URL paths.
evidence: The top-level 'paths:' key in an openapi.yaml/openapi.json file, whose children are keys like '/users/{userId}'.
A root route table that enumerates all URL patterns of the service, e.g. Django root urls.py urlpatterns, Rails config/routes.rb, or an Express app mounting all routers.
Framework-generated spec output exposing a paths dictionary, e.g. FastAPI app.openapi()['paths'] or a springdoc/Swashbuckle-generated document's Paths collection.

distinguish.api.pathitem: the symbol represents one specific URL path pattern and the HTTP methods available on it, rather than the whole collection of paths.
distinguish.api.openapidocument: the symbol is the root specification object carrying openapi version, info, servers, components and security in addition to the paths map.
distinguish.api.operation: the symbol is a single HTTP method handler bound to a path, with its own parameters, request body and responses.
distinguish.api.components: the map holds reusable named definitions (schemas, responses, parameters, etc.) referenced via $ref rather than routable URL paths.

types.title: RateLimit
types.description: A request-throttling policy attached to an API's servers, paths or operations that caps how many requests a consumer, identified by a counting key, may make within a fixed time window. It also states what enforcement happens when that cap is exceeded. Use Header instead when you are modelling the response headers that report quota state to clients (e.g. X-RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After), not the limit policy itself. Use Response instead when you are modelling the documented HTTP outcome returned when a limit trips (typically 429 Too Many Requests or 503), including its description and body. Use SecurityScheme instead when the element defines how a caller is authenticated (an API key, bearer token or OAuth2), even if that identity is later used as the rate-limit key.
evidence: Rate-limiting middleware mounted on an HTTP router with numeric limits, e.g. express-rate-limit `rateLimit({ windowMs: 60000, max: 100, keyGenerator })` or ASP.NET `AddRateLimiter`/`[EnableRateLimiting]`.

Framework throttle declarations on handlers or controllers, e.g. NestJS `@Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60000 } })`, Django REST Framework `throttle_classes` with `DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES = {'user': '1000/day'}`, or Spring/Bucket4j bucket definitions.

API gateway or proxy configuration defining request quotas per route or consumer, e.g. a Kong `rate-limiting` plugin, an AWS API Gateway usage plan throttle, an nginx `limit_req_zone`, or an `x-ratelimit` extension in the OpenAPI file.

distinguish.api.header: you are modelling the response headers that report quota state to clients (e.g. X-RateLimit-Remaining, RateLimit-Reset, Retry-After), not the limit policy itself.
distinguish.api.response: you are modelling the documented HTTP outcome returned when a limit trips (typically 429 Too Many Requests or 503), including its description and body.
distinguish.api.securityscheme: the element defines how a caller is authenticated (an API key, bearer token or OAuth2), even if that identity is later used as the rate-limit key.

types.title: RequestBody
types.description: An API contract element describing the payload a client sends in the body of a single operation's HTTP request, expressed as one or more media-type entries (e.g. application/json, multipart/form-data) plus an optional required flag and description. It covers only the request payload of a body-bearing method; URL, query, header and cookie inputs and anything returned to the client are excluded. Use Parameter instead when the input travels in the path, query string, header or cookie rather than the HTTP message body. Use MediaType instead when modelling the schema, examples and encoding for one specific MIME type inside the body's content map, rather than the body as a whole with its required flag. Use Schema instead when describing the data shape itself (fields, types, constraints) independent of whether it is carried in a request, a response or a parameter. Use Response instead when the payload is sent by the server back to the client for a status code, not by the client to the server.
evidence: A route handler parameter bound from the body, such as Spring @RequestBody, FastAPI Body()/Pydantic model argument, NestJS @Body() or ASP.NET [FromBody].
A 'requestBody:' block under a POST/PUT/PATCH operation, or an entry under 'components/requestBodies', in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file.

Body validation middleware or a DTO class applied to req.body, e.g. express.json() followed by a Joi/Zod/class-validator schema check, or a generated client method that serializes a payload argument with a Content-Type header.

distinguish.api.parameter: the input travels in the path, query string, header or cookie rather than the HTTP message body.
distinguish.api.mediatype: modelling the schema, examples and encoding for one specific MIME type inside the body's content map, rather than the body as a whole with its required flag.
distinguish.api.schema: describing the data shape itself (fields, types, constraints) independent of whether it is carried in a request, a response or a parameter.
distinguish.api.response: the payload is sent by the server back to the client for a status code, not by the client to the server.

types.title: Response
types.description: An OpenAPI description object specifying one possible HTTP outcome of an operation for a single status code (or 'default'). It carries a required description and, optionally, response headers, a body content map keyed by MIME type, and links to follow-on operations. Use Responses instead when the element is the whole status-code-to-response map for an operation rather than a single outcome under one status code. Use MediaType instead when the element describes the schema, examples and encoding for one MIME type entry (e.g. application/json) inside a response's content map. Use Schema instead when the element defines only the data shape of a response body, independent of status code, headers or description. Use Header instead when the element defines one individual response header rather than the response that contains it.
evidence: an @ApiResponse(responseCode="404", description=...) annotation in springdoc/Swagger, or a NestJS @ApiOkResponse/@ApiNotFoundResponse decorator on a controller method
an entry under a status-code key such as '200': or 'default': beneath an operation's 'responses' map, or under 'components/responses', in an openapi.yaml/json file
a FastAPI route declaring responses={404: {"description": ..., "model": ...}}, or a handler returning a fixed status code with a documented body or headers

distinguish.api.responses: the element is the whole status-code-to-response map for an operation rather than a single outcome under one status code
distinguish.api.mediatype: the element describes the schema, examples and encoding for one MIME type entry (e.g. application/json) inside a response's content map
distinguish.api.schema: the element defines only the data shape of a response body, independent of status code, headers or description
distinguish.api.header: the element defines one individual response header rather than the response that contains it

types.title: Responses
types.description: A status-code-keyed map, scoped to exactly one operation, whose keys are HTTP status codes (e.g. '200', '404') or 'default' and whose values are the Response objects describing each possible outcome. It is the container of an operation's outcomes, not any single outcome. Use Response instead when the element describes one outcome (its description, body content, headers, links) under a single status code rather than the whole set of outcomes for an operation. Use Components instead when the element is the reusable registry (components.responses) of named, individually $ref-able Response definitions rather than the status-code map attached to one operation. Use Operation instead when the element is the HTTP method bound to a path that owns the responses map alongside its parameters, request body, security and tags.
evidence: A 'responses:' block nested under an HTTP method in an openapi.yaml/json file, with status-code keys such as '200', '404' or 'default' each pointing to a response definition or $ref.

A Java/Spring handler annotated @ApiResponses({@ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", ...), @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", ...)}), or a NestJS handler stacked with several @ApiResponse({status: ...}) decorators.
A route decorator argument mapping status codes to outcomes, such as FastAPI @app.get(..., responses={404: {...}}) or drf-spectacular @extend_schema(responses={200: Serializer, 404: None}).

distinguish.api.response: the element describes one outcome (its description, body content, headers, links) under a single status code rather than the whole set of outcomes for an operation.
distinguish.api.components: the element is the reusable registry (components.responses) of named, individually $ref-able Response definitions rather than the status-code map attached to one operation.
distinguish.api.operation: the element is the HTTP method bound to a path that owns the responses map alongside its parameters, request body, security and tags.

types.title: Schema
types.description: A data-shape definition, expressed as an OpenAPI 3.0 Schema Object, that constrains the type and structure of a value exchanged over the API, such as a request body, response body, parameter or header value. It is either a named entry under components/schemas or an inline schema nested in a media type, parameter, header or another schema. Use MediaType instead when the element is the MIME-type-keyed content entry (e.g. application/json) that wraps a schema together with examples and encoding, rather than the shape definition itself. Use Parameter instead when the element is a named operation input with a location (path, query, header or cookie), whose value type is merely described by a referenced schema. Use Components instead when the element is the registry that holds reusable schemas, responses and parameters, not an individual type definition. Use Example instead when the element is a concrete sample value illustrating data, rather than the constraints the data must satisfy.
evidence: A DTO or model class used as a route's request or response type and annotated for OpenAPI generation, such as a Pydantic model passed as response_model in FastAPI, a NestJS class with @ApiProperty fields, or a Java class with @Schema.
An entry under '#/components/schemas/' or a 'schema:' block beneath 'content' in an openapi.yaml/json file, containing keywords such as type, properties, required, items, allOf or $ref.
A validation schema object attached to a route definition, such as a Fastify route 'schema: { body, response }', a zod/joi schema converted to OpenAPI, or a model class emitted by openapi-generator.

distinguish.api.mediatype: the element is the MIME-type-keyed content entry (e.g. application/json) that wraps a schema together with examples and encoding, rather than the shape definition itself
distinguish.api.parameter: the element is a named operation input with a location (path, query, header or cookie), whose value type is merely described by a referenced schema
distinguish.api.components: the element is the registry that holds reusable schemas, responses and parameters, not an individual type definition
distinguish.api.example: the element is a concrete sample value illustrating data, rather than the constraints the data must satisfy

types.title: SecurityScheme
types.description: A named declaration in an API description of one mechanism by which clients present credentials: an API key carried in a header, query parameter or cookie; an HTTP authentication scheme such as basic or bearer; a set of OAuth 2.0 flows; or an OpenID Connect discovery URL. It is registered under components.securitySchemes and referenced by name from root-level or operation-level security requirements, which are not themselves instances. Use OAuthFlows instead when modelling the container of grant-type configurations nested inside an oauth2 scheme, rather than the scheme itself. Use OAuthFlow instead when modelling the authorizationUrl, tokenUrl and scopes of a single OAuth 2.0 grant type. Use Parameter instead when a header, query or cookie value is an ordinary operation input rather than a credential the API authenticates, or the API key is only documented as a plain parameter. Use Operation instead when recording that a particular endpoint requires or waives authentication; that is the operation's security requirement referencing this scheme by name.
evidence: An entry under components.securitySchemes in an OpenAPI YAML/JSON file, e.g. bearerAuth: {type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT}.

Framework declarations that emit a scheme into generated OpenAPI, such as FastAPI OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl=...), APIKeyHeader(name='X-API-Key') or HTTPBearer(); springdoc @SecurityScheme(name=..., type=SecuritySchemeType.HTTP, scheme="bearer"); or NestJS DocumentBuilder().addBearerAuth().

Authentication middleware or strategy that reads a credential from a fixed location and is applied across routes, e.g. a passport-jwt/passport-http-bearer strategy, or a middleware checking req.headers['x-api-key'] before handlers run.

distinguish.api.oauthflows: modelling the container of grant-type configurations nested inside an oauth2 scheme, rather than the scheme itself.
distinguish.api.oauthflow: modelling the authorizationUrl, tokenUrl and scopes of a single OAuth 2.0 grant type.
distinguish.api.parameter: a header, query or cookie value is an ordinary operation input rather than a credential the API authenticates, or the API key is only documented as a plain parameter.
distinguish.api.operation: recording that a particular endpoint requires or waives authentication; that is the operation's security requirement referencing this scheme by name.

types.title: Server
types.description: A base-URL declaration in an API description that names a network location (absolute or relative, optionally containing {variable} placeholders) to which operation paths are appended to form request URLs. It is declared in a 'servers' array at document, path or operation scope. Use ServerVariable instead when the element is a single {placeholder} inside a server URL, with its default and allowed values, rather than the URL entry itself. Use PathItem instead when the element is a path template such as /users/{id} appended after the base URL, not the scheme/host/base-path prefix. Use OpenAPIDocument instead when the element is the whole API description that contains the servers array, not one entry within it. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the URL points to human-readable documentation rather than to a location where API requests are sent.
evidence: a 'servers:' list with 'url:' entries in an openapi.yaml/json file, or a @Server(url=...) / @OpenAPIDefinition(servers=...) annotation
a generated API client configured with a basePath or baseURL constant such as 'https://api.example.com/v1', often switched per environment
a framework OpenAPI setup call that sets server URLs, e.g. FastAPI(servers=[{'url': ...}]) or springdoc OpenAPI().servers(List.of(new Server().url(...)))

distinguish.api.servervariable: the element is a single {placeholder} inside a server URL, with its default and allowed values, rather than the URL entry itself
distinguish.api.pathitem: the element is a path template such as /users/{id} appended after the base URL, not the scheme/host/base-path prefix
distinguish.api.openapidocument: the element is the whole API description that contains the servers array, not one entry within it
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the URL points to human-readable documentation rather than to a location where API requests are sent

types.title: ServerVariable
types.description: A substitution rule for a single {placeholder} token in an api.server URL template. It declares the default value, used when no other value is supplied, and may restrict the token to an enumerated set of allowed values. It is identified by the placeholder name used as its key in the parent Server's variables map. Use Server instead when the element is the server URL template itself, or a concrete fixed base URL with no substitutable placeholder, rather than the definition of one placeholder within it. Use Parameter instead when the placeholder sits in a path template such as /users/{id}, or is a query, header or cookie input. Such inputs are supplied per request by the caller, not when the client selects its base URL. Use Example instead when the value is only an illustrative sample for a request, response or parameter, not a default or allowed value constraining a server URL token.
evidence: An OpenAPI YAML/JSON 'servers' entry whose url contains {tenant} or {env}, with a matching 'variables' map entry declaring 'default' and optionally 'enum'.

A springdoc/swagger-annotations @ServerVariable(name=..., defaultValue=..., allowableValues=...) nested inside a @Server annotation. Alternatively, a FastAPI/swagger-jsdoc servers definition carrying a 'variables' dict.
A generated API client exposing a server_variables/serverVariables configuration map, with documented defaults and allowed values used to build the base URL.

distinguish.api.server: the element is the server URL template itself, or a concrete fixed base URL with no substitutable placeholder, rather than the definition of one placeholder within it.
distinguish.api.parameter: the placeholder sits in a path template such as /users/{id}, or is a query, header or cookie input. Such inputs are supplied per request by the caller, not when the client selects its base URL.
distinguish.api.example: the value is only an illustrative sample for a request, response or parameter, not a default or allowed value constraining a server URL token.

types.title: Tag
types.description: A named label in an OpenAPI document, declared in the root 'tags' array or listed in an Operation's 'tags' field, that groups operations into categories for documentation and tooling. It carries only descriptive metadata and has no effect on routing, validation or security. Use PathItem instead when the grouping is defined by a shared URL path pattern, such as all methods on /users/{id}, rather than by a free-form category name. Use ExternalDocumentation instead when the element is the URL and description of an outside documentation resource, even one attached to a tag. Use Components instead when the element is a registry of reusable objects referenced via $ref rather than a categorisation label for operations. Use Info instead when the metadata describes the API as a whole (title, version, terms) rather than one category of operations.
evidence: Controller or router annotations naming a category, e.g. NestJS @ApiTags('users'), springdoc @Tag(name = "Orders"), or Swagger 2 @Api(tags = "...")
Router or decorator arguments listing tag names, e.g. FastAPI APIRouter(tags=["billing"]) or @app.get(..., tags=["items"])
A root-level 'tags:' array in openapi.yaml or openapi.json whose entries have 'name' and 'description' fields, or generated client classes named after tags, such as UsersApi

distinguish.api.pathitem: the grouping is defined by a shared URL path pattern, such as all methods on /users/{id}, rather than by a free-form category name
distinguish.api.externaldocumentation: the element is the URL and description of an outside documentation resource, even one attached to a tag
distinguish.api.components: the element is a registry of reusable objects referenced via $ref rather than a categorisation label for operations
distinguish.api.info: the metadata describes the API as a whole (title, version, terms) rather than one category of operations

layers.name: Data Model Layer
layers.scope: Defines the logical data model: object schemas and their properties, enumerations, validation rules and the relationships between entities, independent of any particular storage technology (JSON Schema Draft 7). Entity classes, ORM models, DTO and record types, and type definitions that describe domain data are evidence for elements here; how that data is persisted belongs to the data-store layer. Modelling rules: data-model elements are passive structure; they are realized, accessed, referenced and mapped, and never serve, trigger or perform behaviour. A subschema written in place is part of what declares it (composes): a schema document composes its root schema and the definitions declared in it, an object schema composes its properties, an array schema its inline item schema, a composition its inline branches, and a property the value constraints it carries. A type declared elsewhere and reached by $ref or by name is referenced (references): a property references the object schema or definition its value takes, an array or composition references a named definition, and a Reference references the definition, object schema or document it points at. Subtyping is specializes. An entity class, an ORM model whatever the framework, or a type whose shape is published as a schema is an object schema; an in-code structure that only carries data between parts of the program is an application data object, which an object schema may realize. Object schemas and definitions realize the application data objects and business objects they give form to (a direct link to the business object is a shortcut through the data object), and map to their counterparts in other layers (maps-to): API schemas, request bodies, responses and parameters, and data-store collections. Behaviour reaches data by accessing it: application functions, components and events access object schemas and definitions, and business behaviour accesses the business objects they realize; a schema does not reference the behaviour that uses it. Schemas satisfy the requirements and constraints that govern the data but do not realize goals. The model is independent of technology: it does not depend on system software or use technology services, and the file that holds a schema document maps to a technology artifact.

types.title: ArraySchema
types.description: A JSON Schema subschema with type 'array' that constrains an ordered list of values: the schema each element must satisfy, how many elements are allowed, whether they must be distinct, and whether at least one element must match a given subschema. Use SchemaProperty instead when you are modelling the named field that holds the list (its name, title, description, readOnly) rather than the constraints on the list value itself. Use ObjectSchema instead when the collection is keyed by name rather than ordered by position, such as a Map<String, T>, dict or record type, which becomes an object with additionalProperties or patternProperties. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the list type is declared once under 'definitions' with a title and reused through $ref. Model the array constraints inside it as an arrayschema. Use SchemaComposition instead when the constraint is a boolean combination (allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not) of subschemas, for example a union of element types, rather than array keywords directly.
evidence: A DTO, entity or record field typed as a collection, such as List<T>, T[], Array<T>, Set<T>, Sequence[T] or repeated in protobuf, where Set or frozenset types imply uniqueItems.

Cardinality validators on a collection field, such as Bean Validation @Size(min, max) or @NotEmpty on a List, Pydantic conlist or Field(min_length=..., max_length=...), or Zod z.array(...).min().max().nonempty().
A JSON Schema or OpenAPI fragment containing "type": "array" together with an "items" keyword, often with minItems, maxItems or uniqueItems.

distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: you are modelling the named field that holds the list (its name, title, description, readOnly) rather than the constraints on the list value itself.
distinguish.data-model.objectschema: the collection is keyed by name rather than ordered by position, such as a Map<String, T>, dict or record type, which becomes an object with additionalProperties or patternProperties.
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the list type is declared once under 'definitions' with a title and reused through $ref. Model the array constraints inside it as an arrayschema.
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: the constraint is a boolean combination (allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not) of subschemas, for example a union of element types, rather than array keywords directly.

types.title: JSONSchema
types.description: A top-level schema document that is the unit of identity and $ref resolution in the data model: it declares a dialect via $schema and a base URI via $id, and contains the root type constraint plus any named subschemas under definitions. Only the outermost schema of a file or registered document qualifies; nested subschemas do not. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the schema is a named, reusable subschema nested under a document's definitions keyword rather than the document itself. Use ObjectSchema instead when you are modelling the object-level constraints (properties, required, additionalProperties) of a schema rather than the document that carries $schema/$id. Use Reference instead when the element is only a $ref pointer to another schema, not a self-contained document with its own $id. Use SchemaComposition instead when the element combines subschemas with allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not rather than being an identified root document.
evidence: a *.schema.json or *.json file whose top-level object contains "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#" and an "$id" URI
a schema registered with a validator by URI, e.g. ajv.addSchema(schema, 'https://example.com/order.json') or compile() called on a loaded file
a build step or decorator that emits a whole schema document per model, e.g. pydantic Model.model_json_schema() or zod-to-json-schema output written to a schemas/ directory

distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the schema is a named, reusable subschema nested under a document's definitions keyword rather than the document itself
distinguish.data-model.objectschema: you are modelling the object-level constraints (properties, required, additionalProperties) of a schema rather than the document that carries $schema/$id
distinguish.data-model.reference: the element is only a $ref pointer to another schema, not a self-contained document with its own $id
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: the element combines subschemas with allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not rather than being an identified root document

types.title: NumericSchema
types.description: A schema constraining JSON number or integer values through validation keywords: inclusive or exclusive lower and upper bounds, or a divisibility step (multipleOf). It describes the value space of a numeric datum, independent of the field that carries it or how the value is stored. Use SchemaProperty instead when the element is a named field of an object (e.g. Order.quantity) carrying its own title, default, readOnly or description; the numeric constraints it applies may be modelled as a NumericSchema that the property composes. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the numeric type is a named, reusable definition under 'definitions' (e.g. a 'Percentage' type referenced via $ref), especially one restricted to an enum of fixed values rather than a range. Use StringSchema instead when the value is serialized as a string even though it looks numeric, e.g. a decimal-as-string money amount, a zero-padded code or a phone number constrained by pattern or length. Use SchemaComposition instead when the numeric constraint is formed by combining subschemas with allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not, e.g. 'positive OR null', rather than by a single set of bounds.
evidence: a JSON Schema or OpenAPI fragment with "type": "integer" or "number" plus minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum or multipleOf keywords
a numeric field annotated with range validators, e.g. Java @Min/@Max/@DecimalMin/@Positive, Pydantic Field(ge=0, le=100) or conint(gt=0), or Zod z.number().int().min(1)
a declared numeric value type or constrained alias with range checks in its constructor or validator, e.g. a Percentage or Quantity class that rejects values outside 0..100 or non-integers

distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: the element is a named field of an object (e.g. Order.quantity) carrying its own title, default, readOnly or description; the numeric constraints it applies may be modelled as a NumericSchema that the property references.
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the numeric type is a named, reusable definition under 'definitions' (e.g. a 'Percentage' type referenced via $ref), especially one restricted to an enum of fixed values rather than a range.
distinguish.data-model.stringschema: the value is serialized as a string even though it looks numeric, e.g. a decimal-as-string money amount, a zero-padded code or a phone number constrained by pattern or length.
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: the numeric constraint is formed by combining subschemas with allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not, e.g. 'positive OR null', rather than by a single set of bounds.

types.title: ObjectSchema
types.description: A schema node of type 'object' that constrains JSON object instances by declaring a set of named, typed properties, which of those properties must be present, and rules for undeclared or dynamically named keys. In code it corresponds to a structured domain record whose shape is part of the data model (an entity class, an ORM model whatever the framework, or a DTO, record or interface whose shape is published as a schema), not to an individual field or to a primitive type alias. Use application DataObject instead when the structure only carries data between parts of the program and is neither persisted as an entity nor published as a schema; an object schema may realize such a data object. Use SchemaProperty instead when the symbol is a single field, column or attribute inside a structure rather than the structure that owns the fields. Use JSONSchema instead when the element is the root schema document or file, identified by $schema and $id and holding definitions, rather than one object shape described within it. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the named reusable type is a primitive alias or enumeration (e.g. a TypeScript enum, a branded string type, a Python Enum) with no named fields of its own. Use SchemaComposition instead when the type is defined only by combining other schemas (union, intersection, discriminated oneOf, negation) rather than by declaring its own properties; plain class inheritance stays an objectschema with a specializes relationship.
evidence: A class annotated @Entity/@Table, a Django models.Model subclass, or a SQLAlchemy declarative class whose attributes declare domain fields
A TypeScript interface or type literal, Pydantic BaseModel, Python @dataclass, Java record, or Go struct with named typed fields used as a DTO or request/response payload
A JSON Schema or OpenAPI components.schemas entry with "type": "object" and a "properties" map, or a z.object()/Joi.object()/yup.object() validator declaration

distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: the symbol is a single field, column or attribute inside a structure rather than the structure that owns the fields
distinguish.data-model.jsonschema: the element is the root schema document or file, identified by $schema and $id and holding definitions, rather than one object shape described within it
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the named reusable type is a primitive alias or enumeration (e.g. a TypeScript enum, a branded string type, a Python Enum) with no named fields of its own
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: the type is defined only by combining other schemas (union, intersection, discriminated oneOf, negation) rather than by declaring its own properties; plain class inheritance stays an objectschema with an extends relationship

types.title: Reference
types.description: A schema node whose only effective content is a $ref keyword holding a URI or JSON Pointer fragment (e.g. '#/definitions/Address') that delegates validation of an instance to another schema, adding no constraints of its own. A usage site that points at a type declared elsewhere, not the declaration of that type. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the element is the named, reusable type being pointed at (the target under 'definitions'), rather than the pointer to it. Use SchemaProperty instead when the element is a named property of an object schema that also carries its own type, description, default or other constraints, even if it uses $ref to obtain its type. Use SchemaComposition instead when the $ref must be combined with further constraints or alternatives, which in Draft 7 requires wrapping it in allOf/anyOf/oneOf. Use JSONSchema instead when the element is the whole root schema document with $schema and $id, not a pointer into or toward one.
evidence: A literal "$ref": "#/definitions/..." or "$ref": "other.schema.json#/..." entry in a JSON/YAML schema or an OpenAPI components file
A field in a DTO, Pydantic model or TypeScript interface typed by another separately declared model class (e.g. 'billing: Address'), which schema generators emit as a $ref

Schema-generator configuration or decorators that hoist nested types into shared definitions, such as Pydantic's ref_template, zod-to-json-schema $refStrategy, or @ApiProperty({ type: () => Address })

distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the element is the named, reusable type being pointed at (the target under 'definitions'), rather than the pointer to it
distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: the element is a named property of an object schema that also carries its own type, description, default or other constraints, even if it uses $ref to obtain its type
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: the $ref must be combined with further constraints or alternatives, which in Draft 7 requires wrapping it in allOf/anyOf/oneOf
distinguish.data-model.jsonschema: the element is the whole root schema document with $schema and $id, not a pointer into or toward one

types.title: SchemaComposition
types.description: A schema node whose validation outcome is computed by applying boolean logic (allOf, anyOf, oneOf, not) to the outcomes of one or more subschemas, rather than by constraining the instance's type, properties, items, length or bounds directly. In code it corresponds to union, intersection, discriminated-variant or negation types built from other data types. Use Reference instead when the node is a single $ref pointer to another schema with no boolean combination; a lone $ref wrapped in a one-element allOf only to attach sibling constraints is still a composition. Use ObjectSchema instead when the structure comes from declared properties, required and additionalProperties on one object, not from merging or choosing among separate subschemas (e.g. a class extending a base is modelled as one object unless the base is a distinct schema combined via allOf). Use SchemaDefinition instead when the subject is the named, reusable entry under definitions itself; a definition whose body is an anyOf/oneOf is a schemadefinition, and the composition is referenced from where it is used. Use StringSchema instead when a set of allowed string literals is expressed with enum or const on one string schema rather than as oneOf over separate subschemas.
evidence: A TypeScript union or intersection type alias (type Payment = Card | BankTransfer; type Admin = User & Permissions), or a Python Union[...]/Annotated discriminated union field in a Pydantic model
Serialization polymorphism annotations such as Jackson @JsonTypeInfo/@JsonSubTypes, a Pydantic Field(discriminator=...), or OpenAPI/JSON Schema files containing allOf, anyOf, oneOf or not keys
Validator-library combinators that join other schemas: zod z.union/z.discriminatedUnion/z.intersection/.and(), Joi alternatives().try(), or io-ts t.union/t.intersection

distinguish.data-model.reference: the node is a single $ref pointer to another schema with no boolean combination; a lone $ref wrapped in a one-element allOf only to attach sibling constraints is still a composition.
distinguish.data-model.objectschema: the structure comes from declared properties, required and additionalProperties on one object, not from merging or choosing among separate subschemas (e.g. a class extending a base is modelled as one object unless the base is a distinct schema combined via allOf).
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the subject is the named, reusable entry under definitions itself; a definition whose body is an anyOf/oneOf is a schemadefinition that aggregates a composition.
distinguish.data-model.stringschema: a set of allowed string literals is expressed with enum or const on one string schema rather than as oneOf over separate subschemas.

types.title: SchemaDefinition
types.description: A named, reusable subschema declared under a JSON Schema document's 'definitions' keyword and addressable as '$ref: #/definitions/{name}'. It describes one domain data type, such as an entity, value object, DTO or enumeration, that other schemas or properties reuse by name rather than declaring inline. Use ObjectSchema instead when you are modelling the structural constraints of an object (its properties, required list, additionalProperties) rather than the named, reusable type entry that carries them. Use SchemaProperty instead when the schema is a single field declared inline within a parent schema's properties and is not reused by name elsewhere. Use JSONSchema instead when the element is the root schema document with its own $schema and $id, not an entry within its definitions. Use Reference instead when the element is only the $ref pointer that points at a definition, not the definition itself.
evidence: an entry under "definitions" (or "$defs", or OpenAPI "components.schemas") in a .schema.json or spec file that is targeted by one or more "$ref": "#/definitions/..." pointers
an exported entity, DTO or record class, a TypeScript interface or type alias, or a Pydantic/zod model that other types import and use as a field type
an exported enum type (e.g. a Java enum, TypeScript enum or Python Enum subclass) whose values represent a fixed domain vocabulary used by several models

distinguish.data-model.objectschema: you are modelling the structural constraints of an object (its properties, required list, additionalProperties) rather than the named, reusable type entry that carries them
distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: the schema is a single field declared inline within a parent schema's properties and is not reused by name elsewhere
distinguish.data-model.jsonschema: the element is the root schema document with its own $schema and $id, not an entry within its definitions
distinguish.data-model.reference: the element is only the $ref pointer that points at a definition, not the definition itself

types.title: SchemaProperty
types.description: A single named field of an object schema, such as one attribute of a domain entity, DTO or record type, together with the subschema that governs its value: type, value restrictions (enum, const, format, default) and annotations (title, description, readOnly, writeOnly, examples). It corresponds to one entry under an ObjectSchema's 'properties' keyword and has no meaning apart from its owning object. Use ObjectSchema instead when the element is the whole entity, class or record that owns several fields, rather than one field of it. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the schema is a named, reusable type declared under 'definitions' (for example a shared enum or value type referenced by several fields) rather than a field belonging to one owning object. Use StringSchema instead when you are modelling the string constraints of the value (minLength, maxLength, pattern, format) apart from the field, which the property then composes; a reusable named string type is a SchemaDefinition. Use NumericSchema instead when you are modelling the numeric bounds or multipleOf rule of the value apart from the field, which the property then composes.
evidence: An attribute declared on an ORM entity class, such as a JPA @Column field, a SQLAlchemy Column(...) or a Django models.CharField.
A typed member of a DTO, Pydantic/dataclass model, TypeScript interface or protobuf message, often carrying a validator, default value or Field(...) metadata.
A key nested under 'properties' in a JSON Schema file or an OpenAPI components/schemas entry, with its own 'type', 'format' or 'enum'.

distinguish.data-model.objectschema: the element is the whole entity, class or record that owns several fields, rather than one field of it.
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the schema is a named, reusable type declared under 'definitions' (for example a shared enum or value type referenced by several fields) rather than a field belonging to one owning object.
distinguish.data-model.stringschema: you are modelling a reusable bundle of string constraints (minLength, maxLength, pattern) that a property points to, rather than the field itself.
distinguish.data-model.numericschema: you are modelling a reusable bundle of numeric bounds or a multipleOf rule that a property points to, rather than the field itself.

types.title: StringSchema
types.description: A JSON Schema subschema whose type is 'string' and which constrains string instances through at least one string-specific keyword: minLength, maxLength, pattern or format. A bare type: 'string' with no such keyword is not enough. Use SchemaProperty instead when the element is the named member of an object (its name, documentation, default, readOnly/writeOnly), rather than the string constraint set that the property composes. Use SchemaDefinition instead when the string type is declared as a named, reusable entry under 'definitions' and referenced via $ref, especially an enumerated string type defined mainly by its enum values. Use Reference instead when the code only points to another schema via $ref and declares no length, pattern or format constraints of its own. Use SchemaComposition instead when string constraints are combined with other subschemas through allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not, and the combination itself is the element being modelled.
evidence: A JSON/YAML schema fragment of the form {"type": "string", "maxLength": 255, "pattern": "^[A-Z]{3}$"} or one carrying a "format" keyword, embedded in a schema file or OpenAPI components
A string field declared with validation constraints, such as Pydantic constr(min_length=…, regex=…) or Field(max_length=…), Zod z.string().min().max().email(), or Joi.string().pattern()
A Java/Kotlin String field annotated with Bean Validation constraints such as @Size(min=…, max=…), @Pattern(regexp=…), or @Email in an entity or DTO class

distinguish.data-model.schemaproperty: the element is the named member of an object (its name, documentation, default, readOnly/writeOnly), rather than the string constraint set that the property references or embeds
distinguish.data-model.schemadefinition: the string type is declared as a named, reusable entry under 'definitions' and referenced via $ref, especially an enumerated string type defined mainly by its enum values
distinguish.data-model.reference: the code only points to another schema via $ref and declares no length, pattern or format constraints of its own
distinguish.data-model.schemacomposition: string constraints are combined with other subschemas through allOf/anyOf/oneOf/not, and the combination itself is the element being modelled

layers.name: Data Store Layer
layers.scope: Describes physical persistence: databases and schemas, tables and collections, columns and fields, indexes, constraints, views, migrations, access patterns and the queries that read and write them (ISO/IEC 9075 SQL with extensions for document, key-value and graph paradigms). Migration scripts, table definitions and repository or DAO code that talks to storage are evidence for elements here. Modelling rules: containment is one level at a time: a database composes namespaces, or collections and views directly when the engine has none; a namespace composes collections, views, stored logic and nested namespaces; a collection composes its fields, indexes, validation rules and event handlers, and may compose partitions. Stored data is passive: collections, views, fields and databases are accessed, referenced and mapped, and never serve or trigger; application components, functions and services access the collections and views they read and write. Behaviour inside the store is stored logic, event handlers and access patterns: event handlers are attached to a collection, reference the fields they watch and trigger stored logic; stored logic accesses collections, triggers other stored logic and refreshes views; access patterns access a collection, use indexes and reference the fields in their key and filter conditions, and serve the application functions that issue them. Validation rules reference the fields they constrain, and a foreign key cascades to the collection it references. Views derive from collections and views; retention policies govern collections and namespaces, archive to collections and trigger the stored logic that purges them. Across layers, the store reaches the business through the application layer and the data model: stored logic realizes application functions, event handlers trigger application events, object schemas map to collections, and a collection may realize a business object as a shortcut; a view maps to the API response it backs.

types.title: AccessPattern
types.description: A single named read or write operation against one collection, characterized by its key condition, optional sort and filter conditions, and operation category, as issued by application code or listed in a data-model design. It describes the request shape the application sends to the store, not a structure or computation stored in the engine. Use StoredLogic instead when the computation is defined and registered inside the database engine (SQL function or procedure, aggregation pipeline saved server-side, Lua script loaded via SCRIPT LOAD) rather than issued as a query from application code. Use View instead when the query is persisted in the schema as a named derived collection (CREATE VIEW, materialized view, search alias) that other queries read from. Use Index instead when the element is the physical lookup structure (CREATE INDEX, GSI, vector index) that makes a lookup efficient, not the lookup itself. Use EventHandler instead when the logic runs reactively in response to a data-change event (trigger, change stream, CDC consumer) rather than being requested by an application call.
evidence: a repository or DAO method that issues one parameterized query against a single table or collection, e.g. Spring Data findByCustomerIdAndStatus, an @Query annotation, or a Mongoose Model.find({customerId}) call
a DynamoDB GetItem/Query/PutItem/BatchWriteItem call, or a Cassandra prepared statement, carrying a KeyConditionExpression or WHERE clause on partition and clustering keys
a data-model design document or single-table-design spreadsheet that enumerates access patterns with their PK/SK expressions, GSI used, and expected request rate

distinguish.data-store.storedlogic: the computation is defined and registered inside the database engine (SQL function or procedure, aggregation pipeline saved server-side, Lua script loaded via SCRIPT LOAD) rather than issued as a query from application code
distinguish.data-store.view: the query is persisted in the schema as a named derived collection (CREATE VIEW, materialized view, search alias) that other queries read from
distinguish.data-store.index: the element is the physical lookup structure (CREATE INDEX, GSI, vector index) that makes a lookup efficient, not the lookup itself
distinguish.data-store.eventhandler: the logic runs reactively in response to a data-change event (trigger, change stream, CDC consumer) rather than being requested by an application call

types.title: Collection
types.description: A named, persistent container that directly stores base records, documents, key-value entries, nodes or edges inside a database or namespace, and whose contents are written to it rather than derived from other containers. It maps to a SQL base table, document collection, key-value bucket or structure, column family, vector collection, time-series measurement or hypertable, graph node label or edge type, and search-engine index. Use View instead when the container's contents are computed from one or more other collections by a query, alias or continuous aggregate rather than written to it directly. Use Namespace instead when the element groups several containers (SQL schema, Cassandra keyspace, MongoDB database, Redis key prefix) and does not itself hold records. Use Index instead when the structure exists only to speed up lookups over another container's fields (B-tree, HNSW, inverted index) and is not queried as the data's home; an Elasticsearch index holding documents remains a collection. Use Field instead when the element is a single named attribute or property of records, such as a column, document path or graph property, rather than the container of records. Use data-model ObjectSchema instead when the symbol is the entity or ORM class that describes the records' logical shape; a table declared by an ORM class is both, and the object schema maps to the collection.
evidence: A CREATE TABLE, CREATE COLUMNFAMILY or create_hypertable statement in a migration or DDL file, or a db.createCollection / client.indices.create call with mappings.

An ORM or ODM mapping that binds a class to a named store container, such as a JPA @Entity/@Table, SQLAlchemy __tablename__, Django Model Meta.db_table, Mongoose model('Order', schema) or Spring @Document(collection=...).

An infrastructure-as-code resource declaring a container with keys or TTL, such as a Terraform aws_dynamodb_table with hash_key/range_key, a Pinecone or Qdrant collection with a vector size, or a Neo4j label used in MERGE (:Label) setup scripts.

distinguish.data-store.view: the container's contents are computed from one or more other collections by a query, alias or continuous aggregate rather than written to it directly.
distinguish.data-store.namespace: the element groups several containers (SQL schema, Cassandra keyspace, MongoDB database, Redis key prefix) and does not itself hold records.
distinguish.data-store.index: the structure exists only to speed up lookups over another container's fields (B-tree, HNSW, inverted index) and is not queried as the data's home; an Elasticsearch index holding documents remains a collection.
distinguish.data-store.field: the element is a single named attribute or property of records, such as a column, document path or graph property, rather than the container of records.

types.title: Database
types.description: A named, independently addressable data store deployment, typically a database or catalog on a specific engine reached through its own connection endpoint or connection string, that contains namespaces and collections. It is the outermost persistence boundary an application connects to, regardless of paradigm. Use Namespace instead when the element is a logical grouping inside a connected deployment. Examples include a PostgreSQL schema, a Cassandra keyspace, a Redis key prefix, or a MongoDB 'database' selected on an already-open client connection. Use Collection instead when the element is a single container of records, such as a table, a DynamoDB table, an Elasticsearch index, or a vector collection, rather than the deployment that hosts it. Use View instead when the element is a derived or virtual container defined by a query over existing collections, not a separately deployed store.
evidence: A connection URL or DSN in configuration or environment variables naming an engine, host and database, e.g. DATABASE_URL=postgres://db:5432/orders, MONGO_URI or spring.datasource.url.

An infrastructure declaration provisioning a store, e.g. a docker-compose service using a postgres/mongo/redis image with POSTGRES_DB, or a Terraform aws_db_instance, aws_dynamodb_table group or google_sql_database resource.

An ORM or driver datasource block registering a named connection, e.g. a Prisma 'datasource db' with a provider, Django DATABASES['default'], or SQLAlchemy create_engine()/Mongoose connect() invoked at application startup.

distinguish.data-store.namespace: the element is a logical grouping inside a connected deployment. Examples include a PostgreSQL schema, a Cassandra keyspace, a Redis key prefix, or a MongoDB 'database' selected on an already-open client connection.
distinguish.data-store.collection: the element is a single container of records, such as a table, a DynamoDB table, an Elasticsearch index, or a vector collection, rather than the deployment that hosts it.
distinguish.data-store.view: the element is a derived or virtual container defined by a query over existing collections, not a separately deployed store.

types.title: EventHandler
types.description: A registered binding, declared in or against a data store, that attaches to a collection or database scope and runs an action automatically when specified data-change events or data conditions occur there (SQL trigger, change-stream or CDC subscription, keyspace notification, watcher or alert rule). It is the activation wiring (event, timing, granularity, filter), not the computation body it invokes. Use StoredLogic instead when the symbol is the function, procedure, Lua script or pipeline body that does the work (e.g. the trigger function created by CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS trigger), not the declaration that binds it to events. Use ValidationRule instead when integrity is enforced declaratively by the engine (CHECK, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, JSON Schema validator) rather than by a BEFORE trigger that runs code to reject or rewrite rows. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the mechanism is a TTL, ILM or downsampling policy that expires or moves data by age, rather than reacting to individual insert, update, delete or expiry events with custom logic. Use View instead when derived data is kept current by a materialized view or continuous aggregate refresh policy rather than by a handler that writes to another collection on each change.
evidence: A migration or DDL file containing CREATE TRIGGER ... BEFORE|AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON <table> FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION <fn>()

Code or config opening a change feed on a store, e.g. MongoDB collection.watch([{ $match: ... }]), a DynamoDB StreamSpecification with a Lambda event source mapping, or a Debezium connector config listing table.include.list
Redis setup issuing CONFIG SET notify-keyspace-events (or notify-keyspace-events in redis.conf) together with a PSUBSCRIBE on __keyspace@*__ or __keyevent@*__ channels

distinguish.data-store.storedlogic: the symbol is the function, procedure, Lua script or pipeline body that does the work (e.g. the trigger function created by CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURNS trigger), not the declaration that binds it to events.
distinguish.data-store.validationrule: integrity is enforced declaratively by the engine (CHECK, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, JSON Schema validator) rather than by a BEFORE trigger that runs code to reject or rewrite rows.
distinguish.data-store.retentionpolicy: the mechanism is a TTL, ILM or downsampling policy that expires or moves data by age, rather than reacting to individual insert, update, delete or expiry events with custom logic.
distinguish.data-store.view: derived data is kept current by a materialized view or continuous aggregate refresh policy rather than by a handler that writes to another collection on each change.

types.title: Field
types.description: A named, typed data element declared in the physical structure of a persisted collection, whose value is stored for each record. Covers a SQL column, document field or path, hash field, wide-column column, time-series tag or field, vector or metadata field, graph property, and search-engine mapping property. Use Collection instead when the symbol declares the container of records (table, collection, bucket, measurement, node label) rather than one named element inside it. Use Index instead when the symbol declares a lookup structure over one or more existing fields (CREATE INDEX, createIndex, mapping index option) rather than the stored element itself. Use ValidationRule instead when the symbol is a separately declared constraint (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, UNIQUE, JSON Schema required list) that restricts field values, rather than the field declaration. Use View instead when the column appears only in a derived query or projection (SELECT list of a view, continuous aggregate) and is not stored in a base collection.
evidence: a column clause inside CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN in a migration script (e.g. 'email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL')
an ORM-mapped attribute such as a JPA @Column field, SQLAlchemy Column(...), Django models.CharField, or Prisma model field line
an entry under a document or search schema definition, such as a Mongoose schema path, a MongoDB $jsonSchema property, or an Elasticsearch mappings.properties key with a type

distinguish.data-store.collection: the symbol declares the container of records (table, collection, bucket, measurement, node label) rather than one named element inside it
distinguish.data-store.index: the symbol declares a lookup structure over one or more existing fields (CREATE INDEX, createIndex, mapping index option) rather than the stored element itself
distinguish.data-store.validationrule: the symbol is a separately declared constraint (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, UNIQUE, JSON Schema required list) that restricts field values, rather than the field declaration
distinguish.data-store.view: the column appears only in a derived query or projection (SELECT list of a view, continuous aggregate) and is not stored in a base collection

types.title: Index
types.description: A lookup structure the data store engine maintains alongside a collection's or view's records, keyed on one or more of its fields with a declared access method (B-tree, hash, inverted, ANN, geospatial and similar). Queries use it to locate matching entries without scanning the whole collection. Use ValidationRule instead when the declaration is a PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY constraint whose purpose is rejecting invalid data, even if the engine backs it with an implicit index; model a separate Index only when the index is declared explicitly. Use Collection instead when the thing called an 'index' is itself the container of documents or vectors, such as an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index (collectionType SEARCH_INDEX) or a Pinecone index, rather than an auxiliary structure over another container's fields. Use AccessPattern instead when the code or documentation describes the shape of a read or write (key condition, filter, frequency) rather than a structure declared to the engine. Use View instead when the structure holds derived rows that are queried directly, such as a materialized view or continuous aggregate, rather than pointers back to the source records.
evidence: A CREATE INDEX / CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statement (optionally with USING gin|hnsw|ivfflat or a WHERE predicate) in a migration script, or a migration-tool call such as op.create_index, add_index, or knex table.index().
An ORM or schema declaration of an index: Prisma @@index, Django Meta.indexes, SQLAlchemy Index(...) in __table_args__, JPA @Table(indexes=@Index(...)), or a Mongoose schema.index({...}) call.

Engine-specific index provisioning: a MongoDB createIndex({...}, {partialFilterExpression, sparse}) call, DynamoDB GlobalSecondaryIndexes/LocalSecondaryIndexes in CloudFormation or Terraform, or a Cassandra CREATE CUSTOM INDEX / SAI statement.

distinguish.data-store.validationrule: the declaration is a PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE or FOREIGN KEY constraint whose purpose is rejecting invalid data, even if the engine backs it with an implicit index; model a separate Index only when the index is declared explicitly.
distinguish.data-store.collection: the thing called an 'index' is itself the container of documents or vectors, such as an Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index (collectionType SEARCH_INDEX) or a Pinecone index, rather than an auxiliary structure over another container's fields.
distinguish.data-store.accesspattern: the code or documentation describes the shape of a read or write (key condition, filter, frequency) rather than a structure declared to the engine.
distinguish.data-store.view: the structure holds derived rows that are queried directly, such as a materialized view or continuous aggregate, rather than pointers back to the source records.

types.title: Namespace
types.description: A named logical container inside a single database instance that scopes the names of collections, views, indexes, stored logic and other database objects, but does not itself hold records. Corresponds to an SQL schema, a MongoDB database, a Cassandra keyspace, a Redis key prefix convention, a vector-store namespace, or a graph named graph. Use Database instead when the element is the deployed engine instance or server/cluster that you connect to (host, engine, version, deployment model), not a name-scoping container within it. Use Collection instead when the element directly stores records, documents, keys or vectors, such as a table, a MongoDB collection, a Cassandra table, or an Elasticsearch index that holds documents. Use View instead when the element is a derived or virtual record set defined by a query or alias over source collections rather than a container that scopes object names.
evidence: a migration or DDL script containing CREATE SCHEMA, CREATE KEYSPACE, or CREATE DATABASE inside a MongoDB/MySQL-style server, or a USE <name> statement
ORM or mapping configuration that qualifies tables with a schema name, e.g. @Table(schema="billing"), SQLAlchemy MetaData(schema="billing"), or Prisma @@schema("billing")

client code selecting a scoped container by name, e.g. mongoClient.getDatabase("orders"), session.execute("USE analytics"), a Pinecone upsert(namespace="tenant-42"), or a constant Redis key prefix such as "cart:" applied to every key

distinguish.data-store.database: the element is the deployed engine instance or server/cluster that you connect to (host, engine, version, deployment model), not a name-scoping container within it
distinguish.data-store.collection: the element directly stores records, documents, keys or vectors, such as a table, a MongoDB collection, a Cassandra table, or an Elasticsearch index that holds documents
distinguish.data-store.view: the element is a derived or virtual record set defined by a query or alias over source collections rather than a container that scopes object names

types.title: RetentionPolicy
types.description: A data lifecycle rule, declared in or enforced by the data store, that sets a maximum age for records in a collection or namespace and names the single action (delete, archive, downsample, move tier or compress) applied to records older than that age. Use ValidationRule instead when the rule constrains or rejects writes, such as a TTL_CONSTRAINT requiring every key to carry an expiry, rather than removing or transforming data that has aged out. Use StoredLogic instead when the symbol is the executable job, function or continuous query that performs the purge or rollup; the policy only declares age and action and triggers that logic. Use View instead when the downsampled result is a queryable derived collection such as a TimescaleDB continuous aggregate; the retention policy governs only when the source data expires. Use EventHandler instead when the code reacts to expiry or deletion events, such as a Redis keyspace EXPIRE notification listener, instead of defining when data expires.
evidence: A migration or setup script containing InfluxDB `CREATE RETENTION POLICY ... DURATION 30d`, TimescaleDB `add_retention_policy('metrics', INTERVAL '90 days')`, or pg_partman `retention` settings on a partitioned table
An Elasticsearch ILM or OpenSearch ISM policy document with phases such as `delete.min_age`, or IaC declaring DynamoDB `TimeToLiveSpecification` or S3 lifecycle rules for a storage bucket
A MongoDB index created with `expireAfterSeconds`, or a scheduled purge job (cron or worker) issuing `DELETE ... WHERE created_at < now() - interval` or dropping old partitions

distinguish.data-store.validationrule: the rule constrains or rejects writes, such as a TTL_CONSTRAINT requiring every key to carry an expiry, rather than removing or transforming data that has aged out
distinguish.data-store.storedlogic: the symbol is the executable job, function or continuous query that performs the purge or rollup; the policy only declares age and action and triggers that logic
distinguish.data-store.view: the downsampled result is a queryable derived collection such as a TimescaleDB continuous aggregate; the retention policy governs only when the source data expires
distinguish.data-store.eventhandler: the code reacts to expiry or deletion events, such as a Redis keyspace EXPIRE notification listener, instead of defining when data expires

types.title: StoredLogic
types.description: A named unit of executable logic that is deployed into and executed by the data store engine itself, such as an SQL function, procedure or package, a Redis Lua script or function, a Cassandra UDF/UDA, a Neo4j procedure, an Elasticsearch ingest pipeline or Painless script, or a scheduled time-series task. It is invoked by name, by an event handler, or on a schedule, rather than shipped as a query text by application code. Use EventHandler instead when the element is the binding that fires on a data-change event (CREATE TRIGGER, a change-stream subscription, a keyspace notification listener), not the routine body that the binding calls. Use View instead when the stored query is exposed as a readable derived collection (CREATE VIEW, a materialized view, a continuous aggregate, a search alias) that clients select from, rather than a routine they invoke. Use AccessPattern instead when the query or aggregation pipeline is built and sent ad hoc by repository/DAO code on each call and is never registered in the engine. Use ValidationRule instead when the integrity check is a declarative constraint (CHECK, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, JSON Schema validator, strict mapping) rather than procedural code.
evidence: A migration or schema file containing CREATE [OR REPLACE] FUNCTION, CREATE PROCEDURE or CREATE PACKAGE with a LANGUAGE clause (plpgsql, tsql, java) and a routine body, e.g. a $$-delimited block
A .lua script file loaded with SCRIPT LOAD and called via EVALSHA, or registered with redis.register_function / ioredis defineCommand

Application code calling a routine by name (JDBC CallableStatement '{call ...}', Python cursor.callproc, Spring @Procedure, Npgsql CommandType.StoredProcedure), or engine config such as PUT _ingest/pipeline/<name> or an InfluxDB task with 'option task = {every: ...}'

distinguish.data-store.eventhandler: the element is the binding that fires on a data-change event (CREATE TRIGGER, a change-stream subscription, a keyspace notification listener), not the routine body that the binding calls
distinguish.data-store.view: the stored query is exposed as a readable derived collection (CREATE VIEW, a materialized view, a continuous aggregate, a search alias) that clients select from, rather than a routine they invoke
distinguish.data-store.accesspattern: the query or aggregation pipeline is built and sent ad hoc by repository/DAO code on each call and is never registered in the engine
distinguish.data-store.validationrule: the integrity check is a declarative constraint (CHECK, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY, JSON Schema validator, strict mapping) rather than procedural code

types.title: ValidationRule
types.description: A declarative integrity constraint, declared in the data store's schema or collection configuration and enforced by the storage engine itself, that restricts which records, field values, keys or cross-collection references a write may produce. Application-side validation that the engine never sees, and imperative checks coded in triggers or procedures, are not instances. Use EventHandler instead when the check is imperative logic fired by a change event, such as a BEFORE INSERT trigger that raises an exception, rather than a declared constraint. Use Index instead when the declaration is an index created mainly to speed up lookups; a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint that the engine happens to back with an index is still a validationrule. Use Field instead when the only restriction is the field's declared dataType, nullable flag, default or generation rule, with no separately named or declared constraint. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the rule governs how long data is kept and expires, deletes, archives or downsamples it, rather than rejecting or flagging invalid writes.
evidence: Migration or DDL statements containing constraint clauses, such as ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT, PRIMARY KEY (...), FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES ... ON DELETE CASCADE, or CHECK (...).

Engine-level validator or constraint commands, such as MongoDB createCollection/collMod with validator: {$jsonSchema: ...} and validationAction, or Neo4j CREATE CONSTRAINT ... REQUIRE n.email IS UNIQUE / IS NOT NULL.

ORM or schema-config declarations that emit engine constraints, such as SQLAlchemy CheckConstraint/UniqueConstraint/ForeignKey, Django Meta.constraints, or an Elasticsearch mapping with "dynamic": "strict".

distinguish.data-store.eventhandler: the check is imperative logic fired by a change event, such as a BEFORE INSERT trigger that raises an exception, rather than a declared constraint.
distinguish.data-store.index: the declaration is an index created mainly to speed up lookups; a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint that the engine happens to back with an index is still a validationrule.
distinguish.data-store.field: the only restriction is the field's declared dataType, nullable flag, default or generation rule, with no separately named or declared constraint.
distinguish.data-store.retentionpolicy: the rule governs how long data is kept and expires, deletes, archives or downsamples it, rather than rejecting or flagging invalid writes.

types.title: View
types.description: A named collection registered in the data store engine whose contents are derived, by a stored query, pipeline or alias, from one or more source collections or views rather than written directly by applications. It is read like a collection and may be computed on each read or precomputed and refreshed. Use Collection instead when the container holds base records that applications insert directly, including a table filled by an ETL job or by a $merge/$out stage, since the engine does not maintain it from a defining query. Use StoredLogic instead when the query or pipeline is invoked procedurally (called with parameters, run as a scheduled task or script) rather than exposed as a named, queryable object, e.g. an InfluxDB continuous query writing into a measurement. Use AccessPattern instead when the query lives only in application or repository code and is not registered in the engine as a named derived object. Use RetentionPolicy instead when the element is the lifecycle rule that downsamples or expires data, not the derived aggregate that results from it.
evidence: a CREATE VIEW, CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW or CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW statement in a migration or schema file, often paired with a REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW job

a MongoDB db.createView(name, source, pipeline) call, an Elasticsearch _aliases or index-template alias definition, or a TimescaleDB CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... WITH (timescaledb.continuous) statement

an ORM entity mapped to a read-only database object, such as a Django model with managed=False whose db_table names a view, a Hibernate @Immutable/@Subselect entity, or an SQLAlchemy Table reflected from a view

distinguish.data-store.collection: the container holds base records that applications insert directly, including a table filled by an ETL job or by a $merge/$out stage, since the engine does not maintain it from a defining query
distinguish.data-store.storedlogic: the query or pipeline is invoked procedurally (called with parameters, run as a scheduled task or script) rather than exposed as a named, queryable object, e.g. an InfluxDB continuous query writing into a measurement
distinguish.data-store.accesspattern: the query lives only in application or repository code and is not registered in the engine as a named derived object
distinguish.data-store.retentionpolicy: the element is the lifecycle rule that downsamples or expires data, not the derived aggregate that results from it

layers.name: UX Layer
layers.scope: Models the user interface: views and screens, library components and their application-specific instances, forms, action and state patterns, component properties and the visual hierarchy they compose (HTML 5.3 vocabulary with component-library conventions). Rendered components, templates and view classes are evidence for elements here; the logic they call belongs to the application layer and the paths that reach them to the navigation layer. Modelling rules: placement is composition. A view composes its sub-views, component instances and action components; a sub-view or library sub-view composes its instances; an instance composes its nested instances, action components, slot references, chart series and table columns, and a menu composes its entries. A UX library aggregates its library components and sub-views, and a library component composes the components and slot references it is built from; an instance or placed sub-view realizes the library definition it places, and a slot reference references the component that fills it. Elements apply their layout configuration; state transitions, state patterns and action patterns use transition templates, which describe motion only. A state pattern aggregates its states; a state composes its outgoing transitions, a transition flows to its destination state, states and transitions trigger state actions, and a state action realizes its template. An action pattern governs the action components it is applied to. A view, sub-view, component instance or action component binds to its data configuration, which maps to the API or data-model data it reads; chart series and table columns bind through their component. Elements use their error configuration. A view realizes the application interface it presents and the product feature it delivers; an action component triggers the API operation or application behaviour it starts. UX does not access stores, operations or services directly, and reaches the business layer through the application interfaces and features it realizes: a view serves the business role it is for and references the business object it shows. A view supports the goals and outcomes it contributes to, and UX elements satisfy requirements and principles.

types.title: ActionComponent
types.description: A user-operable control (button, hyperlink, menu entry, icon button or spoken command) whose activation starts an operation, a navigation or a state change. It is the trigger point that user input reaches, as opposed to the input fields, display components or layout containers around it. Use ActionPattern instead when you are modelling the reusable trigger-plus-feedback behaviour (e.g. confirm-and-delete) that many controls share, rather than one concrete control in the interface. Use LibraryComponent instead when the symbol is the generic, reusable Button/Link/Menu definition in a design system with a props schema, rather than a specific control that triggers a specific action. Use ComponentInstance instead when the element is a configured placement of a non-action library component (table, chart, display, input) inside a View or SubView.
