Use StateTransition instead when you are modelling the state-machine edge that the activation causes (trigger event, destination state, guard), not the control the user operates.
evidence: A <button>, <a href> or design-system <Button>/<IconButton>/<Link> element rendered in a template with an onClick/onSelect/@click handler or a router 'to' target
A menu or toolbar configuration array whose entries carry a label, icon and handler or command id (e.g. items: [{label:'Delete', icon:'trash', onClick: ...}])
A voice or chat intent or command registration (e.g. an Alexa intent handler or a slash-command definition) that maps an utterance to an action invocation

distinguish.ux.actionpattern: you are modelling the reusable trigger-plus-feedback behaviour (e.g. confirm-and-delete) that many controls share, rather than one concrete control in the interface
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the symbol is the generic, reusable Button/Link/Menu definition in a design system with a props schema, rather than a specific control that triggers a specific action
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the element is a configured placement of a non-action library component (table, chart, display, input) inside a View or SubView
distinguish.ux.statetransition: you are modelling the state-machine edge that the activation causes (trigger event, destination state, guard), not the control the user operates

types.title: ActionPattern
types.description: A reusable interaction recipe that pairs a user input modality with a prescribed feedback sequence (toast, modal, route change, etc.) and is applied across multiple action components. It is not tied to one rendered control or one state, and is defined once to be reused wherever the same interaction recurs. Use ActionComponent instead when the element is a single concrete button, link, menu or voice command rendered in a view, rather than the shared interaction convention it follows. Use StateAction instead when the element is one operation (navigate, submit, dispatch…) bound to a specific ExperienceState lifecycle hook, not a user-triggered interaction with feedback reused across components. Use StatePattern instead when the reusable thing is a multi-state machine (wizard, optimistic-update, tab-panel) with states and transitions, rather than a single trigger-and-feedback interaction. Use StateActionTemplate instead when the reusable definition is a parameterized system-side operation executed during state transitions, with no user trigger or feedback mechanism.
evidence: A shared hook or higher-order helper (e.g. useConfirmDelete, withConfirmation, useOptimisticAction) that wraps a click/keyboard handler with a confirmation modal and a success or error toast, and is imported by several components.
A design-system document or Storybook 'Patterns' page describing an interaction such as 'confirm-and-delete' or 'bulk select then act', with its trigger and the feedback the user sees.
A configuration map or registry of named interaction behaviours (e.g. actions: { delete: { confirm: true, toast: 'Deleted' } }) that buttons, table row actions or menus look up by key.

distinguish.ux.actioncomponent: the element is a single concrete button, link, menu or voice command rendered in a view, rather than the shared interaction convention it follows.
distinguish.ux.stateaction: the element is one operation (navigate, submit, dispatch…) bound to a specific ExperienceState lifecycle hook, not a user-triggered interaction with feedback reused across components.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: the reusable thing is a multi-state machine (wizard, optimistic-update, tab-panel) with states and transitions, rather than a single trigger-and-feedback interaction.
distinguish.ux.stateactiontemplate: the reusable definition is a parameterized system-side operation executed during state transitions, with no user trigger or feedback mechanism.

types.title: ChartSeries
types.description: A per-series configuration within a chart component that maps one value field (and optionally one category field) of the chart's bound data to a plotted mark set, with its own legend label, visualization type, color and line style. One chart instance aggregates one or more such series. Use TableColumn instead when the field binding configures a column of a tabular data grid (header, sort, filter, cell rendering) rather than a plotted series in a chart. Use DataConfig instead when the element describes where the chart's data comes from (api, state, storage) and how it is selected, rather than how one field of that data is drawn. Use ComponentInstance instead when the element is the chart component itself placed in a view with its props, rather than one series configured inside it. Use LibraryComponent instead when the element is the reusable chart component definition (e.g. a BarChart wrapper) with its prop schema, not a series configuration passed to it.
evidence: An entry in a chart library's series array, such as Chart.js `datasets: [{ label, data, borderColor }]`, ECharts `series: [{ type: 'bar', encode }]` or Highcharts `series: [...]`.
A series child element in JSX, such as Recharts `<Line dataKey="revenue" stroke="#3B82F6" />`, `<Bar dataKey=...>` or Victory `<VictoryLine x="month" y="count" />`, nested inside a chart container.
A typed config object or constant, such as `SeriesConfig` or `ChartSeries[]`, that pairs a value key and x/category key with a display name and color and is passed as a prop to a chart component.

distinguish.ux.tablecolumn: the field binding configures a column of a tabular data grid (header, sort, filter, cell rendering) rather than a plotted series in a chart.
distinguish.ux.dataconfig: the element describes where the chart's data comes from (api, state, storage) and how it is selected, rather than how one field of that data is drawn.
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the element is the chart component itself placed in a view with its props, rather than one series configured inside it.
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the element is the reusable chart component definition (e.g. a BarChart wrapper) with its prop schema, not a series configuration passed to it.

types.title: ComponentInstance
types.description: A single concrete occurrence of a library component placed inside a specific View, SubView or LibrarySubView, carrying the prop values and render position that configure that one usage. It is identified by its reference to exactly one ux.librarycomponent definition, not by declaring props, slots or events of its own. Use LibraryComponent instead when the symbol defines the reusable component itself (its prop schema, slots, events, implementation) rather than one configured use of it on a screen. Use ComponentReference instead when the element only declares which component fills a named slot of a parent component (a slot or children placeholder), without its own configured props or render order. Use ActionComponent instead when the element's identity is an interactive trigger (button, link, menu, voice command) modelled by its action semantics rather than as a configured usage of a library component. Use SubView instead when the element is a non-routable fragment grouping several components within a View, rather than a single component usage.
evidence: a JSX/TSX, Vue or Angular template tag for an imported design-system component (e.g. <DataTable columns={cols} pageSize={20} />) inside a page or screen component
a declarative layout or page-config entry such as { "component": "Chart", "props": { ... } } in a low-code, CMS or server-driven-UI JSON/YAML file
a component tag inside a parent's render list whose position or explicit order key determines where it appears among sibling components on the screen

distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the symbol defines the reusable component itself (its prop schema, slots, events, implementation) rather than one configured use of it on a screen
distinguish.ux.componentreference: the element only declares which component fills a named slot of a parent component (a slot or children placeholder), without its own configured props or render order
distinguish.ux.actioncomponent: the element's identity is an interactive trigger (button, link, menu, voice command) modelled by its action semantics rather than as a configured usage of a library component
distinguish.ux.subview: the element is a non-routable fragment grouping several components within a View, rather than a single component usage

types.title: ComponentReference
types.description: A composition declaration attached to a parent component that names one of the parent's slots and identifies, by specNodeId, the library component or component instance to be rendered into that slot. It records the slot-filling relationship only; it carries no prop values of its own beyond an optional variant override and is not itself a rendered occurrence. Use ComponentInstance instead when the element is a concrete, configured usage of a library component with its own props and render order inside a View or SubView, rather than a pointer filling a parent's named slot. Use LibraryComponent instead when the element defines a reusable component's props, slots and events schema, rather than declaring what fills one slot of a parent. Use SubView instead when the embedded content is a grouping of several components placed in a View's subViews list, not a single component placed into a named slot of a parent component.
evidence: A child element carrying a slot="header"/slot="actions" attribute, a Vue <template #footer> / v-slot directive, or an Angular <ng-content select=...> projection target being filled.
A React prop typed as ReactNode or render-prop (e.g. header={<Toolbar/>}, actions={<Button variant="compact"/>}) passed to a layout or container component.
A Storybook or design-system doc listing a component's slots together with the allowed child components for each slot (e.g. 'Card.footer accepts Button | Link').

distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the element is a concrete, configured usage of a library component with its own props and render order inside a View or SubView, rather than a pointer filling a parent's named slot.
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the element defines a reusable component's props, slots and events schema, rather than declaring what fills one slot of a parent.
distinguish.ux.subview: the embedded content is a grouping of several components placed in a View's subViews list, not a single component placed into a named slot of a parent component.

types.title: DataConfig
types.description: A data-binding declaration attached to a view, sub-view or component that names where the UI obtains its data (remote API, client state store, local storage, mock or static value) and, optionally, the field path selected from that data. It describes the binding only. The fetching logic belongs to the application layer, and the endpoint or entity it points at belongs to the api or data-model layer. Use ErrorConfig instead when the element describes how a failed load or submit is shown to the user (message, notification type, retry or fallback), rather than where the data comes from. Use ChartSeries instead when the element specifies how one field of already-bound data is drawn in a chart (series label, chart type, color, line style), rather than the origin of the data. Use TableColumn instead when the element specifies the header, field, width, sorting or rendering of a single table column that consumes bound data. Use ComponentInstance instead when the values are fixed, author-supplied prop overrides on a library component placed in a view, rather than values resolved at runtime from a data source.
evidence: A data-fetching hook or service call inside a component, such as useQuery(['orders'], fetchOrders), useSWR('/api/user') or an Angular route resolver, whose result is passed straight into rendered props or a template.

A state-store selector or mapping that wires a store slice into a component, such as useSelector(s => s.user.profile.name), mapStateToProps, or Pinia/Vuex computed getters. These indicate a state source and give the path.
A component whose data is fed from localStorage/sessionStorage (getItem, a useLocalStorage hook) or from imported fixture/mock JSON (MSW handlers, Storybook args, a static constants file).

distinguish.ux.errorconfig: the element describes how a failed load or submit is shown to the user (message, notification type, retry or fallback), rather than where the data comes from.
distinguish.ux.chartseries: the element specifies how one field of already-bound data is drawn in a chart (series label, chart type, color, line style), rather than the origin of the data.
distinguish.ux.tablecolumn: the element specifies the header, field, width, sorting or rendering of a single table column that consumes bound data.
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the values are fixed, author-supplied prop overrides on a library component placed in a view, rather than values resolved at runtime from a data source.

types.title: ErrorConfig
types.description: A display configuration attached to a view, component, route or data binding that specifies how a failure is surfaced to the user: whether a notification appears, its severity, and the specific and fallback message text shown. Use DataConfig instead when the element describes where data comes from and how it is bound (source, target, path), not how a failure to load or save it is presented. Use ExperienceState instead when the error condition is modelled as a distinct state of the experience with its own transitions, enabled/disabled/hidden components and lifecycle actions, rather than as message and notification settings. Use ActionPattern instead when the element describes a reusable trigger-plus-feedback interaction (e.g. confirm-and-delete with a success toast) rather than the failure-specific messaging of a component or view. Use StatePattern instead when the element is a reusable state machine such as optimistic-update with loading, success, error and retry states, rather than the message settings applied in the error case.
evidence: A catch block or onError callback (e.g. a react-query onError or axios interceptor) that calls a toast, snackbar or notification API with a severity such as 'error' or 'warning' and a message string.
An error boundary or fallback component (e.g. React ErrorBoundary, Angular ErrorHandler, Vue errorCaptured) that renders a configured message or generic fallback text when a child component throws.

A component prop or config object with keys such as errorMessage, defaultErrorMessage, showNotification or onErrorNotify, or an i18n message map keyed by error code supplying user-facing failure text.

distinguish.ux.dataconfig: the element describes where data comes from and how it is bound (source, target, path), not how a failure to load or save it is presented.
distinguish.ux.experiencestate: the error condition is modelled as a distinct state of the experience with its own transitions, enabled/disabled/hidden components and lifecycle actions, rather than as message and notification settings.
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: the element describes a reusable trigger-plus-feedback interaction (e.g. confirm-and-delete with a success toast) rather than the failure-specific messaging of a component or view.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: the element is a reusable state machine such as optimistic-update with loading, success, error and retry states, rather than the message settings applied in the error case.

types.title: ExperienceState
types.description: A named, mutually exclusive condition of a user experience's state machine (e.g. idle, loading, editing, submitted, error) that fixes which components are enabled, disabled or hidden while it is active and owns the entry/exit actions and outgoing transitions for that condition. It is a node in the machine, not a screen, route or event. Use StatePattern instead when the thing is a reusable template made of several named states and their transitions (e.g. 'wizard', 'optimistic-update'), rather than one state within a machine. Use StateTransition instead when the thing is the event-driven edge that moves the experience from one state to another, with a trigger, guard and destination. Use View instead when the thing is a routable screen, modal or panel with its own URL or display mode; a state is a condition within or across views, not the container being shown. Use StateAction instead when the thing is a side effect (focus, scroll, dispatch, navigate) executed on entering, exiting or transitioning out of a state, not the state itself.
evidence: a key under 'states' in an XState/Robot/Zag machine config (e.g. states: { loading: { entry: ..., on: { SUCCESS: 'done' } } }) or a state class in a State-pattern implementation
a member of a status union or enum (e.g. type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error') held in useState, useReducer, a Redux/Pinia store or component data and switched on in render logic
conditional rendering or prop toggles keyed on that status value, such as `if (status === 'error') return <ErrorPanel/>` or `disabled={status === 'submitting'}` or `hidden={state.matches('editing')}`

distinguish.ux.statepattern: the thing is a reusable template made of several named states and their transitions (e.g. 'wizard', 'optimistic-update'), rather than one state within a machine
distinguish.ux.statetransition: the thing is the event-driven edge that moves the experience from one state to another, with a trigger, guard and destination
distinguish.ux.view: the thing is a routable screen, modal or panel with its own URL or display mode; a state is a condition within or across views, not the container being shown
distinguish.ux.stateaction: the thing is a side effect (focus, scroll, dispatch, navigate) executed on entering, exiting or transitioning out of a state, not the state itself

types.title: LayoutConfig
types.description: A declarative set of container arrangement rules (CSS layout mode, grid track counts, spacing, alignment and width constraints) applied to a View, SubView or component to position its children. It renders no content of its own and is identified by its layout properties, not by any markup it emits. Use LibraryComponent instead when the layout is a reusable rendered component with its own props, slots or events (e.g. an exported <Grid> or <Stack> primitive of type 'layout'), rather than a set of arrangement values. Use ComponentInstance instead when the symbol is a concrete usage of a layout library component in a particular view, even if the props it receives are layout values. Use LibrarySubView instead when the reusable thing is a grouping of component instances, such as a sidebar-plus-content fragment, rather than the spacing and alignment rules that arrange them. Use View instead when the symbol is a routable screen or page shell, even one named like a layout (e.g. a framework layout.tsx that renders header and outlet).
evidence: A CSS/SCSS rule, CSS module or styled-component on a page or container class that sets display:grid or display:flex together with grid-template-columns, gap, justify-content or max-width.
Layout primitives invoked with arrangement-only props, e.g. <Grid columns={3} gap="md">, <Stack direction="row" align="center">, or Tailwind classes such as 'grid grid-cols-3 gap-4 max-w-screen-xl'.
A named layout entry in theme or route configuration, e.g. a layouts map, container maxWidth and spacing tokens in tailwind.config or theme.ts, or route meta { layout: 'two-column' }.

distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the layout is a reusable rendered component with its own props, slots or events (e.g. an exported <Grid> or <Stack> primitive of type 'layout'), rather than a set of arrangement values.
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the symbol is a concrete usage of a layout library component in a particular view, even if the props it receives are layout values.
distinguish.ux.librarysubview: the reusable thing is a grouping of component instances, such as a sidebar-plus-content fragment, rather than the spacing and alignment rules that arrange them.
distinguish.ux.view: the symbol is a routable screen or page shell, even one named like a layout (e.g. a framework layout.tsx that renders header and outlet).

types.title: LibraryComponent
types.description: A reusable UI component definition that declares an accepted property schema, named content slots and emitted events independently of any particular screen, so it can be instantiated with different configuration in many views or UXSpecs. It is the component type, not a placed, configured occurrence of it. Use ComponentInstance instead when the symbol is a specific usage of a component inside a View, SubView or LibrarySubView with concrete prop values, such as a <DataTable columns={...}/> call site, rather than the component's definition. Use ActionComponent instead when the element is a single interactive trigger, such as a button, link, menu item or voice command, modelled for the action it fires rather than as a reusable component with its own props, slots and events. Use LibrarySubView instead when the reusable unit is an ordered arrangement of several component instances, such as a filter bar plus a table, rather than one component with its own prop schema. Use View instead when the component is a routable page, modal or screen reached via a navigation route rather than a building block embedded by other components or views.
evidence: A component exported from a shared design-system or components package index, such as packages/ui/src/index.ts, with a typed props contract (TypeScript Props interface, PropTypes, Vue defineProps or an Angular @Input set) and imported by several screens.
A Storybook story file (*.stories.tsx or *.stories.mdx) or design-system documentation page that catalogues the component and its prop, slot and event variants.

A customElements.define('x-foo', ...) registration, or a component declaring <slot name=...>, children or render props and emitting custom events (emit, dispatchEvent, onXxx callback props) without registering any route.

distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the symbol is a specific usage of a component inside a View, SubView or LibrarySubView with concrete prop values, such as a <DataTable columns={...}/> call site, rather than the component's definition.
distinguish.ux.actioncomponent: the element is a single interactive trigger, such as a button, link, menu item or voice command, modelled for the action it fires rather than as a reusable component with its own props, slots and events.
distinguish.ux.librarysubview: the reusable unit is an ordered arrangement of several component instances, such as a filter bar plus a table, rather than one component with its own prop schema.
distinguish.ux.view: the component is a routable page, modal or screen reached via a navigation route rather than a building block embedded by other components or views.

types.title: LibrarySubView
types.description: A reusable, non-routable composition of configured component instances, published in a UX library and embedded by reference into multiple Views or SubViews. It is distinguished from a SubView by being the shared definition rather than its placement in a particular parent, and from a LibraryComponent by being an assembly of existing components rather than a primitive with its own prop, slot and event contract. Use SubView instead when the fragment is a specific placement inside one parent View (with an order), either referencing a library sub-view via 'ref' or defined inline and not reused elsewhere. Use LibraryComponent instead when the unit is a single primitive or widget with its own declared props, slots and events, rather than an arrangement of several already-configured component instances. Use View instead when the grouping is reachable by a route or URL, or is opened as a page, modal, dialog or drawer in its own right. Use StatePattern instead when what is being reused is a sequence of states and transitions (wizard, optimistic update) rather than a visual arrangement of components.
evidence: A component file in a shared or design-system package (e.g. src/shared/sections/, packages/ui/patterns/) that renders a fixed arrangement of several other library components, has no route registration and is imported by two or more page components.
A Storybook story grouped under a 'Patterns', 'Sections' or 'Compositions' heading, as opposed to 'Components', that renders a multi-component block such as a FiltersWithTable or AddressFormSection.

A reusable template partial (e.g. Angular ng-template, Django {% include %} partial, Rails shared partial, Blade @include, or HTML <template> element) that contains several component tags and is included from multiple page templates.

distinguish.ux.subview: the fragment is a specific placement inside one parent View (with an order), either referencing a library sub-view via 'ref' or defined inline and not reused elsewhere.
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the unit is a single primitive or widget with its own declared props, slots and events, rather than an arrangement of several already-configured component instances.
distinguish.ux.view: the grouping is reachable by a route or URL, or is opened as a page, modal, dialog or drawer in its own right.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: what is being reused is a sequence of states and transitions (wizard, optimistic update) rather than a visual arrangement of components.

types.title: StateAction
types.description: A side-effect operation (navigate, submit, open, close, dispatch, validate) bound to one specific ExperienceState or StateTransition and executed automatically by that element's lifecycle hook (on-enter, on-exit, on-transition), rather than invoked directly as a user-facing control. Use StateActionTemplate instead when the action is a parameterized, reusable definition that is not yet bound to a particular state and lifecycle hook. Use ActionPattern instead when describing a recurring user-initiated interaction recipe (input trigger plus feedback such as toast or modal) rather than an effect fired by a state lifecycle. Use StateTransition instead when modelling the edge itself, meaning its trigger event, destination state and guard, rather than the effect executed while it fires. Use ActionComponent instead when the element is the rendered button, link or menu the user activates, not the effect run as part of a state's entry, exit or transition.
evidence: Named actions listed in a state-machine config's entry/exit arrays or in a transition's actions array (e.g. XState `entry: ['scrollToTop','focusFirstField']`, `exit: 'trackStepExit'`).
A useEffect, watch or ngOnInit/ngOnDestroy handler keyed on the current step or state value that calls router.push, form.submit, store.dispatch, element.focus or window.scrollTo.
Wizard or step components whose onEnter/onLeave callbacks, or route-leave guards such as beforeRouteLeave, emit analytics events or run form validation when the step changes.

distinguish.ux.stateactiontemplate: the action is a parameterized, reusable definition that is not yet bound to a particular state and lifecycle hook
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: describing a recurring user-initiated interaction recipe (input trigger plus feedback such as toast or modal) rather than an effect fired by a state lifecycle
distinguish.ux.statetransition: modelling the edge itself, meaning its trigger event, destination state and guard, rather than the effect executed while it fires
distinguish.ux.actioncomponent: the element is the rendered button, link or menu the user activates, not the effect run as part of a state's entry, exit or transition

types.title: StateActionTemplate
types.description: A reusable, parameterized definition of a state-machine side-effect operation that is not bound to any particular ExperienceState or lifecycle hook. It declares the operation kind and its named input parameters, and StateActions instantiate it with concrete values on specific states. Use StateAction instead when the action is attached to a specific ExperienceState or StateTransition with a lifecycle hook (on-enter, on-exit, on-transition) and concrete argument values, even if it reuses a template. Use ActionPattern instead when the reusable thing is a user-initiated interaction recipe defined by input trigger (click, swipe, voice, keyboard) and user-facing feedback (toast, modal), not a side effect run by the state machine. Use TransitionTemplate instead when the reusable definition describes motion or animation (fade, slide, duration, easing) applied during a state or page change rather than an operation executed. Use StatePattern instead when the reusable unit is a whole state machine of ExperienceStates and transitions rather than a single action used inside one.
evidence: Named, parameterized actions declared once in a state-machine options block (e.g. XState setup({ actions: { scrollTo: (_, params) => ... } })) and referenced by name from the entry/exit arrays of several states.

An action-creator or effect factory taking arguments (e.g. focusField(fieldId), trackEvent(eventName)) exported from a shared module and called from the lifecycle hooks of multiple steps, screens or states.
A design-system or state-library catalogue entry (JSON/YAML or docs page) listing a reusable state action with a parameter table of name, type and default value.

distinguish.ux.stateaction: the action is attached to a specific ExperienceState or StateTransition with a lifecycle hook (on-enter, on-exit, on-transition) and concrete argument values, even if it reuses a template.
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: the reusable thing is a user-initiated interaction recipe defined by input trigger (click, swipe, voice, keyboard) and user-facing feedback (toast, modal), not a side effect run by the state machine.
distinguish.ux.transitiontemplate: the reusable definition describes motion or animation (fade, slide, duration, easing) applied during a state or page change rather than an operation executed.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: the reusable unit is a whole state machine of ExperienceStates and transitions rather than a single action used inside one.

types.title: StatePattern
types.description: A reusable, named state machine definition: an ordered set of ExperienceStates and the transitions between them that encodes a recurring interaction flow (e.g. wizard, loading/success/error, tab panel, auth gate). It is not bound to any single View or component and is meant to be applied by several of them. Use ExperienceState instead when the symbol represents one state node (e.g. 'loading' or 'step-2') rather than the whole reusable machine that contains it. Use StateTransition instead when the symbol is a single trigger→destination edge with an optional guard, not a complete set of states. Use ActionPattern instead when the reusable thing is one trigger-plus-feedback interaction (e.g. confirm-and-delete) with no states of its own. Use UXSpec instead when the states are the top-level, one-off state machine of a single experience rather than a template reused across experiences.
evidence: A state machine factory or definition (e.g. XState createMachine, a createWizardMachine(steps) function) exported from a shared module and imported by multiple views or components

A generic hook or store (e.g. useAsync, useWizard, useTabs) exposing a finite status union such as 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error' plus transition functions (next, back, retry), reused across features
A shared reducer typed with a discriminated union of states, or a design-system doc page describing the flow and its states (e.g. 'Optimistic update pattern')

distinguish.ux.experiencestate: the symbol represents one state node (e.g. 'loading' or 'step-2') rather than the whole reusable machine that contains it
distinguish.ux.statetransition: the symbol is a single trigger→destination edge with an optional guard, not a complete set of states
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: the reusable thing is one trigger-plus-feedback interaction (e.g. confirm-and-delete) with no states of its own
distinguish.ux.uxspec: the states are the top-level, one-off state machine of a single experience rather than a template reused across experiences

types.title: StateTransition
types.description: A directed edge in an ExperienceState machine that moves the experience from its owning source ExperienceState to one destination ExperienceState when a named UI event occurs. It may carry a guard condition that must hold and an ordered list of StateActions run as side effects when it fires. Use TransitionTemplate instead when the element describes reusable motion or animation (fade, slide, duration, easing) applied to a state or page change, not which state the event leads to. Use StateAction instead when the element is the side-effect operation itself (navigate, submit, dispatch, validate) bound to a lifecycle hook, rather than the edge between two states. Use ExperienceState instead when the element is a node the experience can rest in (loading, error, confirmed), with entry and exit actions and component visibility, rather than the move between such nodes. Use ActionPattern instead when the element is a reusable trigger-plus-feedback interaction recipe (e.g. confirm-and-delete) applied to components, not a specific source-to-destination edge in one state machine.
evidence: An XState or similar statechart config entry such as `on: { SUBMIT: { target: 'confirmed', guard: 'isValid', actions: ['track'] } }` inside a state node

A reducer or useReducer case that switches on the current status together with an event or action type and returns a different status value (e.g. `case 'editing': if (action.type === 'SAVE') return 'saving'`)
A transitions table or map literal of `{ from, event, to }` records, or a `canTransition(from, event)` / `transition(state, event)` helper that a component's onClick or onSubmit handler calls

distinguish.ux.transitiontemplate: the element describes reusable motion or animation (fade, slide, duration, easing) applied to a state or page change, not which state the event leads to
distinguish.ux.stateaction: the element is the side-effect operation itself (navigate, submit, dispatch, validate) bound to a lifecycle hook, rather than the edge between two states
distinguish.ux.experiencestate: the element is a node the experience can rest in (loading, error, confirmed), with entry and exit actions and component visibility, rather than the move between such nodes
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: the element is a reusable trigger-plus-feedback interaction recipe (e.g. confirm-and-delete) applied to components, not a specific source-to-destination edge in one state machine

types.title: SubView
types.description: A non-routable region of a parent View that groups several component instances and is rendered only as part of that View. It is either a placement of a reusable LibrarySubView (ref set) or a one-off composition defined inline (ref absent). Use View instead when the fragment has its own route or URL, or is opened independently as a page, modal, dialog or drawer. Use LibrarySubView instead when you are modelling the reusable fragment definition exported from a UX library, not its placement inside a particular View. Use ComponentInstance instead when the element is a single configured library component with props, not a grouping of several components. Use ComponentReference instead when the element only declares which component fills a named slot of a parent component, rather than being a rendered region of a View.
evidence: A component file under a page's local folder (e.g. pages/Orders/components/OrderFiltersPanel.tsx) that is imported and rendered only by that route-level page and has no route registration of its own.
A template partial or include inside a page template, e.g. {% include 'orders/_summary.html' %}, @Html.Partial("_Summary"), or <ng-container *ngTemplateOutlet="summary">.

A named section of a page's render tree, e.g. <SidebarSection/> or a renderSidebar() helper, that composes several library components such as Table, Button and Input. A shared-fragment import from a design-system package indicates the library-instance mode.

distinguish.ux.view: the fragment has its own route or URL, or is opened independently as a page, modal, dialog or drawer.
distinguish.ux.librarysubview: you are modelling the reusable fragment definition exported from a UX library, not its placement inside a particular View.
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the element is a single configured library component with props, not a grouping of several components.
distinguish.ux.componentreference: the element only declares which component fills a named slot of a parent component, rather than being a rendered region of a View.

types.title: TableColumn
types.description: A declarative configuration entry for one column of a tabular data component, binding a header label to a single field of each row record and specifying that column's width, alignment, cell rendering type, default sort direction and filter operation. It describes column structure, not a rendered component, and exists only as part of a table-type ComponentInstance or LibraryComponent. Use ChartSeries instead when the field binding drives a plotted data series (line, bar, pie) in a chart rather than a column of cells in a table. Use ComponentInstance instead when the symbol is the table itself or a component rendered inside a cell (e.g. a badge or action menu), rather than the column definition that hosts it. Use DataConfig instead when the configuration describes where the table's row data comes from (API, state, static) and how it is selected, not how one field is displayed as a column. Use ActionComponent instead when the element is an interactive control (button, link, icon-button) placed in an actions column, rather than the column definition containing it.
evidence: An object literal in a columns array passed to a table/grid component, e.g. { header: 'Name', accessorKey: 'name', size: 200 } for TanStack Table or { field: 'price', headerName: 'Price', width: 120 } for MUI DataGrid/AG Grid columnDefs.

A declarative column child element in a template, such as <el-table-column prop="date" label="Date" sortable>, <mat-header-cell *matHeaderCellDef> paired with matColumnDef="status", or <Column field="code" header="Code"> in PrimeReact.

A column definition carrying cell rendering or sort/filter options, e.g. a cellRenderer/render function returning a badge, sortable: true with sortingOrder, or filter: 'agNumberColumnFilter' on a single field.

distinguish.ux.chartseries: the field binding drives a plotted data series (line, bar, pie) in a chart rather than a column of cells in a table.
distinguish.ux.componentinstance: the symbol is the table itself or a component rendered inside a cell (e.g. a badge or action menu), rather than the column definition that hosts it.
distinguish.ux.dataconfig: the configuration describes where the table's row data comes from (API, state, static) and how it is selected, not how one field is displayed as a column.
distinguish.ux.actioncomponent: the element is an interactive control (button, link, icon-button) placed in an actions column, rather than the column definition containing it.

types.title: TransitionTemplate
types.description: A reusable motion definition specifying the animation type, duration and easing applied when a UI change occurs, such as a state change, route change, or component enter/leave. It describes how the change is animated, not which change occurs, and can be shared by many state transitions, patterns and views. Use StateTransition instead when the element is a concrete edge in an ExperienceState machine with a source state, destination state, trigger and guard, whether or not it is animated. Use ActionPattern instead when the reusable artifact describes the interaction itself (trigger modality, feedback such as toast or modal, target), rather than the motion curve and duration of the visual change. Use StateActionTemplate instead when the reusable definition is an operation executed during a transition (navigate, submit, dispatch, validate), not an animation. Use StatePattern instead when the reusable artifact is a whole state machine of named states and transitions, such as a wizard or optimistic update.
evidence: Named, shared animation definitions such as Angular `trigger('fadeIn', [transition(':enter', [animate('300ms ease-in')])])` or exported Framer Motion `variants` objects imported by several components

CSS classes or @keyframes reused across components for enter/leave or route changes (e.g. `.fade-enter-active { transition: opacity 300ms ease-in-out }` used with Vue `<Transition name="fade">` or react-transition-group `CSSTransition classNames="slide"`)

Motion design tokens or theme entries defining duration and easing values (e.g. `motion.duration.medium: 300ms`, `motion.easing.standard: cubic-bezier(0.4,0,0.2,1)`) referenced by page-transition or modal-open animations

distinguish.ux.statetransition: the element is a concrete edge in an ExperienceState machine with a source state, destination state, trigger and guard, whether or not it is animated.
distinguish.ux.actionpattern: the reusable artifact describes the interaction itself (trigger modality, feedback such as toast or modal, target), rather than the motion curve and duration of the visual change.
distinguish.ux.stateactiontemplate: the reusable definition is an operation executed during a transition (navigate, submit, dispatch, validate), not an animation.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: the reusable artifact is a whole state machine of named states and transitions, such as a wizard or optimistic update.

types.title: UXApplication
types.description: A top-level, independently deployable user-facing client for one delivery channel that aggregates one or more UXSpecs and fixes the settings they share: theme, design system, and default locale. It corresponds to a single front-end app root, such as an SPA bundle, mobile app, or voice skill, not to a reusable package or a single experience. Use UXSpec instead when the artifact describes a single experience (its views and state machine) within an app rather than the deployable app root that bundles experiences and carries app-wide theme, locale and design-system settings. Use UXLibrary instead when the artifact is a versioned package of reusable components, sub-views or patterns consumed by applications (e.g. a published npm design-system package) rather than an end-user application itself. Use View instead when the artifact is a single routable screen, page, modal or dialog rather than the whole application containing many screens.
evidence: A front-end entry point that mounts the root component and wires app-wide providers, e.g. ReactDOM.createRoot(...).render(<ThemeProvider><IntlProvider locale=...><App/>), createApp(App).use(router).mount('#app'), or an Angular bootstrapApplication/AppModule

An application manifest or build descriptor defining a distinct deliverable, e.g. manifest.json/manifest.webmanifest with name and start_url, AndroidManifest.xml or Info.plist, an Alexa skill.json, or a separate app package in a monorepo apps/ folder

App-level configuration declaring shared settings, such as a theme/design-token selection, i18n config with defaultLocale (next.config.js i18n, i18next init), and a dependency on an internal design-system package

distinguish.ux.uxspec: the artifact describes a single experience (its views and state machine) within an app rather than the deployable app root that bundles experiences and carries app-wide theme, locale and design-system settings
distinguish.ux.uxlibrary: the artifact is a versioned package of reusable components, sub-views or patterns consumed by applications (e.g. a published npm design-system package) rather than an end-user application itself
distinguish.ux.view: the artifact is a single routable screen, page, modal or dialog rather than the whole application containing many screens

types.title: UXLibrary
types.description: A versioned, distributable package of UI building blocks that exports library components, library sub-views, state patterns and action patterns for consumption by one or more UX applications or specs. It is identified by its package boundary (manifest, version, export index), not by any rendered screen or route of its own. Use UXApplication instead when the artifact is a deployable product that consumes components, targets a delivery channel and groups UXSpecs, rather than a package exporting reusable parts. Use LibraryComponent instead when the symbol is a single reusable component definition with props, slots and events, not the package or index that exports many of them. Use LibrarySubView instead when the symbol is one reusable composition of component instances, not the collection that publishes it. Use UXSpec instead when the artifact describes the views and states of one concrete experience instead of exporting reusable parts for others to assemble.
evidence: A package.json (or equivalent manifest) for a UI package with name, version, license and author fields whose main/exports entry is a barrel index re-exporting many components (e.g. `export * from './Button'`).

A Storybook configuration or design-system documentation site cataloguing components of a single package, or a monorepo workspace such as packages/ui or @org/design-system that is imported by multiple apps.

Consumer code importing components from a shared package specifier (e.g. `import { DataTable } from '@acme/ui'`) rather than a relative path, often with the package listed as a peer or regular dependency in several applications.

distinguish.ux.uxapplication: the artifact is a deployable product that consumes components, targets a delivery channel and groups UXSpecs, rather than a package exporting reusable parts.
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the symbol is a single reusable component definition with props, slots and events, not the package or index that exports many of them.
distinguish.ux.librarysubview: the symbol is one reusable composition of component instances, not the collection that publishes it.
distinguish.ux.uxspec: the artifact describes the views and states of one concrete experience instead of exporting reusable parts for others to assemble.

types.title: UXSpec
types.description: A specification artifact that groups the routable views and top-level experience states making up one user experience (a feature area or user journey) delivered in a single modality: visual, voice, chat or SMS. It is aggregated by a UXApplication and is the unit that satisfies UX requirements. Use UXApplication instead when the element groups several experiences and carries application-wide settings such as theme, design system, default locale or target channel. Use View instead when the element is a single routable screen, page, modal or dialog rather than the collection of screens and states for a whole experience. Use StatePattern instead when the state machine is a reusable template (wizard, optimistic-update, tab-panel) meant to be applied across experiences rather than the top-level states of one concrete experience. Use UXLibrary instead when the element is a shareable package of library components, sub-views and patterns with no routes or experience-specific states of its own.
evidence: A feature module or route-group directory (e.g. Angular module calling RouterModule.forChild, Next.js app/(checkout)/ group, React Router nested route tree) that bundles the routes and screens of one user journey.
A top-level flow state machine (e.g. XState createMachine or a Redux slice for a flow) whose states correspond to the screens or steps of a single experience such as onboarding or checkout.

A per-experience design or interaction artifact: a Figma page or Storybook section named for a journey, or for non-visual modalities a voice skill interaction model (Alexa/Dialogflow JSON) or chatbot flow definition.

distinguish.ux.uxapplication: the element groups several experiences and carries application-wide settings such as theme, design system, default locale or target channel.
distinguish.ux.view: the element is a single routable screen, page, modal or dialog rather than the collection of screens and states for a whole experience.
distinguish.ux.statepattern: the state machine is a reusable template (wizard, optimistic-update, tab-panel) meant to be applied across experiences rather than the top-level states of one concrete experience.
distinguish.ux.uxlibrary: the element is a shareable package of library components, sub-views and patterns with no routes or experience-specific states of its own.

types.title: View
types.description: A top-level UI surface (page, screen, modal, dialog, drawer, panel or overlay) that composes component instances and sub-views into one complete display unit. It is either the target of a navigation route or opened as a standalone surface; it is not a fragment owned by another view's region, which is a SubView. Use SubView instead when the fragment is rendered inside a parent view's region, cannot be shown on its own, and has no route or independent open/close lifecycle. Use LibrarySubView instead when the grouping is a reusable, non-routable composition unit meant to be embedded in many views rather than a destination screen. Use UXSpec instead when the element describes an entire experience (a set of views and its state machine) rather than one screen within it. Use LibraryComponent instead when the code is a generic modal, drawer or dialog widget definition with props and slots, not a specific application screen built from it.
evidence: A component or template file registered as the target of a router entry, for example a React Router <Route element={...}>, a Next.js app/**/page.tsx, a Vue Router `component:` entry, or an Angular Routes `component` property.
A server-side controller action that renders a full template or page (Django render(request, 'orders/list.html'), Rails `render :index`, a Spring MVC @Controller method returning a view name).

A file under a pages/, views/, screens/ or modals/ directory, or a mobile Activity, Fragment or UIViewController destination in a navigation graph, that sets a page or dialog title and mounts several child components.

distinguish.ux.subview: the fragment is rendered inside a parent view's region, cannot be shown on its own, and has no route or independent open/close lifecycle.
distinguish.ux.librarysubview: the grouping is a reusable, non-routable composition unit meant to be embedded in many views rather than a destination screen.
distinguish.ux.uxspec: the element describes an entire experience (a set of views and its state machine) rather than one screen within it.
distinguish.ux.librarycomponent: the code is a generic modal, drawer or dialog widget definition with props and slots, not a specific application screen built from it.

layers.name: Navigation Layer
layers.scope: Describes how a user moves through the application: routes and route parameters, navigation flows and their steps, guards and redirects, menus, deep links and the transitions between views (single-page-application navigation patterns). Router configuration and route tables are the usual evidence; the views reached belong to the UX layer and server-side HTTP endpoints to the API layer. Modelling rules: a navigation graph composes its routes and transitions and aggregates its flows, guards and breadcrumb configurations; a route composes its route meta and may contain child routes; a flow composes its steps and aggregates the context variables it carries. A transition leaves its source route (the route flows to it) and navigates to its destination route; a flow step navigates to its route, and a guard action redirects by navigating to a route. A guard evaluates its condition, triggers its action on denial and protects what it guards (routes, transitions, flows and flow steps); the condition and the action do not link to each other. Context variables are passive state: the steps, guards, conditions, actions and transitions that read or write them access them, and their value types map to data-model schema properties or reference data objects and schema documents. A breadcrumb configuration references the route meta it reads labels from, its home route and the flows it shows progress for. Across layers, a route maps to the UX view it renders and may lazy-load or depend on application components; routes, steps and guards use application services, access the data-model schemas they load or check, and are served by the API operations they call; they never reach the data store directly. Navigation reaches the business and motivation layers through the product user workflows and workflow steps that flows and steps realize, and satisfies requirements, constraints and principles.

types.title: BreadcrumbConfig
types.description: A navigation-scope configuration object that governs how the breadcrumb location trail is derived from the active route hierarchy and rendered. It covers label resolution, the home link, separators and truncation, and applies to every route in a NavigationGraph or NavigationFlow rather than to one route. Use RouteMeta instead when the evidence is a breadcrumb label or flag set on a single route's meta/data object rather than a shared rule for building the whole trail. Use NavigationFlow instead when the trail being shown is a progress indicator through ordered wizard or checkout steps rather than the user's position in the route hierarchy. Use NavigationGraph instead when the object is the overall route table or router instance and breadcrumb settings are only one incidental option inside it.
evidence: An options object or provider passed to a breadcrumb library or component (e.g. xng-breadcrumb BreadcrumbService config, use-react-router-breadcrumbs options, MUI <Breadcrumbs separator maxItems itemsBeforeCollapse>) defined once and reused across pages
A breadcrumb service or composable that walks the router's matched route chain (route.matched, ActivatedRoute.parent, useMatches) and builds items from meta.breadcrumb or a title template
Shared constants or settings such as BREADCRUMB_SEPARATOR, HOME_BREADCRUMB = { label: 'Home', to: '/' } or a showHome flag imported by a layout-level breadcrumb component

distinguish.navigation.routemeta: the evidence is a breadcrumb label or flag set on a single route's meta/data object rather than a shared rule for building the whole trail
distinguish.navigation.navigationflow: the trail being shown is a progress indicator through ordered wizard or checkout steps rather than the user's position in the route hierarchy
distinguish.navigation.navigationgraph: the object is the overall route table or router instance and breadcrumb settings are only one incidental option inside it

types.title: ContextVariable
types.description: A named, typed item of client-side state that a NavigationFlow carries between its FlowSteps across route transitions, declared with a schema, a lifetime scope and a storage mechanism such as session storage, local storage, memory or URL query string. It is runtime data written by one step and read by later steps or guards, not static per-route configuration or a path parameter of a single route. Use RouteMeta instead when the value is static configuration declared on one route (layout, roles, keepAlive, breadcrumb) rather than data produced and consumed at runtime as the user moves through a flow. Use Route instead when the value is a path segment parameter (e.g. ':orderId') that is part of a single route's URL pattern and identifies the resource that route addresses, rather than state carried across several steps. Use FlowStep instead when the thing being modelled is a position in the flow bound to a route, not the data passed between such positions. Use GuardCondition instead when the symbol is the boolean predicate that reads session or flow state to permit or deny access, rather than the state item itself.
evidence: A wizard or checkout store (Redux slice, Pinia/Vuex module, NgRx feature, or XState machine context) whose fields are written in one route's component and read in subsequent routes of the same flow
Calls such as sessionStorage.setItem('checkout.shippingAddress', ...), localStorage writes, or a useSessionStorage hook keyed by flow name, with the value read back on a later step page

Navigation calls that pass values forward, such as router.push({ query: { planId } }), navigate('/step-2', { state: { orderId } }), or Angular NavigationExtras.state, read on arrival via useLocation().state or getCurrentNavigation()

distinguish.navigation.routemeta: the value is static configuration declared on one route (layout, roles, keepAlive, breadcrumb) rather than data produced and consumed at runtime as the user moves through a flow
distinguish.navigation.route: the value is a path segment parameter (e.g. ':orderId') that is part of a single route's URL pattern and identifies the resource that route addresses, rather than state carried across several steps
distinguish.navigation.flowstep: the thing being modelled is a position in the flow bound to a route, not the data passed between such positions
distinguish.navigation.guardcondition: the symbol is the boolean predicate that reads session or flow state to permit or deny access, rather than the state item itself

types.title: FlowStep
types.description: An ordered position within a NavigationFlow that binds a sequence index to one route the user visits as part of a multi-step process, together with whether the step may be skipped and how the flow waits on it before advancing. It exists only as a member of a flow; the same route outside any ordered process is not a step. Use Route instead when the symbol declares a URL path pattern and the component it resolves to, independent of any position in an ordered multi-step process. Use NavigationFlow instead when the symbol is the whole ordered wizard, checkout or onboarding sequence that contains the steps, not a single position within it. Use NavigationTransition instead when the symbol describes the edge between two routes and what triggers it (click, redirect, back) rather than a numbered stop in a flow. Use ContextVariable instead when the symbol is state carried between steps (e.g. a cart or form draft held in sessionStorage) rather than the step itself.
evidence: An entry in a steps array of a wizard or stepper configuration (e.g. `steps: [{ path: '/checkout/shipping', ... }, { path: '/checkout/payment', ... }]`) whose position or explicit index defines order
A stepper component child (e.g. `<Step>`, `<mat-step>`, `<el-step>`) bound to a route path, carrying an `optional` or `required` flag or a completion or validation gate
Next/previous step logic, such as `goToStep(n)`, `currentStep + 1` or a state-machine state in an onboarding or checkout flow, that resolves a step index to a router push of a specific path

distinguish.navigation.route: the symbol declares a URL path pattern and the component it resolves to, independent of any position in an ordered multi-step process
distinguish.navigation.navigationflow: the symbol is the whole ordered wizard, checkout or onboarding sequence that contains the steps, not a single position within it
distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: the symbol describes the edge between two routes and what triggers it (click, redirect, back) rather than a numbered stop in a flow
distinguish.navigation.contextvariable: the symbol is state carried between steps (e.g. a cart or form draft held in sessionStorage) rather than the step itself

types.title: GuardAction
types.description: A denial-handling outcome attached to a NavigationGuard that specifies what the router does when the guard's condition fails. It either redirects to a route or URL, cancels navigation in place, shows a message, or asks for confirmation, and it records whether the attempted route is kept so the user can return to it later. Use NavigationGuard instead when you are modelling the interceptor itself: its mechanism type (auth, role, feature-flag), its execution order, and the routes it protects, rather than what happens on denial. Use GuardCondition instead when you are modelling the boolean predicate the guard evaluates (e.g. 'user.isAuthenticated'), not the response executed when that predicate is false. Use NavigationTransition instead when you are modelling a standing edge between two routes in the navigation graph (including one with trigger 'redirect') rather than a guard's conditional denial response. Use Route instead when the redirect is unconditional, such as a route of type 'redirect' whose router entry always forwards (e.g. { path: '/', redirectTo: '/home' }) regardless of any access check.
evidence: The denied branch of a beforeEach/canActivate guard that returns a redirect location carrying the attempted path, e.g. return { name: 'login', query: { redirect: to.fullPath } } or router.createUrlTree(['/login'], { queryParams: { returnUrl: state.url } }).
A guard branch that aborts navigation with next(false), return false, or event.preventDefault(), optionally preceded by a toast or notification call explaining the denial.
A window.confirm(...) or modal-dialog prompt inside a canDeactivate or beforeRouteLeave hook, or a React protected-route wrapper rendering <Navigate to="/login" state={{ from: location }} replace />.

distinguish.navigation.navigationguard: you are modelling the interceptor itself: its mechanism type (auth, role, feature-flag), its execution order, and the routes it protects, rather than what happens on denial.
distinguish.navigation.guardcondition: you are modelling the boolean predicate the guard evaluates (e.g. 'user.isAuthenticated'), not the response executed when that predicate is false.
distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: you are modelling a standing edge between two routes in the navigation graph (including one with trigger 'redirect') rather than a guard's conditional denial response.
distinguish.navigation.route: the redirect is unconditional, such as a route of type 'redirect' whose router entry always forwards (e.g. { path: '/', redirectTo: '/home' }) regardless of any access check.

types.title: GuardCondition
types.description: A boolean predicate, possibly asynchronous with a millisecond timeout, that a NavigationGuard evaluates against session state, roles, permissions, feature flags, route metadata or flow context to decide whether activation of a target route is allowed. It is the test only: it neither registers interception on routes nor specifies what happens on denial. Use NavigationGuard instead when the symbol is the interceptor registered with the router (beforeEach hook, canActivate class, route-level beforeEnter) that carries a guard type and execution order, rather than the predicate expression it calls. Use GuardAction instead when the code describes the denial response, such as a redirect to '/login', returning false to block, showing a toast, or prompting for confirmation, rather than the true/false test that precedes it. Use RouteMeta instead when the symbol is declarative per-route data like requiresAuth, roles or permissions that a predicate reads, rather than the logic that evaluates that data. Use ContextVariable instead when the symbol is the flow-scoped state value itself (e.g. a stored cartId or wizard progress) that a condition may inspect, rather than a predicate over it.
evidence: A named function or method returning boolean, Promise<boolean> or Observable<boolean> (e.g. isAuthenticated(), hasRole(route.meta.roles), isFeatureEnabled('beta')) that is invoked from inside a router guard hook.

An inline conditional expression in a beforeEach/canActivate/loader body, such as `if (!store.user || !to.meta.roles.includes(store.user.role))`, whose result selects between next()/true and a redirect or block.

An awaited token or permission check (e.g. `await authService.validateToken()`), often wrapped in Promise.race or a timeout option, that returns false or throws on expiry before a route is allowed to activate.

distinguish.navigation.navigationguard: the symbol is the interceptor registered with the router (beforeEach hook, canActivate class, route-level beforeEnter) that carries a guard type and execution order, rather than the predicate expression it calls.
distinguish.navigation.guardaction: the code describes the denial response, such as a redirect to '/login', returning false to block, showing a toast, or prompting for confirmation, rather than the true/false test that precedes it.
distinguish.navigation.routemeta: the symbol is declarative per-route data like requiresAuth, roles or permissions that a predicate reads, rather than the logic that evaluates that data.
distinguish.navigation.contextvariable: the symbol is the flow-scoped state value itself (e.g. a stored cartId or wizard progress) that a condition may inspect, rather than a predicate over it.

types.title: NavigationFlow
types.description: A named, ordered grouping of FlowSteps that links two or more routes into a single multi-step user process, such as a checkout, onboarding sequence or wizard, with a defined first step, a defined final step and an imposed traversal order. It is the container for the journey as a whole, not for any individual step, route or edge. Use FlowStep instead when the symbol is one position in the sequence, binding a single index to a single route, rather than the whole ordered journey. Use NavigationGraph instead when the symbol is the application's complete route table or router instance, covering all routes, rather than one bounded multi-step process. Use NavigationTransition instead when the symbol is a single from-to route change with a trigger, such as a next button handler or a redirect, rather than an ordered set of steps. Use Route instead when the symbol is one URL path pattern resolving to a view, even if that view internally renders a stepper without changing route.
evidence: A configuration array or object listing ordered step entries, each naming a route path (e.g. steps: [{path: '/checkout/cart'}, {path: '/checkout/shipping'}, ...]), consumed by a stepper or wizard component or hook.
A parent route with ordered child routes that share a flow layout showing a progress indicator, plus next/back handlers that compute the following child path from the current index.

A state machine or flow store (e.g. XState machine, Redux slice, useWizard hook) whose states map to routes and that exposes start, next, previous and complete transitions, often carrying shared flow state between steps.

distinguish.navigation.flowstep: the symbol is one position in the sequence, binding a single index to a single route, rather than the whole ordered journey.
distinguish.navigation.navigationgraph: the symbol is the application's complete route table or router instance, covering all routes, rather than one bounded multi-step process.
distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: the symbol is a single from-to route change with a trigger, such as a next button handler or a redirect, rather than an ordered set of steps.
distinguish.navigation.route: the symbol is one URL path pattern resolving to a view, even if that view internally renders a stepper without changing route.

types.title: NavigationGraph
types.description: A root container representing one application's complete router configuration, the single top-level route table or router instance whose scope covers every Route, NavigationTransition, NavigationGuard, NavigationFlow and BreadcrumbConfig reachable in that application. Exactly one exists per independently bootstrapped router, as opposed to a subset, journey or single entry. Use NavigationFlow instead when the symbol describes an ordered, goal-directed subset of routes, such as a wizard or checkout, rather than the whole route table of the application. Use Route instead when the symbol is a single path entry, including a parent route with nested children or a lazily loaded child route module, rather than the root router configuration. Use BreadcrumbConfig instead when the symbol only configures breadcrumb trail rendering for a navigation scope rather than defining the routes themselves.
evidence: A root router bootstrap call that receives the full routes array, such as createRouter({ history, routes }), RouterModule.forRoot(routes), createBrowserRouter([...]) or provideRouter(routes), which is mounted once on the app instance.
A top-level routing file, such as router/index.ts, app-routing.module.ts or routes.tsx, that imports and assembles all feature route modules and registers global guards like router.beforeEach.
The root directory of a file-system routing convention, such as Next.js app/ or pages/, Nuxt pages/ or SvelteKit src/routes, treated as one application's complete route tree.

distinguish.navigation.navigationflow: the symbol describes an ordered, goal-directed subset of routes, such as a wizard or checkout, rather than the whole route table of the application.
distinguish.navigation.route: the symbol is a single path entry, including a parent route with nested children or a lazily loaded child route module, rather than the root router configuration.
distinguish.navigation.breadcrumbconfig: the symbol only configures breadcrumb trail rendering for a navigation scope rather than defining the routes themselves.

types.title: NavigationGuard
types.description: A client-side router interceptor that runs during route resolution, before the target view renders, and decides whether a navigation to one or more routes may proceed, by evaluating a GuardCondition and, on denial, triggering a GuardAction. It is the executable hook registered with the SPA router (global, per-route or per-flow), not the predicate it evaluates, the response it takes on denial, or the route metadata it reads. Use GuardCondition instead when the symbol is only the boolean predicate or expression (e.g. isAuthenticated(), hasRole('admin')) and is not itself registered with the router as an interceptor. Use GuardAction instead when the symbol is only the denial response: the redirect target, block, notification message or confirmation prompt returned or executed when access is refused. Use RouteMeta instead when the symbol is declarative per-route data (meta.requiresAuth, data.roles, canDeactivate flags) that a guard reads but which performs no evaluation itself. Use NavigationTransition instead when the symbol models the edge between two routes and its trigger, rather than the check that permits or denies traversing that edge.
evidence: a function or class implementing CanActivate, CanActivateChild, CanMatch or CanDeactivate (or a CanActivateFn) listed in a route's canActivate/canMatch array
a callback registered via router.beforeEach, router.beforeResolve or a route's beforeEnter that calls next(false), next('/login') or returns a redirect location

a React Router loader or wrapper component such as <RequireAuth>/<ProtectedRoute> that checks session, role or feature flag and returns redirect('/login') or <Navigate> before rendering the child route

distinguish.navigation.guardcondition: the symbol is only the boolean predicate or expression (e.g. isAuthenticated(), hasRole('admin')) and is not itself registered with the router as an interceptor
distinguish.navigation.guardaction: the symbol is only the denial response: the redirect target, block, notification message or confirmation prompt returned or executed when access is refused
distinguish.navigation.routemeta: the symbol is declarative per-route data (meta.requiresAuth, data.roles, canDeactivate flags) that a guard reads but which performs no evaluation itself
distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: the symbol models the edge between two routes and its trigger, rather than the check that permits or denies traversing that edge

types.title: NavigationTransition
types.description: A directed edge between exactly one source Route and one destination Route that records a single permitted route change in the client-side router, together with the mechanism that initiates it (user click, programmatic call, timeout, browser history, or redirect). It represents the move between routes, not either route, and carries no sequence position in a multi-step process. Use Route instead when the element is the addressable URL pattern or route-table entry itself, including a route declared with type 'redirect' or 'alias', rather than the move from one route to another. Use FlowStep instead when the element is an ordered position in a multi-step process (it has a sequence index and a required/wait behavior) rather than an edge between two routes. Use GuardAction instead when the redirect or block is the response a NavigationGuard executes on denial, with a message and preserveRoute setting, rather than a modeled edge between two routes. Use RouteMeta instead when 'transition' refers to the CSS or animation effect applied on entering or leaving a route (e.g. 'fade'), not to a route-to-route edge.
evidence: A router link component (<Link to="/orders">, <router-link :to="{name:'checkout'}">, [routerLink]) rendered in the view of one route and targeting another route

An imperative navigation call such as router.push(), navigate('/x'), history.replace(), Navigator.pushNamed() or this.router.navigateByUrl() inside an event handler, effect, form-submit callback, or setTimeout
A route-table entry or loader/guard return that forwards one path to another, e.g. { path: '/old', redirect: '/new' }, <Navigate to="/login" replace/>, or return redirect('/dashboard')

distinguish.navigation.route: the element is the addressable URL pattern or route-table entry itself, including a route declared with type 'redirect' or 'alias', rather than the move from one route to another
distinguish.navigation.flowstep: the element is an ordered position in a multi-step process (it has a sequence index and a required/wait behavior) rather than an edge between two routes
distinguish.navigation.guardaction: the redirect or block is the response a NavigationGuard executes on denial, with a message and preserveRoute setting, rather than a modeled edge between two routes
distinguish.navigation.routemeta: 'transition' refers to the CSS or animation effect applied on entering or leaving a route (e.g. 'fade'), not to a route-to-route edge

types.title: Route
types.description: A client-side router entry that binds a URL path pattern, with any route parameters, to the view or component the single-page-application router renders, lazily loads, or forwards to when the browser location matches it. It is one entry in a front-end route table, not a server-side HTTP endpoint. Use NavigationTransition instead when the element is a movement from one route to another, such as a Link, router.push call or redirect between two paths, rather than the destination path itself. Use FlowStep instead when the element is an ordered position in a multi-step wizard or checkout that refers to a route, rather than the route definition itself. Use RouteMeta instead when the element is the meta or data object attached to a route entry, holding layout, keepAlive, transition, breadcrumb or role hints, rather than the path-to-component mapping. Use NavigationGuard instead when the element is a beforeEnter, canActivate or loader function that decides whether a route may be activated, rather than the route entry it protects.
evidence: An object in a client-side router's routes array, such as Vue Router createRouter({routes}), Angular Routes or React Router createBrowserRouter, that has a path property together with component/element, loadComponent/lazy, redirect/redirectTo, or alias.

A file in a file-system routing convention whose location defines a URL path, such as Next.js app/**/page.tsx, SvelteKit +page.svelte, Nuxt pages/*.vue or Remix routes/*.tsx, including dynamic segments like [id] or $id.
A named path constant or route-name enum, such as ROUTES.USER_DETAIL = '/users/:id', that is passed to router.push, navigate(), <Link to> or <router-link :to> elsewhere in the front-end code.

distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: the element is a movement from one route to another, such as a Link, router.push call or redirect between two paths, rather than the destination path itself.
distinguish.navigation.flowstep: the element is an ordered position in a multi-step wizard or checkout that refers to a route, rather than the route definition itself.
distinguish.navigation.routemeta: the element is the meta or data object attached to a route entry, holding layout, keepAlive, transition, breadcrumb or role hints, rather than the path-to-component mapping.
distinguish.navigation.navigationguard: the element is a beforeEnter, canActivate or loader function that decides whether a route may be activated, rather than the route entry it protects.

types.title: RouteMeta
types.description: A declarative metadata record attached to a single Route that the SPA router reads at runtime. It sets how that route's view is rendered (layout wrapper, keep-alive caching, enter/leave animation, breadcrumb label) and exposes access hints (requiresAuth, roles, permissions) for guards to read; it carries no URL path and no executable logic of its own. Use Route instead when the symbol defines the addressable path pattern and the component it resolves to, rather than the auxiliary meta/data object hanging off that route record. Use NavigationGuard instead when the symbol is executable interception logic (beforeEach, canActivate, a loader redirect) that evaluates and enforces access, rather than the static hints such logic reads. Use BreadcrumbConfig instead when the configuration sets breadcrumb generation rules, separators or home-link behaviour for a whole navigation scope rather than one route's breadcrumb label. Use NavigationTransition instead when modelling a directed change from one route to another with a trigger, not the CSS/animation name stored in a route's meta 'transition' field.
evidence: a `meta: { requiresAuth: true, layout: 'AuthLayout', keepAlive: true }` object inside a Vue Router route record, or a `declare module 'vue-router' { interface RouteMeta { ... } }` type augmentation
an Angular route definition with `data: { roles: ['admin'], breadcrumb: 'Reports' }` that is read through ActivatedRoute.snapshot.data or in a guard
a root shell that wraps `<router-view>` in `<keep-alive>` or `<transition :name="route.meta.transition">`, or that picks a layout component from `route.meta.layout` / `useMatches()[i].handle`

distinguish.navigation.route: the symbol defines the addressable path pattern and the component it resolves to, rather than the auxiliary meta/data object hanging off that route record
distinguish.navigation.navigationguard: the symbol is executable interception logic (beforeEach, canActivate, a loader redirect) that evaluates and enforces access, rather than the static hints such logic reads
distinguish.navigation.breadcrumbconfig: the configuration sets breadcrumb generation rules, separators or home-link behaviour for a whole navigation scope rather than one route's breadcrumb label
distinguish.navigation.navigationtransition: modelling a directed change from one route to another with a trigger, not the CSS/animation name stored in a route's meta 'transition' field

layers.name: APM Observability Layer
